# TO THE PRINCIPAL
## OF THE
### UNIVERSITY OF ST. ANDREWS

*Dear* PRINCIPAL DONALDSON,

I hope you will permit me to dedicate to the University of St. Andrews these chapters on the early History of Religion, in acknowledgment of the kindness she has shown to her former student throughout my life. These chapters may be considered a representation of the Gifford Lectures <note>The Gifford Lectures are a prestigious series of lectures established in 1887 at Scottish universities to promote the study of natural theology and religion.</note> which I delivered, although in reality they contain very little of what was actually spoken from Lord Gifford’s chair. I wish they were more worthy of a nourishing mother <note>original: "Alma Mater"</note> that nurtured in the past the leaders of desperate missions <note>original: "forlorn hopes"</note> that were destined to succeed, as well as the supporters of lost causes who fought bravely against fate—Patrick Hamilton, Cargill, and Argyll, Beaton, Montrose, and Dundee. <note>Lang lists famous figures from Scottish history associated with St. Andrews who stood on opposing sides of religious and political conflicts: Patrick Hamilton (a Protestant martyr), Donald Cargill (a Covenanter martyr), the Marquess of Argyll (a Covenanter leader), Cardinal Beaton (a Catholic prelate), the Marquess of Montrose (a Royalist general), and Viscount Dundee (a Jacobite leader).</note>

->Believe me,<-
->Very sincerely yours,<-
->ANDREW LANG.<-

# PREFACE

---

The person primarily responsible for this work <note>original: "The Only Begetter"—a reference to the dedication of Shakespeare's Sonnets</note> is Mr. Lefébure <note>original: Monsieur Lefébure</note>, author of *The Eyes of Horus* <note>original: *Les Yeux d’Horus*</note> and other studies in Egyptology. He suggested writing this book, but he is in no way responsible for the opinions expressed within it.

The author cannot pass up the opportunity to thank Mr. Frederic Myers for his kindness in reading the proof sheets of the earlier chapters and suggesting several corrections. Mr. Myers, however, probably does not agree with the author on certain points—for example, in the chapter on "Possession." Since the second part of the book differs significantly from the opinions usually held by most anthropological writers on early religion, the author must state here (as he does later) that no harm can come from seeing how facts look from a new point of view. He certainly did not expect the facts to fall into the shape he now presents for criticism.

ST. ANDREWS: *April 3, 1898.*

# THE MAKING OF RELIGION

---

## I

### INTRODUCTORY CHAPTER

<margin>Tylor <note>Edward Burnett Tylor (1832–1917) was a founding figure of modern anthropology, famous for his theory that religion began with "animism"—the belief in individual souls and spirits.</note></margin>
The modern science of the history of religion <note>Now commonly known as Comparative Religion or Religious Studies.</note> has reached conclusions that already seem to be firmly established. These conclusions may be briefly stated as follows: Humanity derived the conception of "spirit" or "soul" from reflections on the phenomena of sleep, dreams, death, shadows, and from the experiences of trances and hallucinations. By first worshipping the departed souls of their ancestors, humans later expanded the doctrine of spiritual beings in many directions. Ghosts, or other spiritual existences fashioned in the same way, thrived until they became gods. Finally, as the result of various processes, one of these gods became supreme and, at last, was regarded as the only God. Meanwhile, humanity retained a belief in the existence of the individual soul, surviving after the death of the body, and so reached the concept of immortality. Thus, the ideas of God and of the soul are the result of early, flawed reasoning <note>original: "fallacious reasonings"</note> about misunderstood experiences.

It may seem almost reckless <note>original: "wanton"</note> to suggest that we should revise a system that is at once so simple, so logical, and apparently so well-supported by facts <note>original: "well bottomed on facts"</note>. But there can

<summary>This page introduces the prevailing 19th-century scientific theory of the origin of religion, which suggests that beliefs in souls and God evolved from early humans misinterpreting natural phenomena like dreams and shadows.</summary>
<keywords>Anthropology, Animism, E.B. Tylor, Origin of Religion, Soul, Monotheism, Comparative Religion</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory argument, specifically outlining the author's plan to challenge E.B. Tylor's established theories on the origins of religious belief.</meta>

never be any real harm in studying masses of evidence from fresh points of view. At worst, the failure of a critique <note>original: "adverse criticism"</note> will only help to establish the doctrines being challenged. Now, as we shall show, there are two points of view from which the evidence regarding religion in its early stages has not been consistently examined. Therefore, we intend to ask, first: what, if anything, can be discovered about the nature of the "visions" and hallucinations which—according to **Mr. Tylor** in his celebrated work **"Primitive Culture"**—helped form the idea of "spirit"? Second, we shall collect and compare the accounts we have of the High Gods and creative beings worshipped or believed in by the most primitive societies <note>original: "backward races"</note>. We shall then ask whether these relatively Supreme Beings, conceived of by people in very basic social conditions, can truly be—as anthropology declares—mere developments from a belief in the ghosts of the dead.

We shall conclude by venturing to suggest that the early human <note>original: "savage"</note> theory of the soul may be based, at least in part, on experiences which cannot, at present, be made to fit into any purely materialistic system of the universe. We shall also bring evidence tending to prove that the idea of God, in its earliest known form, does not logically have to be derived from the idea of "spirit," regardless of how that idea of spirit itself may have been reached or evolved. The conception of God, then, does not need to be evolved out of reflections on dreams and "ghosts."

If these two positions can be defended with any success, it is obvious that the entire theory of the Science of Religion <note>Now commonly called Religious Studies or Comparative Religion.</note> will need to be reconsidered. But it is no less evident that our two positions do not depend on each other. The first may be regarded as far-fetched <note>original: "fantastic"</note> or improbable, and may be set aside <note>original: "masked"</note> and ignored. However, the strength of the second position, which is derived from evidence of a different character, will not be weakened because of that.

### INTRODUCTORY

Our first claim <note>original: "position"</note> can only be argued for by using evidence that is highly unpopular and, as a general rule, condemned by modern science. However, this evidence is obtained through what is, in any case, a legitimate anthropological method. We may follow the example of **Mr. Tylor** <note>Edward Burnett Tylor (1832–1917), a founding figure of modern anthropology and author of "Primitive Culture."</note> and collect primitive <note>original: "savage"</note> beliefs about visions, hallucinations, "clairvoyance," and the gaining of knowledge that apparently cannot be reached through the normal senses. We may then compare these primitive beliefs with documented records of similar experiences among living and educated modern <note>original: "civilised"</note> people. 

Even if we reach no conclusion—or a negative one—regarding the reality or the supernatural <note>original: "supernormal"</note> nature of these alleged experiences, it is still a valid part of anthropological science to compare the data of primitive and modern psychology, or even their illusions and fables. This has, until now, been a neglected area of study. The results, whether or not they support our first claim, will certainly be curious and educational, if only as a chapter in the history of human error. 

That chapter, moreover, deals with no small matter, but with what we might call the "X region" <note>The author uses "X" to represent the mysterious, unknown, or subconscious aspects of human nature.</note> of our nature. From that region—from miracles, prophecy, and visions—the great religions of Christianity and Islam have certainly emerged. So too have the great religious innovators and leaders: our Lord Himself <note>Referring to Jesus Christ.</note>, St. Francis, John Knox, and Joan of Arc <note>original: "Jeanne d’Arc"</note>, down to the founder of the new faith of the Sioux and Arapaho <note>Likely a reference to Wovoka and the Ghost Dance movement of the 1890s.</note>. 

Therefore, it cannot be unscientific to compare primitive <note>original: "barbaric"</note> and modern beliefs and experiences regarding a subject that is so poorly understood and yet so full of powerful influence. In this work, the topic will be examined using the methods of anthropology rather than psychology. It is possible that we may have something to learn (as has happened before) from the raw observations and quick conclusions of the most primitive cultures <note>original: "backward races"</note>.

# THE MAKING OF RELIGION

We may illustrate this by an anecdote:

> ‘The Northern Indians call the *Aurora Borealis* “Edthin,” that is “Deer.” Their ideas in this respect are founded on a principle one would not imagine. Experience has shown them that when a hairy deer-skin is briskly stroked with the hand on a dark night, it will emit many sparks of electrical fire.’

So says Hearne in his *Journey*, published in 1795 (p. 346). <note>Samuel Hearne (1745–1792) was an English explorer, fur-trader, and naturalist known for his travels across northern Canada.</note>

This observation of the Indigenous people <note>original: "Red Men"</note> is a kind of parable representing a part of the meaning of the following treatise. The Indians, making a hasty inference from a trivial phenomenon, arrived unaware at a probably correct conclusion that was long unknown to civilized science. They connected the *Aurora Borealis* with electricity, supposing that multitudes of deer in the sky rubbed the sparks out of each other! Meanwhile, even in the last century, a puzzled populace spoke of the phenomenon as ‘Lord Derwentwater’s Lights.’ <note>James Radcliffe, 3rd Earl of Derwentwater, was a Jacobite leader executed in 1716. The brilliant aurora that occurred shortly after his death was popularly linked to him in Northern English folklore.</note> The cosmic pomp and splendor shone to welcome the loyal Derwentwater into heaven, after he had given his life for his exiled king.

Now, my purpose in the earlier portion of this essay is to suggest that certain phenomena of human nature—apparently as trivial as the sparks rubbed out of a deer’s hide on a dark night—may indicate, and may be allied to, a force or forces which, like the *Aurora Borealis*, may shine from one end of the heavens to the other, strangely illuminating the darkness of our destiny. Science has ignored such phenomena, just as it so long ignored the sparks from the stroked deer-skin and the attractive power of rubbed amber. These trivial things were not known to be allied to the lightning, or to indicate a force which man could tame and use. But just as the Indians, by a rapid, careless inference, attributed the *Aurora Borealis* to electric in-

# INTRODUCTORY

...influences, so (as anthropology assures us) primitive peoples <note>original: "savages"</note> everywhere have inferred the existence of a soul or spirit—an intelligence that:

> ‘Does not know the bond of Time,
> Nor wear the manacles of Space,’

in part from certain apparently trivial phenomena of human faculty. These phenomena, as Mr. Tylor says, ‘the great intellectual movement of the last two centuries has simply thrown aside as worthless.’¹ I refer to alleged experiences—merely odd, sporadic, and, for commercial purposes, useless—such as the transference of thought from one mind to another by no known channel of sense, the occurrence of hallucinations which, at first glance <note>original: "*prima facie*"</note>, correspond coincidentally with unknown events at a distance, all that is called ‘second sight’ or ‘clairvoyance,’ and other things even more obscure. Reasoning on these real or alleged phenomena, and on other quite normal and accepted facts of dreams, shadows, sleep, trance, and death, primitive peoples <note>original: "savages"</note> have inferred the existence of a spirit or soul, exactly as the Northern Indians arrived at the notion of electricity (not so called by them, of course) as the cause of the *Aurora Borealis*. But, just as the Indians thought that the cosmic lights were caused by the rubbing together of crowded deer in the heavens (a theory that is quite childishly absurd), so the primitive person <note>original: "savage"</note> has expressed his conclusion about the existence of spirit in unrefined and fantastic ways. He believes in wandering, separable souls of men that survive death, and he has peopled the whole inanimate universe with his dreams.

My suggestion is that, in spite of his fantasies, the primitive person <note>original: "savage"</note> had possibly drawn from his premises an inference that was not wholly, or at least not demonstrably, erroneous. Just as the sparks from the deer-skin indicated electricity, so the strange lights in the night of human nature may indicate faculties...

# THE MAKING OF RELIGION

which science, until recently and in only a few instances, has laughed at, ignored, and ‘thrown aside as worthless.’

It should be observed that I am not speaking of ‘spiritualism,’ a word associated with the worst things, inextricably entangled with fraud, bad logic, and the blindest credulity. Some of the phenomena alluded to have, however, been claimed as their own province by ‘spiritists,’ and need to be rescued from them. Mr. Tylor writes:

> ‘The issue raised by the comparison of primitive <note>original: "savage"</note>, barbaric, and civilized spiritualism is this: Do the Red Indian medicine man, the Tatar necromancer, the Highland ghost-seer, and the Boston medium share the possession of belief and knowledge of the highest truth and importance, which, nevertheless, the great intellectual movement of the last two centuries has simply thrown aside as worthless?’

*Distinguo!* <note>Latin: "I make a distinction!"</note> That does not seem to me to be the issue. In my opinion the issue is: ‘Have the Red Indian, the Tatar, the Highland seer, and the Boston medium (the least reputable of the group) observed, and reasoned wildly from, and counterfeited, and darkened with imposture, certain genuine by-products of human faculty, which do not at first glance <note>original: "*prima facie*"</note> deserve to be thrown aside?’

That, I venture to think, is the real issue. That science may toss aside as worthless some valuable observations of primitive peoples <note>original: "savages"</note> is now universally admitted by people who know the facts. Among these observations is the whole topic of Hypnotism, with the use of suggestion for healing purposes, and the phenomena, no longer denied, of ‘alternating personalities.’ For the truth of this statement we may appeal to one of the greatest of Continental anthropologists, Adolf Bastian.<sup>1</sup> The missionaries, like Livingstone, usually supposed that the primitive <note>original: "savage"</note> seer’s—

They thus make themselves judges of what is possible and practically regard themselves as all-knowing. Science has had to accept so many things once mocked as "impossible" that this attitude of hers—as we shall show in chapter 2—ceases to command respect.

My suggestion is that the trivial, rejected, or ignored phenomena supported by the evidence defended here may, quite possibly, be of considerable importance. But, to put it at its simplest, even if we are only concerned with illusions and fables, it is certainly interesting to note their persistent uniformity in both primitive and civilized life.

## II

### SCIENCE AND ‘MIRACLES’

->*Historical Sketch*<-

Research in the <term>X region</term> is not something new under the sun. When Saul disguised himself before his meeting with the Witch of Endor, he made a basic attempt at a scientific test of the supernatural. King Croesus went much further when he tested the clairvoyance of the oracles of Greece by sending an embassy to ask what he was doing at a specific hour on a specific day, and by then doing something very strange. We do not know how the Delphic oracle found the correct answer, but various easy methods of fraud immediately come to mind. However, Croesus’s procedure, provided he took certain precautions, was relatively scientific. The inquiry of Porphyry was also relatively scientific, and his position is quite likely to be compared to our own. Unable or reluctant to accept Christianity, Porphyry "sought a sign" of an element of supernormal truth in Paganism. But he began at the wrong end—specifically, at Pagan spiritualistic séances, with the usual accompaniments of darkness and fraud. His confused letter to Anebo, along with the reply attributed to Iamblichus, reveal Porphyry wandering puzzled among mediums, floating lights, strange noises, and dubious "physical phenomena." He did not begin with accurate experiments regarding the existence of rare and apparently supernormal human faculties, and he seems to

Something more similar to modern research began around the time of the Reformation and lasted until about 1680. The craze for burning witches led men of reason, learning, and humanity to ask whether there was any reality in witchcraft and, more generally, in the wonders of popular belief. The investigations of Thyræus, Lavaterus, Bodin, Weyer, Le Loyer, Reginald Scot, and many others tended, on the whole, toward the negative side regarding the wilder stories about witches, but left the problems of ghosts and haunted houses much as they were before. It may be noted that Lavaterus (around 1580) had already proposed a version of the telepathy hypothesis (that "ghosts" are hallucinations produced by the direct influence of one mind, or brain, upon another), while Thyræus wondered if the noises heard in "haunted houses" were not simply hallucinations of the sense of hearing. But all these early writers, like Cardan, were very careless about first-hand evidence; indeed, they preferred ghosts vouched for by classical authorities like Pliny, Plutarch, or Suetonius. With the Reverend Joseph Glanvil, F.R.S. (around 1666), a more careful examination of evidence began. Among the marvels in Glanvil’s writings and other tracts usually published together in his *Sadducismus Triumphatus*, one finds letters showing that he and his friends, such as Henry More and Boyle, worked to collect first-hand evidence for second sight, haunted houses, ghosts, and wraiths. Their admitted goal was to provide a "Whip for the Droll"—a response to the mocking skepticism of the Restoration period. The result was that Glanvil was descended upon by a crowd of bores—he was

With Henry More, Baxter, and Glanvil, the attempt to investigate these topics scientifically practically died out for a time, although a sense of doubt remained in the mind of Addison. Witchcraft ceased to be believed in and was abolished as a crime in 1736. Some of the Scottish clergy and John Wesley clung fondly to the old faith, but Wodrow and Cotton Mather (around 1710–1730) were exceptionally careless and unsuccessful in providing anything like evidence for their accounts. Ghost stories continued to be told but were no longer investigated.

Then one of the most brilliant philosophers decided that investigation should never even be attempted. This scientific attitude toward *X* phenomena—refusing to examine them and denying them without investigation—was established by David Hume in his famous essay on 'Miracles.' Hume mocked the observation and study of what he called 'miracles' in the realm of experience; he sought an *a priori* argument that would settle the question forever without any examination of the facts. In an age of experimental philosophy that mocked *a priori* methods, this was Hume's major contribution to knowledge. His famous argument, which has delighted many an honest soul, is a collection of fallacies that could be given to beginners in logic as an elementary exercise in identifying errors. In announcing his discovery, Hume amusingly displays the self-satisfaction and lack of humor for which we Scots are commonly criticized by our critics:

> 'I pride myself on having discovered an argument which, if correct, will serve the wise and learned as an everlasting check against all kinds of superstitious delusions,

and consequently will be useful as long as the world lasts.'

However, he does not expect to convince the masses. Until the end of the world, 'accounts of miracles and wonders, I suppose, will be found in all histories, sacred and secular.' Without explaining here what he means by a miracle, Hume argues that 'experience is our only guide in reasoning.' He then defines a miracle as 'a violation of the laws of nature.' By a 'law of nature' he means a consistency—not of all experience, but of the specific experience he chooses to acknowledge; meanwhile, he excludes, without examination, all evidence of experience where such consistency is absent. That kind of experience cannot be considered. 'There must be a consistent experience against every miraculous event; otherwise, the event would not deserve that name.' If there is any experience in favor of the event, that experience does not count. A miracle goes against universal experience; no event goes against universal experience; therefore, no event is a miracle. If you produce evidence for what Hume calls a miracle (we shall see examples), he replies that the evidence is not valid unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the fact itself. Now, no error in human evidence can be more miraculous than a 'miracle.' Therefore, there can be no valid evidence for 'miracles.' Fortunately, Hume now provides an example of what he means by 'miracles.' He says:

> 'For, first, there is not to be found in all history any miracle attested by a sufficient number of men of such unquestioned good sense, education, and learning as to protect us against all self-delusion; of such undoubted integrity as to place them beyond all suspicion of any intent to deceive others; of such credit and reputation in the eyes of mankind as to have much to lose in case they were detected in any falsehood; and at

Hume added a note at the end of his book in which he contradicted every assertion he had made in the passage just cited; indeed, he contradicted himself before he had written six pages.

But what is more extraordinary, many of the miracles were *immediately proven on the spot* before judges of unquestioned integrity, and attested by *witnesses of credit and distinction* in a learned age, and on the most eminent stage now in the world. Nor is this all. An account of them was published and spread everywhere; even the Jesuits—a learned group supported by civil authorities and determined enemies of the opinions in favor of which the miracles were supposedly performed—were never able to clearly refute or expose them. Where shall we find such a number of circumstances agreeing to corroborate a single fact? And what do we have to oppose such a cloud of witnesses, other than the absolute *impossibility* or the miraculous nature of the events they relate? And this, surely, in the eyes of all reasonable people, will alone be regarded as a sufficient refutation.’

Having done this, he abandons (as Mr. Wallace observes) his original claim that the evidence does not exist, and instead takes refuge in alleging "the absolute impossibility" of the events that the evidence supports. Thus, Hume poses as a perfect judge of what is possible, as if he possessed a kind of omniscience. He bases his position on the uniformity of all experience that does not conflict with his idea of the possible, and he dismisses all testimony regarding other experiences, even when it meets his own standard of evidence. He is quite far indeed from Virchow’s position "that what we call the laws of nature must change according to our frequent new experiences."¹ In his note, Hume reinforces and confirms his evidence for the Jansenist miracles. They even have a martyr, M. Montgeron, who wrote an account of the events and, as Hume mentions casually, "is now said to be somewhere in a dungeon because of his book." Hume adds his own testimony regarding the character of these *priests*. Thus, according to Hume, it is wise to dismiss the most public and well-attested "miracles" without any examination. This is a strange kind of experimental science.

But the Church continues to have an interest in the matter. As the class of facts which Hume declined to examine begins to be gradually admitted by science, the matter becomes clear. The evidence which could safely convey these now admittedly possible facts—say, from the time of Christ—is so far proved to be not necessarily mythical; it is proved to be not incapable of carrying statements that are probably correct, which once seemed absolutely false. If so, where, precisely, does its power of carrying facts end? Thus considered, the kinds of marvelous events recorded in the Gospels, for example, are no longer to be dismissed on *a priori* grounds as 'mythical.' We cannot now discard evidence as necessarily false because it clashes with our present ideas of the possible, when we have to acknowledge that the very same evidence may safely convey to us facts which clashed with our fathers' notions of what is possible, but which are now accepted. Our notions of the possible cease to be a criterion of truth or falsehood, and our contempt for the Gospels as myths must slowly die, as 'miracle' after 'miracle' is brought within the realm of acknowledged law. With each such admission, the hypothesis that the Gospel evidence is mythical must grow weaker, and the negative certainty of popular science must also grow weaker.

We return to Hume. He next argues that the pleasures of wonder make all accounts of "miracles" worthless. He has just given an example of the equivalent pleasures of dogmatic disbelief. Then religion is a disturbing force; but so, clearly, is irreligion. "The wise and learned are content to mock the absurdity without informing themselves of the particular facts." The wise and learned are praised for their scientific attitude. Furthermore, miracles cancel each other out, for all religions have their miracles, yet all religions cannot be true. This argument no longer carries weight with people who view "miracles" as "X phenomena," not as divine evidence for the truth of one creed or another. "The staring populace accepts, without examination, whatever soothes superstition," and Hume’s entire purpose is to make the wise and learned imitate the staring populace by rejecting alleged facts "without examination." The common people investigated more than the wise and learned did.

A "miracle" may result from the operation of some as yet unascertained law of nature (for instance, self-suggestion), and our business, at present, is to examine such events, not to account for them.

It may fairly be said that Hume is arguing against men who wished to make so-called "miracles" a test of the truth of Jansenism, for example, and that he could not be expected to answer, by anticipation, ideas not current in his day. But he remains guilty of denouncing the investigation of apparent facts. No attitude can be less scientific than his, or more common among many men of science.

According to the humorous custom of things in this world, the whole question of the marvelous had no sooner been settled forever by David Hume than it was reopened by Emanuel Swedenborg. Now, Kant was familiar with certain works of Hume, whether he had read his "Essay on Miracles" or not. Far from declining to examine the portentous "visions" of Swedenborg, Kant interested himself deeply in the topic. As early as 1758, he wrote his first remarks on the seer, containing some reports of stories or legends about Swedenborg’s "clairvoyance." The first seventy pages of the *Dreams* are devoted to a perfectly serious discussion of the metaphysics of "Spirits." On page 73, he pleasantly remarks, "Now we shall understand that everything said so far is superfluous," and he will not reproach the reader who regards seers *not* as citizens of two worlds (Plotinus), but as candidates for Bedlam.

Kant’s irony is uniquely Scottish. He does not know himself how far he is in earnest, and, to preserve his self-respect and reputation for shrewdness, he "jokes with difficulty." He amuses himself by trying to see how far he can carry speculations on metaphysics (not yet reformed by himself) into the realm of the supernatural. He admits to his own tendency to think that he has an immaterial soul, and that these points are, or may be, or one day will be, scientifically solved. These admissions are eagerly welcomed by Du Prel in his *Philosophy of Mysticism*; however, they are only part of Kant’s joke, and Kant himself does not know how far they are serious. If spiritualists understood their own interests, they would translate and publish the first seventy pages of Kant’s *Dreams*. Something like telepathy—the action of spirit, even discarnate, on spirit—is alluded to, but the idea is at least as old as Lavaterus (p. 52). Like Scott in his *Demonology*, Kant has a good deal to say on the physics of Hallucination, but it is outdated material. He thinks the entire topic of spiritual existence is only important in how it relates to hopes for a future life. For some reason, modern manuals are prone to overlook these German researches and speculations. (Compare Mr. Vincent’s ‘Elements of Hypnotism,’ p. 34.) The Schellings were interested; Ritter thought he had detected a new force, ‘<term>Siderism</term>.’ Mr. Wallace, in his preface to Hegel’s ‘*Philosophie des Geistes*,’ speaks as if Ritter had conducted experiments in telepathy. He may have done so, but his ‘*Siderismus*’ (Tübingen, 1808) is a report undertaken for the Academy of Munich on the activities of an Italian water-finder, or ‘<term>dowser</term>.’ Ritter provides details of seventy-four experiments in ‘<term>dowsing</term>’ for water, metals, or coal. He believes in the ability, but not in ‘psychic’ explanations or the Devil. He discusses ‘electricity’ (pp. 170, 190). He describes his precautions to avoid common fraud, but he took no precautions against unconscious thought-transference. He regarded the faculty as ‘temperamental’ and useful.

Probably the most important philosophical result of the early German research into the hypnotic sleep is to be found in the writings of Hegel. Due to his peculiar use of a terminology, or scientific language, that was entirely his own, it is extremely difficult to make Hegel’s meaning even moderately clear. Perhaps we may partially clarify it by using an analogy from Mr. Frederic Myers. Suppose we compare the ordinary everyday consciousness of each of us to a spectrum, whose ends fade out of our view toward each extremity.

Beyond the range of sight, one may imagine a lower or physiological end; for our ordinary consciousness, of course, is unaware of many physiological processes which are constantly occurring within us. Digestion, as long as it is healthy, is an obvious example. But hypnotic experiments make it certain that a patient, in the hypnotic state, can consciously, or at least purposefully, affect physiological processes to which the *ordinary* consciousness is blind—for example, by raising a blister when it is suggested that a blister must be raised. Again (granting the facts hypothetically and merely for the sake of argument), at the *upper* end of the spectrum, beyond the view of ordinary everyday consciousness, knowledge may be acquired of things which are outside the view of everyday consciousness. For example (admitting it for the sake of argument), unknown and remote people and places may be seen and described by <term>clairvoyance</term>, or <term>*vue à distance*</term> <note>Vision at a distance, or remote viewing.</note>.

Now Hegel accepted as genuine the facts which we cite here merely for the sake of argument and as illustrations. But he did not regard the clairvoyant consciousness (or whatever we call it) which, <term>*ex hypothesi*</term> <note>By the very nature of the hypothesis.</note>,

He gives (without date or source) a case of a girl in Germany who saw her brother lying dead in a hospital at Valladolid. Her brother was at the time in the hospital, but it was another man in the next bed who was dead. "It is thus impossible to determine whether what the clairvoyants actually see outweighs the things in which they are mistaken."

The hypnotized patient sees the absent object which he is told to see; the sleeper sees things not really present.

The years which have passed between the date of Hegel’s *Philosophy of Mind* and our own time have seen the long dispute over the existence, the nature, and the causes of the hypnotic condition, and over the reality and limits of the phenomena. The Report (1831) attested to the development, under 'magnetism,' of 'new faculties,' such as clairvoyance and intuition, and also the production of 'great changes in the physical economy,' such as insensibility and a sudden increase of strength. The Report declared it to be 'demonstrated' that sleep could be produced 'without suggestion'—as we say now, though the term was not then in use. The Academy did its best to suppress this Report, which attests to the phenomena that Hegel accepted—phenomena that are still disputed. Six years later (1837), a Committee reported against the claims of a certain Berna, a 'magnetizer.' No person served on both Committees, and this Report was accepted. Later, a number of people tried to read a letter in a box and failed. 'This,' says Mr. Vincent, 'settled the question with regard to clairvoyance'; though it might be more logical to say that it settled the claims of the competitors on that occasion. The Academy now decided that, because certain persons did not satisfy the expectations raised by their preliminary advertisements, the question of magnetism was therefore definitely closed.

We often have cause to regret that scientific eminence is not always accompanied by scientific logic. Where science neglects a subject, charlatans and dupes take it up. He was persecuted as only doctors know how to persecute; but in 1841, Braid of Manchester discovered that the so-called 'magnetic sleep' could be produced without any 'magnetism.' A hypnotized patient is told that the middle finger of his left hand will become rigid and lose all feeling. This happens, and it is explained as 'suggestion,' though how 'suggestion' produces such an astonishing effect is another problem. The late Mr. Gurney, however, conducted several experiments in which no suggestion was spoken, and the patients did not know which of their fingers was meant to become rigid and immune to pain. The patient's hands were placed through a screen, on the other side of which the hypnotist made hand movements over the finger that was to become rigid. The observers chose the finger, and the lack of sensation was tested with a strong electric current. The effect was also produced without hand movements; the operator simply pointed at the chosen finger and 'willed' the result. If he did not 'will' it, nothing happened; similarly, nothing happened if he willed it without pointing. The closeness of the operator's hand had no effect if he did not 'will' the result, nor was his 'willing' successful if he did not bring his hand near the patient’s. Other people's hands, placed in the same position, had no effect.

We also see that the stranger and rarer phenomena which Hegel accepted as facts and interwove with his general philosophy are still matters of dispute. Admitted by some men of science, they are doubted by others; by others, again, they are denied, while most of the journalists and authors of cheap introductory books, who inspire popular tradition, regard the phenomena as frauds or fables of superstition. But it is plain that these phenomena, like the more ordinary facts of hypnotism, *may* finally be admitted by science. The scientific world laughed, not so long ago, at Ogham inscriptions, meteorites, and paleolithic weapons as impostures or freaks of nature. Now nobody has any doubt about these matters, and clairvoyance, thought-transference, and telepathy may, not inconceivably, be as successful in the long run as meteorites, or as the more usual phenomena of hypnotism.

It is only Lord Kelvin who now maintains, or lately maintained, that in hypnotism there is nothing at all but fraud and poor observation. In years to come it may be that only some similar belated voice will cry that in thought-transference there is nothing but poor observation and fraud. # III

## ANTHROPOLOGY AND RELIGION

AMONG the various forms of science which are reaching and affecting the new popular tradition, we have included Anthropology. Interestingly enough, Anthropology itself has only recently emerged from that limbo of the unrecognized in which Psychical Research is still languishing. The British Association used to reject anthropological papers as "vain dreams based on travelers' tales." No doubt the British Association would reject a paper on clairvoyance as a vain dream based on old wives' fables, or on hysterical imposture. Undeniably, the study of such themes is hampered by fable and fraud, just as anthropology must be constantly on its guard against "travelers' tales," against European misunderstandings of savage ideas, and against civilized notions and scientific theories unconsciously read into barbaric customs, rites, traditions, and usages. Man, *ondoyant et divers*, is the subject alike of anthropology and of psychical research. Man (especially savage man) cannot be secluded from disturbing influences and watched like the materials of a chemical experiment in a laboratory. Nor can man be caught in a "primitive" state: his intellectual beginnings lie very far behind the stage of culture in which we find the lowest known races. Consequently, the matter on which anthropology works is fluctuating; the evidence on which it rests needs the most skeptical criticism, and many of its conclusions, in the

For these sound reasons, official science long looked askance at Anthropology. Its followers were not regarded as genuine scholars, and, perhaps as a result of this contempt, they were often "broken men," intellectual outlaws, people of one wild idea. To the scientific mind, anthropologists or ethnologists were a horde who darkly muttered about serpent worship, phallus worship, Arkite doctrines, and the Ten Lost Tribes that kept turning up in the most unexpected places. Anthropologists were said to gloat over the dirty rites of dirty savages and to seek reason where there was none. The exile, the outcast, the pariah of Science is, indeed, apt to find himself in odd company. Around the campfire of Psychical Research too, in the unofficial, unstaked wasteland of Science, hover odd, menacing figures of Esoteric Buddhists, *Satanists*, Occultists, Christian Scientists, Spiritualists, and Astrologers, just as the Arkites and Lost Tribesmen haunted the cradle of anthropology.

But there was found at last to be reason in the thing, and method in the madness. Evolution was involved. The acceptance, after long ridicule, of Paleolithic weapons as relics of human culture probably helped to bring Anthropology within the sacred circle of permitted knowledge. Its topic was full of illustrations of the doctrine of Mr. Darwin. Modern writers on the theme had been anticipated by the less systematic students of the eighteenth century—Goguet, de Brosses, Millar, Fontenelle, Lafitau, Boulanger, or even Hume and Voltaire. As pioneers, these writers correspond to the early mesmerists and magnetists—Puységur, Amoretti, Ritter, Elliotson, Mayo, and Gregory—in the history of Psychical Research. They were on the same track, in each case, as Lubbock, Tylor,

You only have to skim a few books of travel, pencil in hand, and pick out what suits your case. You can find evidence for that. Or suppose you want to show that they have no religious ideas at all; you can find evidence for that also. Your testimony is often derived from observers who are ignorant of the language of the people they talk about, or who are themselves prejudiced by one theory or another, or by bias. How can you pretend to build a science on such foundations, especially since the "savage" informants wish to please or to mystify inquirers, or they answer at random, or deliberately conceal their most sacred institutions, or have never paid any attention to the subject?

Mr. Tylor has replied to all these perfectly natural objections.¹ Evidence must be collected, sifted, and tested, just as in any other branch of inquiry. A writer, "of course, is bound to use his best judgment as to the trustworthiness of all authors he quotes, and, if possible, to obtain several accounts to certify each point in each locality." Mr. Tylor then cites "the test of recurrence"—the undesigned coincidence in testimony—as Millar had already

An exception among anthropologists is Mr. Tylor. He has not suppressed the existence of these barbaric parallels to our modern problems of this kind. But his interest in them practically ends when he has shown that the phenomena helped to originate the savage belief in "spirits," and when he has displayed the "survival" of that belief in later culture. He does not ask, "Are the phenomena real?"; he is concerned only with the savage philosophy of the phenomena and with its relics in modern spiritism and religion. My purpose is to do, by way only of an *outline*, what neither anthropology nor psychical research nor psychology has done: to put the savage and modern phenomena side by side. Such evidence as we can give for the actuality of the modern experiences will, so far as it goes, raise a presumption that the savage beliefs—however erroneous, however darkened by fraud and fancy—rest on a basis of real observation of actual phenomena.

Anthropology is concerned with man and what is in man—*humani nihil a se alienum putat* <note>"it considers nothing human to be foreign to itself"</note>. These researches, therefore, are within the anthropological province, especially as they bear on the prevalent anthropological theory of the "Origin of Religion." By "religion" we mean, for the purpose of this argument, the belief in the existence of an Intelligence, or Intelligences, that are not human and not dependent on a physical mechanism of brain and nerves, which may or may not powerfully control human fortunes and the nature of things. ...related to these Intelligences that it can transcend the knowledge obtained through the known bodily senses, and may possibly survive the death of the body. These **two** beliefs at present (though not necessarily in their origin) appear chiefly as the **faith in God and in the Immortality of the Soul.**

It is important, then, to trace, if possible, the origin of these two beliefs. If they arose in actual communion with Deity (as the first at least did, according to the theory of the Hebrew Scriptures), or if they could be proved to arise in an unanalyzable <term>*sensus numinis*</term>, or even in ‘**a perception of the Infinite**’ (**Max Müller**), religion would have a divine, or at least a necessary source. To the Theist, what is inevitable cannot help but be divinely ordained; therefore, religion is divinely preordained. Therefore, in essentials, though not in accidental details, religion is true. The atheist, or non-theist, of course, draws no such inferences.

<margin>Truth of religion</margin>
But if religion, as now understood among men, is the latest evolutionary form of a series of mistakes, fallacies, and illusions—if its seed is a blunder, and its present form is only the result of progressive but unessential refinements on that blunder—the inference that religion is untrue (that nothing actual corresponds to its hypothesis) is very easily drawn. The inference is not, perhaps, logical, for all our science itself is the result of progressive refinements upon hypotheses that were originally erroneous, fashioned to explain facts that were misconceived. Yet our science is true within its limits, though it is very far from being exhaustive of the truth. In the same way, it might be argued, our religion—even granting that it arose out of primitive fallacies and false hypotheses—may yet have been refined, as science has been, through many causes, into an approximate truth.

We have also shown that the Australians make an essential distinction between waking hallucinations (ghosts seen by a person when awake) and the common hallucinations of sleep. Anyone can have these; the person who sees ghosts while awake is marked out as a wizard.

It was not only the dreams of sleep, which are so easily forgotten, that the savage considered in his early speculations about life and the soul. He included in his evidence the much more striking and memorable experiences of waking hours, as both I and Mr. Tylor agree.

Reflecting on these things, the earliest savage thinkers would decide: (1) that man has a "life" (which leaves him temporarily during sleep, and permanently at death); (2) that man also possesses a "phantom" (which appears to other people in their visions and dreams). The savage philosopher would then "combine his information," like a celebrated writer on Chinese metaphysics. He would simply "combine the life and the phantom" as "manifestations of one and the same soul." The result would be an "apparitional soul" or "ghost-soul."

When the earliest thinkers—in an era and in mental conditions about which we have no historical record—had developed the hypothesis of this conscious, powerful, and separable soul that was capable of surviving the body's death, it was not difficult for them to develop the rest of religion, as Mr. Tylor suggests. <note>The following sentence is underlined in pencil</note> A powerful ghost of a dead man might flourish until, long after its original owner was forgotten, it became a god. <note>End of annotation</note> Furthermore, once the concept of souls was established, it would perhaps not be a very difficult logical leap to imagine souls, or spirits, that had never been human at all. Nevertheless, when we remember that Mr. Tylor is theorizing about primitive people in the distant background of human evolution—people whom we know nothing about through experience, and who are far less advanced than the Australians and Bushmen (who already have gods)—we must admit that he attributes great ingenuity and strong powers of abstract reasoning to them. He may be right in his opinion. In the same way, just as early humans were sharp thinkers, perhaps early bees—more clever than modern bees—developed the system of hexagonal cells; and perhaps only an exceptionally gifted early fish could have first hit on the plan, now instinctive, of killing a fly by blowing water at it.

I have no objection to this theory of metaphysical genius in very primitive people. Later, we will find astonishing examples of primitive abstract speculation, <note>The following phrase is underlined in pencil</note> definitely not taken from missionary sources, <note>End of annotation</note> because they were entirely outside the missionary’s scope of duty and reflection.

His reasoning appears to have proceeded from the more abstract (the idea of Life) to the more concrete: to a life that was first shadowy and vaporous, then clothed in the very appearance of the real man.

Mr. Tylor has thus (whether or not we follow his logic) provided humanity with a theory of active, intelligent, separable souls which can survive the death of the body. Early man arrived at this theory by speculating on the nature of life and on the causes of phantasms of the dead or living seen in ‘dreams and visions.’ However, our author by no means ignores the effects of alleged supernormal phenomena believed in by primitive people, along with their parallels in modern civilization. These supernormal phenomena, whether real or illusory, are, he believes, facts within that mass of experiences from which primitive people constructed their belief in separable, enduring, intelligent souls or ghosts—the foundation of religion.

But the savages who, by hypothesis, evolved the doctrine of souls lie beyond our knowledge, far behind the modern savages, among whom we find belief not only in souls and ghosts, but also in moral gods. Concerning the psychical condition of the savages who worked out the theory of souls and founded religion, we necessarily know nothing. If such experiences as clairvoyance, telepathy, and so on exist, these unknown ancestors of ours may (for all we can tell) have been especially open to them, and therefore especially inclined to believe in separable souls. In fact, when we write about these far-off founders of religion, we are guessing in the dark, or by the flickering light of analogy. The lower animals have faculties (such as their power of finding their way home through new unknown regions, and the ways ants acquire and communicate knowledge to each other) which remain mysteries to us. The terror of dogs in "haunted houses" and of horses passing "haunted" scenes has often been reported, and is briefly mentioned by Mr. Tylor. Balaam’s ass, and the dogs which crouched and whined before Athene—whom Eumaeus could not see—are "classical" examples.

The weakness of the anthropological argument here <note>The text from "the mental condition..." to the end of the sentence is underlined in pencil; the word "Souls" is circled.</note> is, we must repeat, that we know little more about the mental condition and experiences of the early thinkers who developed the doctrine of Souls than we know about the mental condition and experiences of the lower animals.

# ANTHROPOLOGY AND RELIGION

And the more firmly a philosopher believes in the <term>Darwinian hypothesis</term>, the less, he must admit, can he claim to know about the twilight ages between the lower animals and fully evolved humans. What kind of creature was man when he first conceived the seeds, or received the light, of Religion? All is guesswork here! We may simply refer to Hegel's theory that clairvoyance and hypnotic phenomena are produced by a kind of temporary <term>atavism</term>, or "throwing back" to a remotely ancient condition of the "<term>sensitive soul</term>" (*Fühlende Seele*). The "sensitive" <note>unconditioned, clairvoyant</note> faculty or "soul" is "a disease when it becomes a state of the self-conscious, educated, self-possessed human being of civilization." <note>Philosophy of Spirit, pp. 406, 408.</note> "<term>Second sight</term>," Hegel thinks, was a product of an earlier time and an earlier mental condition than ours.

Approaching this almost untouched subject—the early psychic condition of humanity—not from the perspective of metaphysical speculations like Hegel's, but with the tools of modern psychology and physiology, Dr. Max Dessoir of Berlin (following, indeed, M. Taine) has arrived, as we have seen, at somewhat similar conclusions. "This fully conscious life of the spirit," in which we modern people now live, "seems to rest upon a base of reflex action of a hallucinatory type." Our actual modern condition is not "fundamental," and "hallucination represents, at least in its early stages, the main trunk of our psychic existence." <note>See also Mr. A. J. Balfour's Presidential Address to the Society for Psychical Research, Proceedings, vol. 10. See, too, Taine, On Intelligence, i. 78, 100, 139.</note>

Now, suppose that those remote and unknown ancestors of ours who first developed the <term>doctrine of souls</term> had not yet moved far from "the main trunk of our psychic existence"—far from constant hallucination. In that case

If early humans were ever in a condition where telepathy and clairvoyance (assuming they are possible) were prevalent, one might expect that such useful faculties would be developed during the struggle for survival. We know that they are deliberately cultivated by modern primitive peoples. The Native American foster mother of John Tanner used to put herself into a hypnotic state when food was needed, so that she became *clairvoyant* regarding the whereabouts of game. Tanner, an English boy captured by the Indians at a young age, was skeptical at first, but eventually came to practice the same art himself, not without success.¹ His memoirs, which he dictated upon his return to civilization, were certainly not faked to support any particular theories. But it could be argued that the most telepathic human groups should, <term>ceteris paribus</term> <note>all else being equal</note>, have been the most successful in the struggle for survival. We may infer that other factors were not equal, as the clairvoyant state is not exactly the best for the practical business of living. But in reality, we know nothing about the psychic state of the earliest humans. They may have had experiences leading toward a belief in "spirits" about which we can say nothing. We are forced to guess while remaining largely ignorant of the actual conditions, and this historical ignorance inevitably plagues all anthropological speculation regarding the origin of religion.

Recognizing our own <term>nescience</term> <note>ignorance or lack of knowledge</note> regarding the psychic condition of our first thinking ancestors should make us hesitate to take it for granted that early man was on the same "psychic" level as ourselves or modern primitive peoples.

Of course, the shadow in the sunlight does not resemble the phantom in a dream. The two, however, were combined and identified by early thinkers, while breath and heart were used as symbols of "that in men which makes them live," a phrase found among the natives of Nicaragua in 1528. The admittedly symbolic character of the phrase, "it is *not* precisely the heart, but that in them which makes them live," proves that to the speaker life was *not* "heart" or "breath," but that these terms were known to be material placeholders for the concept of life.<gloss>1</gloss> Whether the earliest thinkers identified heart, breath, and shadow with life, or whether they consciously used words of material origin to denote an immaterial concept, of course we do not know. # THE MAKING OF RELIGION

We are next presented with many cases in which primitive people attribute sickness or lethargy to the absence of the patient’s spirit, or one of his spirits. This idea of a migratory spirit is then used by tribal peoples to explain certain actions of the sorcerer, priest, or seer. His soul, or one of his souls, is thought to travel to distant places in search of information, while the seer himself perhaps remains in a lethargic state. Probably, in the struggle for survival, he lost more by being lethargic than he gained by being clairvoyant!

Now, here we reach the first point in Mr. Tylor’s theory where a critic may ask: Was this belief in the wandering of the seer’s spirit a theory that was not only false in its form (as it probably is), but also completely unsupported by experiences that might suggest the existence of truly supernormal phenomena? By “supernormal” experiences, I mean the acquisition of knowledge by a human mind that could not be obtained through the recognized channels of sensation. Suppose, for the sake of argument, that a person—whether from a tribal or civilized society—obtains information while in a trance about distant places or events that are unknown and, through the senses, unknowable to him. The primitive man will explain this by saying that the seer’s soul, shadow, or spirit wandered out of the body to the distant location. This is currently an unverified theory. But still, for the sake of argument, suppose that the seer did honestly obtain this information in a trance, lethargy, hypnotic sleep, or any other state. If so, the modern tribal person (or his more gifted ancestors) would have had grounds for his theory of the wandering soul other than those provided by normal occurrences, such as ordinary dreams, shadows, and so forth. Again, if such things occur, there would be a potentiality in human nature for experiences other and stranger

But it will give the primitive man a better excuse for his theory than normal experiences provide; and it will even suggest a possibility that reflection on mere ordinary experiences—death, shadows, or trances—is not the sole origin of his theory. For a primitive person as sharp as Mr. Tylor’s hypothetical early reasoner might refuse to believe that his own or a friend’s soul had been absent on an expedition, unless it brought back information that could not normally be acquired. However, we cannot reason *beforehand* <note>Translating the Latin term *a priori*.</note> about how far the logic of a primitive person might or might not go at times.

In any case, a scientific reasoner might be expected to ask: 
> ‘Is this alleged acquisition of knowledge, not through the ordinary channels of sense, something that exists *in the nature of things*?’ 
Because, if it is, we must obviously expand our list of the primitive man’s reasons for believing in a soul: we must include ‘psychical’ experiences in those reasons, and there must be an X region to investigate.

Jung-Stilling (though he wrote before modern "Spiritualism" began) is not a very reliable authority; there is plenty of better evidence than his, but Mr. Tylor passes it by, merely remarking that "modern Europe has kept closely enough to the lines of early philosophy." Modern Europe has indeed done so, if it explains the supernormal acquisition of knowledge, or the hallucinatory appearance of a distant person to his friend, by a theory of wandering "spirits." But facts do not cease to be facts because wrong interpretations have been put upon them by primitive people, by Jung-Stilling, or by anyone else. The real

<page-num>71</page-num>
<header>ANTHROPOLOGY AND RELIGION</header>

The question is: Do such events occur among lower and higher races, beyond explanation by fraud and accidental coincidence? We gladly admit that the belief in Animism, when it takes the form of a theory of "wandering spirits," is probably unsustainable, as it is certainly of primitive origin. But we are not entirely sure that, in this respect, the theory is not based on actual experiences of an abnormal and extraordinary kind. If so, primitive philosophy and its supposed survivals in belief will appear in a new light. And we are inclined to believe that an examination of the massive evidence to which *Mr. Tylor* makes only a slight allusion here will at least make it wise to suspend our judgment, not only regarding the origins of the primitive theory of spirits, but also regarding the materialistic hypothesis that there is no psychical element in man.

I may seem to have already exceeded the limits of acceptable hypothesis. It may appear absurd to suggest that there could exist in humans—whether primitive or civilized—a faculty for acquiring information not accessible through the known senses, a faculty attributed by primitive philosophers to the wandering soul. But one may be permitted to quote the opinion of *M. Charles Richet*, *Professor of Physiology* in the Faculty of Medicine in Paris. He is not cited because M. Richet is a professor of physiology, but because he reached his conclusion after six years of meticulous experimentation. He says: "There exists in certain people, at certain moments, a faculty of acquiring knowledge which has no connection with our normal faculties of that kind."<sup>1</sup>

Instances tending to support *M. Richet’s* idea may now be sought in primitive and civilized life.

## IV

### ' OPENING THE GATES OF DISTANCE '

'To open the Gates of Distance' is the poetic Zulu phrase for what is called <term>clairvoyance</term>, or *vue à distance*. This, if it exists, is the result of a faculty of an undetermined nature, by which knowledge of remote events may be acquired through something other than the normal channels of the senses. As the Zulus say: '*Isiyezi* is a state in which a man becomes slightly unresponsive. He is awake, but still sees things which he would not see if he were not in a state of ecstasy (*nasiyesi*).'¹ The Zulu description of *isiyezi* includes what is technically called '<term>dissociation</term>.' No psychologist or pathologist will deny that visions of an hallucinatory sort may occur in dissociated states, such as in the *petit mal* of epilepsy. The question, however, is whether any such visions convey actual information that could not otherwise be acquired, beyond what chance coincidence can explain.

A Scottish example, from the records of a court of law, exactly illustrates the Zulu theory. At the moment when the husband of Jonka Dyneis was in danger in his boat six miles from her house, Jonka 'was found and seen standing against her own house wall in a trance; and when she was approached, she could not give an answer, but stood as if bereft of her senses, and when she was asked why she

---

<note>¹ Callaway, *Religion of the Zulus*, p. 232.</note>

The belief in "opening the Gates of Distance" is, of course, very widely widespread. The gift is attributed to Apollonius of Tyana, to Plotinus, to many Saints, to Catherine de’ Medici, to the Reverend Mr. Peden,² and to Joan of Arc, while the faculty is the standard practice of tribal seers in all regions.³

<margin>||</margin>
The question, however, which Mr. Tylor does not address, is: *Are any of the stories true?* If they are, they would certainly confirm the tribal theory of the wandering soul in the mind of the practitioner. Currently, finding documented cases of successful <term>clairvoyance</term> among indigenous peoples is a difficult task. White men either dismiss the idea, are afraid of appearing superstitious if they give examples, or, if they *do* give examples, are accused of having sunk to the degraded level of Zulus or Native Americans. Even where travelers, like Scheffer, have told about their own experiences, the narratives are omitted by modern writers on tribal divination.⁴ We must therefore conduct our own research, and it is to be noted that the stories of successful tribal clairvoyance are given as illustrations only, not as evidence of facts, for we cannot cross-examine the witnesses.

Mr. Tylor dismisses the topic in a rather dismissive manner:

> ‘Without discussing the merits of the accounts of what is called “second sight,”⁵ it may be pointed out that

> ‘There is among black men something which is divination within themselves. Finally, it says he will find it; finally, he sees it, and himself approaching it; before he begins to move from where he is, he sees it very clearly indeed, and there is an end of doubt. That sight is so clear that it is as if it were not an inner sight, but as if he saw the very thing itself, and the place where it is; so he quickly rises and goes to the place. If it is a hidden place, he throws himself into it, as though there were something that impelled him to go as swiftly as the wind; and, in fact, he finds the thing, if he has not acted by mere head-guessing. If it has been done by real inner divination, he really sees it. But if it is done by mere head-guessing and the knowledge that he has not gone to such a place and such a place, and that therefore it must be in such another place, he generally misses the mark.’

It is unusual for European travelers and missionaries to provide anecdotes that might seem to “confirm the delusions of ignorant savages.” Such anecdotes, again, are among the hidden mysteries of these wild philosophers and are not easily shared with strangers. When successful cases are reported, it is natural to claim that they come from Europeans who have fallen into primitive superstition, or that they may be explained by fraud and collusion. It is certain, however, that indigenous practitioners believe in their own powers, though they will just as certainly supplement them with trickery. Seers are chosen in Zululand, as among the Eskimos and Samoyeds, from the class of people who in Europe used to be—though are no longer—the most favored hypnotic subjects: “abnormal children,” the epileptic, and the hysterical. These individuals are subjected to “a long and methodical course of training.”¹ Stoll, speaking of Guatemala, says that “certainly most of the induced and spontaneous phenomena with which we are familiar occur among primitive peoples,” and he appeals to travelers for their observations.² Information is likely to increase as educated travelers pay more attention to the topic.

Dr. Callaway translates some Zulu communications that indicate the strength of belief among this very practical and skeptical people. Amusing illustrations of their skepticism will be quoted later, under the section on “Possession,” but they do accept certain hysterical patients as seers. These

are tested by their skill in finding objects that have been hidden without their knowledge. The point is that, while the primitive conjurer will undoubtedly use fraud whenever possible, the experience of these cultures favors employing as seers the same class of people who in Europe were, until recently, supposed to make the best hypnotic subjects. Thus, in West Africa, "the presiding elders, during your initiation into the secret society of your tribe, discover this gift <note>of Ebumtupism, or second sight</note>, and so select you as a 'witch doctor.'" $^1$ Among the Karens, the "Wees," or prophets, "are nervous, excitable men, the kind who would become mediums," $^2$ as mediums are described by Mr. Tylor.

In short, not to multiply examples, there is an element of actual observation and of good faith entangled in the trickery of primitive practice. Although the subjects may be selected partly because of the physical phenomena of convulsions which they exhibit—and which favorably impress their clients—they are also the type of subjects who occasionally show evidence of that supernormal faculty which is investigated by modern psychologists, like Richet, Janet, and William James.

The following example, by no means unique, shows the view taken by indigenous people of their own magic after they have become Christians. Catherine Wabose, a converted Native American seeress, described her preliminary fast at the age of puberty. After six days of abstaining from food, she was carried away to an unknown place where a radiant being welcomed her. Later, a dark, round object promised her the gift of prophecy. She found her natural senses greatly sharpened by the lack of food. She first exercised her powers when many of her kinsfolk were starving. A <term>medicine-lodge</term> (or "tabernacle," as Lafitau calls it) was built for her, and she crawled inside. As is well known, these lodges are violently shaken during the magician’s stay within them, which the early Jesuits at first attributed to the muscular efforts of the seers. In 1637, Père Lejeune was astonished by the violent motions of a large lodge occupied by a small man. One sorcerer, with an appearance of candor, vowed that "a great wind entered boisterously," and the Father was assured that if he went in himself, he would become <term>clairvoyant</term>. He did not perform the experiment. The Methodist convert, Catherine, gave the same description of her own experience: "The lodge began shaking violently by supernatural means. I knew this by the compressed current of air above and the noise of motion." She had been beating a small drum and singing; now she lay quiet. The radiant "orbicular" spirit then informed her that they "must go westward for game; how short-sighted you are!" The advice was taken and followed by instant success. This established her reputation.¹ Catherine’s conversion was preceded by a dream of her dying son, who saw a Sacred Figure and received white clothing from Him.

> ->Speak, man, ah say<-
> ->What Spirit, or Body, is this Body?’<-

It is like an indigenous hymn to Hegel’s <term>fühlende Seele</term>: the all-pervading Sensitive Soul. We are reminded, too, of the doctrine of the <term>Sanskrit Upanishads</term>: "There is no limit to the knowing of the Self that knows." <note>Brinton’s *Religions of Primitive Peoples*, p. 57.</note>

Unfortunately, Catherine was not asked to give other examples of what she considered her successes.

Acosta, who does not have the best possible reputation as an authority, informs us that Peruvian clairvoyants "tell what has passed in the farthest parts before news can come. At a distance of two or three hundred leagues, they would tell what the Spaniards did or suffered in their civil wars." To Du Pont, in 1606, a sorcerer "rendered a true oracle of the coming of Poutrincourt, saying his Devil had told him so." <note>Purchas, p. 629.</note>

We now give a modern case, from a scientific laboratory, of knowledge apparently acquired in no normal way, by a person of the sort usually chosen to be a prophet, or wizard, by indigenous people.

Professor Richet writes: <note>S.P.R. *Proceedings*, vol. vi. 69.</note>

> "On Monday, July 2, 1888, after having passed the whole day in my laboratory, I hypnotized Léonie at 8 P.M., and while she tried to make out a diagram concealed in an envelope, I said to her quite suddenly: 'What has happened to M. Langlois?' Léonie knows M. Langlois from having seen him two or three times some time ago in my physiological laboratory, where he acts as my assistant."

The results, however, when successful, would naturally suggest the belief in the wandering soul to the primitive thinker, or corroborate it if it had already been suggested by the common phenomena of dreaming.

To these instances of knowledge acquired through means other than the recognized channels of sense, we might add the Scottish tales of 'second sight.' That phrase is merely a local term covering examples of what is called 'clairvoyance'—visions of things remote in space, visual hallucinations that coincide with some notable event, premonitions of future things, and so on. From their clothing, most of the mourners seemed to be farm laborers—indeed, the young woman recognized some of them as people from Dull who had moved to live and work near Dunkeld. Comments were naturally made by my grandfather and the young couple about the unusual hour for a funeral; and, quickly filling in the papers, my grandfather went out to get the key to the churchyard, which was kept in the manse, as the procession could not enter God's acre without the key. Wondering why he had received no notice of the funeral, he took a shortcut to the manse, got the key, and hurried down to the churchyard gate, where he naturally expected to find the procession waiting. Not a single person was there except the young couple, who were just as amazed as my grandfather!

> ' Well, at the same hour in the evening of the same day the following week, the funeral—this time in reality—arrived quite unexpectedly. The facts were that a boy, a native of Dull, had been gored by a bull at Dunkeld and was so terribly mangled that his remains were gathered, placed into a coffin, and taken without delay to Dull. A grave was dug as quickly as possible—since the poor lad had no relatives—and the remains were buried. My grandfather and the young couple recognized several of the mourners as being among those whom they had seen from the session clerk's room exactly a week earlier in the phantom procession. The young woman knew some of them personally and told them what she had seen, but they, of course, denied any knowledge of the matter, as they had been in Dunkeld at that time.'

> ‘ The parishioners in Skye were evidently largely filled with a belief, similar to that of Catholics, in the powers of intercession held by their clergyman; so when they had a “warning” or “vision,” they usually consulted my father about what they could do to prevent the coming disaster from happening to their relatives or friends. In this way, my father had the opportunity to note down the minute details of the “warning” or “vision” immediately after it was told to him. Having had the benefit of medical training before his theological training, he was able to record solid facts without the addition of imaginary details. Approaching this method of taking notes with a perfectly open mind, except for a slight touch of skepticism, he was greatly surprised to discover how very frequently these visions were realized exactly according to the details recorded in his notebook. Finally, he was compelled to set aside his skepticism and admit that some people undoubtedly possessed this uncanny gift. Almost the first case he recorded (Case X) was that of a woman who one day had a vision of her son falling over a high cliff at Uig, in Skye, with a sheep or lamb.
>
> ‘ CASE X.—She heard her son exclaim in Gaelic, “This is a fatal lamb for me.” As her son lived several miles from Uig and was a fisherman, it seemed very unlikely to my father that this would come true; however, one month later, the realization occurred only too accurately. Unknown to his mother, who had warned him against having anything to do with sheep or lambs, the son one day decided to take a holiday inland instead of going out in his boat. He went off to Uig, where a farmer asked for his help in separating some lambs from the ewes. One of the lambs ran away, and the fisherman lad ran headlong after it; not looking where he was going, he caught the lamb but was pulled by it to the edge of one of the very picturesque but exceedingly dangerous cliffs at Uig. Realizing his dangerous position too late, he exclaimed, “This is a fatal lamb for me,” but moving with such momentum, he was unable to stop himself in time. Along with the lamb, he fell over into the ravine below and was, of course, killed instantly. When the farmer saw the lad’s danger, he ran to help him, but he was only in time to hear him cry out in Gaelic before disappearing over the edge of the precipice. This had been predicted by the mother a month earlier. Was this simply a coincidence? ’

Dr. Macgregor’s remarks on the involuntary and unwelcome nature of these visions are supported by what Scheffer says concerning the Lapps, as already quoted.

In addition to visions that come unsought—contributing knowledge of remote or even future things—we may look at visions that are provoked by various methods. Drugs (*impepo*) are used, seers whirl in a wild dance until they fall unconscious, or a trance is induced by various kinds of self-suggestion or "auto-hypnotism." Fasting is also practiced. In modern life, the self-induced trance is common among "mediums"—a subject to which we will return later.

So far, it will be observed, our evidence proves that precisely similar beliefs regarding man’s occasional power of "opening the gates of distance" have been held in a great variety of lands and eras, and by races in every state of culture.<note>The examples in the Old Testament and in the *Life of St. Columba* by Adamnan need only be mentioned, as they are too familiar to require quotation.</note> These alleged experiences are still said to occur and have been investigated by physiologists as eminent as M. Richet. The question of the truth behind these narrations inevitably arises, and it continues to arise.

In the following chapter, we discuss a method of inducing hallucinations that interests anthropologists because it is practiced universally. We believe the broad extent of its range among savage races has not been previously noted. We then add facts from modern experience, the authenticity of which we personally do not doubt; the provisional conclusion appears to be that savages have observed a psychological phenomenon that has been ignored by professional psychologists, and which certainly does not fit into the standard materialistic hypothesis.

### V

## CRYSTAL VISIONS, SAVAGE AND CIVILIZED

Among savage methods of inducing hallucinations from which knowledge may be supernormally obtained, various forms of "crystal-gazing" are the most curious. We find the habit of looking into water—usually in a vessel, and preferably a glass one—among Red Indians (Lejeune), Romans (Varro, cited in *Civitas Dei*, iii. 457), and the Africans of Fez (Leo Africanus); while the Maori use a drop of blood (Taylor), Egyptians use ink (Lane), and Australian savages employ a ball of polished stone into which the seer "projects himself" to perceive the results of an expedition.¹

I have already provided, in the Introduction, Ellis’s record of the Polynesian case. After a hole is dug in the floor of his house and filled with water, the priest looks for a vision of the thief who has carried off stolen goods. The Polynesian theory is that the god carries the spirit of the thief over the water, in which it is reflected. Lejeune’s Red Indians have their patients gaze into the water, in which they will see images of the things in the way of food or medicine that will do them good. In modern terms, the instinctive knowledge existing implicitly in the patient’s subconscious is thus brought into the range of his ordinary consciousness.

In 1887 the late Captain J. T. Bourke, of the U.S.

Cavalry, an original and careful observer, visited the Apaches on behalf of the Bureau of Ethnology. He learned that one of the chief duties of the medicine-men was to find the location of lost or stolen property. Na-a-cha, one of these *jossakeeds*, possessed a magic quartz crystal which he highly valued. Captain Bourke presented him with an even finer crystal. "He could not give me an explanation of its magical use, except that by looking into it he could see everything he wanted to see." Captain Bourke appears never to have heard of the modern experiments in crystal-gazing. Captain Bourke also discovered that the Apaches, like the Greeks, Australians, Africans, Maori, and many other races, use the bull-roarer, turndun, or *rhombos*—a piece of wood which, when whirled around, causes a strange windy roar—in their mystic ceremonies. The widespread use of the *rhombos* was known to Captain Bourke; that of the crystal was not.

For the Iroquois, Mrs. Erminie Smith provides information about the crystal. "Placed in a gourd of water, it could make visible the apparition of a person who has bewitched another." She gives a case from the era of European contact of a medicine-man who found the witch’s home, but obtained only a blurry view of her face. the Malagasies, says that they *squillent* (a word not found in the Littré dictionary), that is, they divine by crystals which "fall from heaven when it thunders."
