of geographical distribution. We also find the practice in Greece (Pausanias, VII. xxi. 12), in Rome (Varro), in Egypt, and in India.

Though anthropologists have paid no attention to the subject, it was, of course, familiar to later Europe. ‘Miss X’ <note>Ada Goodrich-Freer, a researcher for the Society for Psychical Research</note> has traced it among early Christians, in early Councils, in episcopal condemnations of *specularii* <note>those who practice divination by looking into mirrors or crystals</note>, and so to Dr. Dee, under James VI; Aubrey; the Regent d’Orléans in St.-Simon’s Memoirs; the modern mesmerists (Gregory, Mayo) and the mid-Victorian spiritualists, who, as usual, explained the phenomena in their prehistoric way, by ‘spirits.’¹ Until this lady examined the subject, nobody had thought of remarking that a belief so universal likely had some basis in fact—or at least nobody except for two professors of chemistry and physiology, Drs. Gregory and Mayo. Miss X conducted experiments, beginning by accident when she was a child, just as George Sand did.

The hallucinations which appear to her eyes in ink or crystal are:

1. Revived memories ‘arising thus, and only thus, from the subconscious layers;’
‘2. Objectification of ideas or images—(*a*) consciously or (*b*) unconsciously—in the mind of the percipient;
‘3. Visions, possibly telepathic or clairvoyant, implying the acquisition of knowledge by supernormal means.’²

The examples given of the last category—the category which would be so useful to a priest or medicine man asked to find lost items—are of very little interest.³

of people, sane and healthy, can see vivid landscapes and figures of persons in motion in glass balls and other vehicles. Dr. Parish attributes this faculty to "dissociation," which is practically drowsiness. However, he speaks by conjecture and without having witnessed experiments, as will be shown later. I now offer a series of experiments with a glass ball, coming under my own observation, in which knowledge was apparently acquired in no ordinary way. I am personally convinced of the absence of fraud, not only by the character of everyone involved but by the nature of the circumstances. I feel certain that adaptive memory did not later alter the narratives as they were originally told, because they were reported to me—even when I was not present—within less than a week, exactly as they are given here, except in cases specifically noted.

Early in the present year (1897), I met a young lady who told me of three or four curious hallucinatory experiences of her own, which were sufficiently corroborated. She was unaware of psychical studies and personally was, and is, in perfect health; the "pale cast of thought" <note>An allusion to Shakespeare's *Hamlet*, meaning she is not overly intellectual or prone to brooding</note> is remote from her. I obtained a glass ball and was present when she first looked into it. I remember she saw the interior of a house with a full-length portrait of an unknown person. There were, I think, one or two other imaginary pictures of the familiar kind. But she presently (living as she was among strangers) developed a power of "seeing" persons and places unknown to her, but familiar to them. These experiences do seem to me to be good examples of what is called "thought transference"; indeed, I never before could move past a state of balanced doubt on that subject—a balance which now leans considerably to the affirmative side. There may be an abundance of better evidence, but knowing the persons and circumstances, and being present once at what seemed to me a crucial...

We cannot tell what clues may be accidentally given in experiments in thought transference. But, in these cases of crystal-gazing, the detail was too abundant to be conveyed by a bystander through a wink or a cough. I do not mean to say that success was invariable. I thought of <term>Dr. W. G. Grace</term> <note>A famous and easily recognizable English amateur cricketer of the era</note>, and the <term>scryer</term> saw an old man crawling along with a stick. But I doubt if Dr. Grace is very deeply seated in that mystic entity, my subconscious self. The "<term>scries</term>" which were correct were sometimes, but not always, those that the "<term>agent</term>" (or person for whom the vision was seen) was consciously thinking of. But the examples will illustrate the various kinds of occurrences.

Here one should first consider the arguments against accepting the recognition of objects merely described by another person. The <term>crystal-gazer</term> may know the inquirer so intimately as to have a very good guess at the subject of his thoughts. Again, a man is likely to be thinking of a woman, and a woman of a man, so the field of guesswork is limited. In answer to the first objection, I may say that the crystal-gazer was among strangers, all of whom—myself included—she was meeting now for the first time. Nor could she have studied their histories beforehand, for she could not normally know, when she left home, that she was about to be shown a glass ball or whom she would meet. The second objection is met by the circumstance that ladies were not usually picked out for men, nor men for women. Indeed, these choices were the exceptions, and in each case they were marked by extremely specific details. A third objection is that credulity, or the love of strange novelties, or the desire to be helpful, biases the inquirers and makes them anxious to

recognize something familiar in the <term>scryer’s</term> descriptions. In the same way, we know how people recognize faces in the most blurred and vague of <term>spiritist</term> photographs, or see family resemblances in the most basic dough-faced babies. Consider the descriptions of people in a passport, or in a proclamation describing the personal appearance of a criminal. These fit the men or women intended, but they also fit a crowd of other people. The description given by the <term>scryer</term>, then, may be correct by a lucky coincidence, or may be too easily accepted as a match by someone wanting to believe.

The complex of coincidences, however, could not be attributed to chance selection out of the entire possible field of guesswork. We must also remember that a series of such "hits" increases, at an enormous rate, the odds against accidental guesswork. I can give an example of such mere luck. I was writing a story in which the hero was <term>George Kelly</term>, one of the <term>‘Seven Men of Moidart.’</term> <note>A group of seven followers who accompanied Prince Charles Edward Stuart to Scotland in 1745</note> A year after writing my tale, I found the Government description of Mr. Kelly (from 1736). It exactly matched my purely imaginary sketch, down to the eyes, teeth, and face, except that I made my hero "about six feet tall," whereas the Government listed him as five feet ten. But I knew beforehand that Mr. Kelly was a clergyman; his remarkable career proved him to be a person of great activity and cheerfulness—and he was of Irish birth. Even a dozen such guesses, equally correct, could not suggest any powers of "vision," when so much was already known beforehand about the person being guessed. > ‘A great black ship,’ anchored in ‘a river or lake,’ naturally suggests the Suez Canal, where, in fact, Mr. Pembroke’s brother was just arriving. In February 1898, Miss Angus again visited the place where I was staying. Together, we visited the scene of a historical crime, and Miss Angus looked into the glass ball. It was easy for her to ‘visualize’ the incidents of the crime (the murder of Cardinal Beaton), for they are familiar enough to many people. What she actually saw in the ball was a tall, pale lady, ‘about forty, but looking thirty-five,’ with hair drawn back from her brow, standing beside a high chair and dressed in a wide <term>farthingale</term><note>A hooped skirt or petticoat worn under a dress in the 16th and 17th centuries.</note> of stiff gray brocade, without a ruff. The costume corresponds well (as we found) with that of 1546, and I said, ‘I suppose it is Mariotte Ogilvy’—to whom Miss Angus’s historical knowledge (and perhaps that of the general public) did not extend. Mariotte was the Cardinal’s lady-love and was in the Castle on the night before the murder, according to Knox. She had been in my mind, from where (according to the theory of <term>thought transference</term>) she may have passed to Miss Angus’s mind; however, I had never speculated on Mariotte’s costume. Nothing but conjecture, of course, comes from these apparently ‘retrospective’ pictures, though a most singular and picturesque coincidence occurred which may be told in a very different context.

In these Indian cases, ‘thought transference’ may account for the connection between the figures seen by Miss Angus and the ideas in the minds of Mr. and Mrs. Bissett. But the hypothesis of thought transference, while it would cover the wooden huts at Bombay (Mrs. Bissett knowing that her brother was about to leave that place), can scarcely explain the scene in the garden by the river and the scene with the trees. In the Introductory Chapter, it was observed that the phenomena which apparently point to some unaccountable, supernormal faculty of acquiring knowledge are ‘trivial.’ These anecdotes illustrate that triviality; but the facts certainly left a number of people, who were completely unfamiliar with such experiments, with the impression that Miss Angus’s glass ball was like Prince Ali’s magical telescope in the *Arabian Nights*.² These experiments, however, occasionally touch on intimate personal matters and cannot be reported in such instances.

It will be noted that the faculty is unpredictable and does not always respond to the conscious exertion of thought.

However, I do not precisely understand how that is meant to account for some of the cases provided.

Anyone who can accept the assurance of my personal belief in the good faith of everyone involved will see how very useful this faculty of crystal-gazing must be to an Apache or Australian medicine man, or a Polynesian priest. Unpredictable as the faculty is, a few real successes, well exploited and supplemented by fraud, would establish a wizard’s reputation. That the faculty of being affected in this way is genuine seems proved—aside from modern evidence—by the worldwide prevalence of crystal-gazing in various cultures. ## VI
### ANTHROPOLOGY AND HALLUCINATIONS

We have been examining cases, whether primitive or civilized, in which knowledge is believed to be acquired through no known sensory channel. All such instances among primitive peoples—whether involving simple clairvoyance, the aid of gazing into a smooth surface, dreams, trances, or second sight—would confirm, if they did not actually originate, the belief in the separable soul. It was argued that if the soul is to visit distant places and collect information, it must leave the body, and must therefore be capable of leading an independent life. Perhaps we should next study cases of "possession," where knowledge is supposedly conveyed by an alien soul, ghost, spirit, or god taking up residence in a person and speaking through their lips. However, it seems better first to consider the alleged supernatural phenomena that may have led the primitive thinker to believe that *he* was not the only owner of a separable soul, and that other people were equally gifted.

The sense of separation that a primitive dreamer or seer would feel after a dream or vision in which he visited remote places would satisfy him that *his* soul, at least, was volatile. However, some experience of what he would take to be visits from the spirits of others would be needed before he recognized that other men, as well as himself, had the ability to send their souls on journeys.

<header>THE MAKING OF RELIGION</header>

Now, ordinary dreams—in which the dreamer seemed to see people who were actually far away—would provide the primitive reasoner with a certain amount of supporting evidence. It is part of Mr. Tylor’s argument that primitive people (like some children) struggle with the difficulty, which most of us may have occasionally felt, of deciding: "Did this really happen, or did I dream it?" Therefore, ordinary dreams would offer the early thinker some evidence that other people’s souls could visit him, just as he believes that his own soul can visit them.

But we may assume that people, even at that stage of thought, were not so deluded as to fail to make a major practical distinction between sleeping and waking experiences on the whole. As has been shown, this distinction is made by even the most primitive groups we know. On the other hand, a single clear *waking* hallucination of the presence of a person who is actually absent would surely carry more weight with the early philosopher than twenty dreams, for the essence of a dream is to be easily forgotten. Indeed, primitive people, oddly enough, have arrived at our own theory: "dreams go by opposites." Dr. Callaway illustrates this regarding the Zulus, and Mr. Scott does so for the Mang’anza. Therefore, they *do* distinguish between sleeping and waking. We must, therefore, examine waking hallucinations within the field of actual experience, using whatever recent evidence is available. If these hallucinations correspond—at a frequency beyond what mere coincidence can explain—with real but unknown events, then such hallucinations would greatly strengthen the primitive theory in the mind of an early thinker: that a person far away may, voluntarily or involuntarily, project their spirit on a journey and be seen where they are not physically present.

When Mr. Tylor wrote his book, the study of occasional waking hallucinations in sane and healthy people

was in its infancy. Indeed, much had been written about hallucinations, but these were mainly the chronic false perceptions of lunatics, of drunkards, and of people in poor health, such as Nicolai and Mrs. A. The hallucinations of people of genius—Jeanne d’Arc, Luther, Socrates, and Pascal—were attributed by some to insanity in these famous individuals. Hardly any writers before Mr. Galton had recognized that hallucinations might occur once in a lifetime, perhaps, among healthy, sober, and mentally sound people. If these were known to occur, they were dismissed as dreams of an unconscious sleep. This is still essentially the hypothesis of Dr. Parish, as we shall see later. But in the last twenty years, the infrequent hallucinations of the sane have been recognized by Mr. Galton and discussed by Professor James, Mr. Gurney, Dr. Parish, and many other writers.

Two results have followed. First, "ghosts" are shown to be hallucinations—when they are not illusions caused by mistaking one object for another. As these most frequently represent a living person who is not present, by the same logic, the appearance of a dead person is on the same level; it is not a physical "ghost" occupying space, but merely an hallucination. Such an appearance can, *prima facie*, suggest no reasonable conclusion regarding the continued existence of the dead. On the other hand, new studies have raised the perhaps unanswerable question: "Do not hallucinations of the sane representing the living coincide more frequently than mere luck can account for with the death or other crisis of the person apparently seen?" If this could be proved, then there would seem to be a causal *nexus*, a relationship of cause and effect between the hallucination and the coinciding crisis. That connection would be tentatively explained by some misunderstood action of the mind or brain of the person in the crisis upon that of the

In the meantime, the reader who has persevered this far is likely to go no further. The prejudice against "wraiths" and "ghosts" is very strong; but, then, our innocent phantasms are (as we understand their nature) neither ghosts nor wraiths. Kant blunted his metaphysical tools not against these phantasms, but against the logically inconceivable entities which were simultaneously material and non-material, both "spiritual" and "space-filling." There is no such difficulty with hallucinations, which, whatever else may be said about them, are familiar facts of experience. The only real objections are the claims that hallucinations are always *morbid* <note>In this context, morbid means relating to disease or an unhealthy mental state.</note> (which is no longer the universal belief of physiologists and psychologists), and that the alleged coincidences of a phantasm of a person with the unknown death of that person at a distance are "pure flukes." That is the question to which we will return later.

Of these, (1) the emotional effect is, of course, the vaguest. We may all have had a sudden fit of gloom which we could not explain. People rarely act on such impressions, and when they do, they are often wrong. For example, a friend of my own was suddenly so overwhelmed with inexplicable misery while playing golf (even though he was winning his match) that he apologized to his opponent and walked home from the ninth hole. Nothing was wrong at home. Probably some real reason for anxiety had vaguely occurred to his mind and expressed itself through his emotions.

Cases where a person feels compelled to perform an action (2) are also documented. In fact, the lawyer’s experience in our story is such an example. Without getting bogged down (3) with "voices," visual hallucinations that coincide with a distant, unknown crisis have been traced from a mere feeling that someone is in the room, followed by a mental image—or "mind's eye" picture—of a person dying far away, up to a kind of "vision" of a person or scene, and even to hallucinations that affect touch, sight, and hearing all at once. Since hundreds of these accounts of coincidental hallucinations of every level have been gathered directly from witnesses—often individuals known to the researcher and usually questioned in person—it is hard to deny that there is a *prima facie* <note>at first sight; based on the first impression</note> case for investigation.<note>See "Phantasms of the Living" and "A Theory of Apparitions," *Proceedings*, S.P.R., vol. ii., by Messrs. Gurney and Myers.</note>

This is not a matter of "spirits," with all the physical and metaphysical problems they present. Nor is there any attempt to avoid the fact that many "premonitions" and hallucinations experienced by sane people do not correspond to any discoverable event. We are only suggesting the possibility of an influence—unknown in its nature—of one mind on another across a distance, where that influence expresses itself as a hallucination. An investigation into this subject, within both the ethnographic and modern fields, may be new, but it involves no "superstition."

We now return to Mr. Tylor, who discusses hallucinations along with other experiences that led early primitive thinkers to believe in ghosts or souls that can leave the body—which he considers the origin of religion.

As to the causes of hallucinations in general, Mr. Tylor has something to say, but it is not systematic. "Sickness, exhaustion, and excitement" cause savages to see "human specters," in whose "objective reality" they believe. But if an educated modern person—who is neither sick, exhausted, nor excited—has a hallucination of a friend's presence, he also believes that it is "objective" (that it is his friend in the flesh) until he discovers his mistake through investigation or reflection. As Professor William James remarks in his *Principles of Psychology*, such solitary hallucinations occurring to sane and healthy people once in a lifetime are difficult to explain, and they are by no means rare. "Sometimes," Mr. Tylor observes, "the phantom has the characteristic quality of not being visible to everyone in a gathered company," and he adds, "to assert or imply that they are visible sometimes, and to some persons, but not always, or to everyone, is to offer an explanation of <margin>Not public.</margin>facts which is not, indeed, our usual modern explanation, but which is a perfectly rational and intelligible product of early science."

It is indeed; nor has later science produced any rational and intelligible explanation of collective hallucinations—those shared by several people at once and perhaps not perceived by others who are present. Mr. Tylor, it is true, asserts that "in civilized countries, a rumor of someone having seen a phantom is enough to make others see it if their minds are in a properly receptive state." But this is circular reasoning. What is "a properly receptive state"? If illness, overwork, or "expectant attention" create "a properly receptive state," I should have seen several phantoms in several "haunted houses." But the only experience of that sort I ever had occurred when I was thinking of anything but that, when I was in good health, and when I did not know

Mr. Tylor treats waking hallucinations in much the same manner as he deals with "traveling clairvoyance." He does not study them "in the field of experience." He is not concerned with the truth of the facts—important as we think it would be—but with his theory that hallucinations, among other causes, would naturally give rise to the belief in spirits, and thus to the early philosophy of <term>Animism</term>. Now, certainly, the hallucination of a person’s presence—say at the moment of his death at a distance—would suggest to a savage that something of the dying man’s, something symbolized by the word "shadow" or "breath" (<term>spiritus</term>), had come to say farewell. The modern "spiritualistic" theory, again, that the dead man’s "spirit" is actually present to the perceiver in space, corresponds to and is derived from the animistic philosophy of the savage. But we may believe in such "death-wraiths," or hallucinatory appearances of the dying, without being either savages or spiritualists. We may believe without pretending to explain, or we may propose the theory of "<term>Telepathy</term>," Hegel’s "magical tie," according to which the distant mind somehow impresses itself, in a more or less perfect hallucination, on the mind of the person who perceives the wraith. If this is so, or even if no explanation is offered, the truth of the stories of coincidental apparitions becomes important, as pointing toward a new region of psychical inquiry. The hallucinations we hear about most are those in which a person sees the phantom of another person who, unknown to him, is at or near the hour of death. Mr. Tylor, in addition to his three instances in civilized life, refers to one in savage life, with references to other cases.<note>Primitive Culture, vol. i, p. 450.</note> We turn to his savage instance, providing it in full from the original.<note>From Shortland’s Traditions of New Zealand, p. 140.</note>

‘Among the Maoris,’ says Mr. Shortland, ‘it is always ominous to see the figure of an absent person. If the figure is very shadowy and its face is not seen, death, although it may soon be expected, has not yet seized its prey. If the face of the absent person is seen, the omen warns the observer that he is already dead.’

The following statement is from the mouth of an eyewitness:
‘A party of natives left their village with the intention of being absent for some time on a pig-hunting expedition. One night, while they were seated in the open air around a blazing fire, the figure of a relative who had been left ill at home was seen to approach. The apparition appeared to only two of the party and vanished immediately when they made a cry of surprise. When they returned to the village, they asked about the sick man and then learned that he had died around the time he was said to have been seen.’

In filling the gap in Mr. Tylor’s anthropological work, and in asking questions about the proportion of phantasms of the living that coincide with a crisis in the experience of the person seen compared to those that do not, it is obviously necessary to reject all evidence from people who were ill, anxious, overworked, or in deep grief at the time of the hallucination. It will be seen later that neither grief nor romantic passion (dominating the association of our ideas as they do) produce many phantasms. Our business, however, is with the false perceptions of people who are trustworthy, as far as we know, sane, healthy, not usually prone to visions, and in a calm state of mind.

There remains a normal cause of subjective hallucinations: expectancy. This appears to be a real cause of hallucination or, at least, of illusion. While waiting for the sound of a carriage, you may often hear it before it arrives, as you mistake other sounds for the one you desire. Furthermore, in an inquiry involving 17,000 people, the S.P.R. <note>Society for Psychical Research</note> collected thirteen cases where a person appeared as a hallucination to another who was *expecting* their arrival. Again, it is very conceivable that a small thing—the accidental opening of a door, or a familiar noise in an unfamiliar place—may trigger the brain into creating a hallucination of a person passing through the door, or of the place where the sound now heard used to be familiar. Expectancy and nervousness could also undoubtedly cause a hallucination for someone who felt uncomfortable in a house with a reputation for being “haunted,” though, as we have seen, the effect is far less common than the cause. All these types of causes are undoubtedly more likely to be prevalent among superstitious savages than among educated Europeans.

Yet collective hallucinations, which are shared by several persons at once, are especially puzzling. Even if they occur when everyone is in a strained state of expectancy, it is odd that they all see them in the same way.<note>It will, of course, be said that they adjusted their stories to agree with each other.</note> Examples will occur later. Again, only one person—and that based on doubtful evidence—is claimed to have shared, on one occasion, the visions of Jeanne d’Arc. In both cases, all the conditions said to produce collective hallucination were present in the highest degree. Yet no collective hallucination occurred.

Narratives about hallucinations occurring at the same time as a death—well-attested narratives—are abundant in modern times, so abundant that one need only refer the curious to Mr. Gurney and Mr. Myers’s two large volumes, *Phantasms of the Living*, and to the S.P.R. <note>Society for Psychical Research</note> *Report of Census of Hallucinations* (1894). As Mr. Tylor observes, "Man, while still in a low intellectual condition, came to associate in thought those things which he found by experience to be connected in fact." <note>¹ *Primitive Culture*, volume 1, page 116.</note> Did early man, then, find through experience that apparitions of his friends were "connected in fact" with their deaths? We have seen that this belief exists in New Zealand, and it is confirmed by this instance—one of "many such accounts," according to the author. A Maori chief was away for a long time on the warpath. One day he entered his wife’s hut and sat silently by the hearth. She ran to bring witnesses, but upon her return, the phantasm was no longer visible. Soon afterward, the woman married again. Her husband then returned in perfect health and pardoned the lady, as she had acted on what, to a Maori mind, seemed like good legal evidence of his death. Of course, even if she had made up the story, it is evidence of the existence of the belief. <note>² *Polack’s Manners of the New Zealanders*, volume 1, page 268.</note>

What, then, is the cause of the belief that a phantom of a person is a sign of their death? Based on the theory of primitive philosophy, as explained by Mr. Tylor himself, a person’s soul may leave their body and become visible to others, not only at death, but on many other occasions—in dreams, trances, or lethargy. All of these are much more frequent conditions in any person’s life than the act of dying. Why, then, is the phantasm supposed by primitive peoples to announce death? Is it because, in a high enough ratio of cases to provoke notice, early man found the appearance and the death to be "things connected in fact"?

I will provide an instance in which the philosophy of primitive peoples would lead them *not* to connect a phantasm of a living man with his death.

The Woi Worung, an Australian tribe, believe that ‘the Murup [wraith] of an individual could be sent from him by magic, as, for instance, when a hunter carelessly went to sleep when out hunting.’¹ In this case the hunter is exposed to the magic of his enemies. But the Murup, or detached soul, would be visible to people at a distance when its owner is only asleep—according to primitive philosophy. Why, then, when the wraith is seen, is the owner believed to be dying? Are the events bound to be ‘connected in fact’?

As is well known, the Society for Psychical Research has attempted a small census for the purpose of discovering whether hallucinations representing people at a distance coincided, within twelve hours, with their deaths, in a larger ratio than the laws of chance allow as possible. If this were so, the Maori might have some ground for their theory that such hallucinations indicate a death. I do not believe that any such census can enable us to reach a positive conclusion which science will accept. In spite of all precautions taken, all warnings given beforehand, and ‘allowances’ made later, collectors of evidence will ‘select’ positive cases already known—or (which is equally fatal) will be suspected of doing so. Again, lapses of memory that increase the closeness of the coincidence will occur—or it will be easy to say that they occurred. ‘Allowances’ for them will not be accepted.

Once more, 17,000 cases, though a larger number than is usual in biological inquiries, are decidedly not enough for a general argument on probabilities; a million, it will be said, would not be too many. Finally, granting honesty, accurate memory, and non-selection (none of which will be granted by opponents), it is easy to say that odd things *must* occur, and that the large proportion of positive

Other objections are put forward by teachers of popular science who have either not examined—or, having examined, misrepresent—the results of the Census in detail. I can provide an example of their method.

Mr. Edward Clodd is the author of several science handbooks—‘The Story of Creation,’ ‘A Manual of Evolution,’ and others. In a signed review of a book, a critique published in ‘The Sketch’ (October 13, 1897), Mr. Clodd wrote about the Census: ‘Thousands of people were asked whether they had ever seen apparitions, and out of these some hundreds, mostly unintelligent foreigners, replied in the affirmative. In weighing evidence we have to take into account the competency as well as the integrity of the witnesses.’ Mr. Clodd has very frankly and good-naturedly acknowledged the errors in his remark. But, if by "snakes" Mr. Clodd means purely subjective hallucinations, not known to coincide with any event—and this is his meaning—his statement agrees with that of the Census. His observations, of course, were purely accidental errors.

The number of hallucinations representing living or dying recognized persons in the answers received was 352. Of first-hand cases, in which the coincidence of the hallucination with the death of the person apparently seen was affirmed, there were 80, of which 26 are given.

The non-coincidental hallucinations were multiplied by four to allow for the forgetfulness of "misses." The results being compared, it was decided that the hallucinations collected coincided with death 440 times more often than should be the case by the law of probabilities. Therefore, there was proof, or a presumption, in favor of some relation of cause and effect between A’s death and B’s hallucination.

If we were to attack the opinion of the Committee on Hallucinations, that "Between deaths and apparitions of the dying a connection exists which is not due to chance alone," the assault should be made not only on the method, but on the details. The events were never very recent, and often were of remote occurrence. The remoteness was less than it seems, however, as the questions were often answered several years before

These mental conditions, therefore, occur only in twelve percent of the instances. On the whole, it does not seem fair to argue that anxiety produces so much hallucination that it will account by itself for those which we have analyzed as coincidental.

We find ourselves able to understand the Master of Ravenswood’s reflections after he saw the best wraith in fiction:

> "She died expressing her eager desire to see me. Can it be, then—can strong and earnest wishes, formed during the last agony of nature, survive its end, surmount the formidable boundaries of the spiritual world, and place before us its inhabitants in the hues and coloring of life? And why was that manifested to the eye, which could not unfold its tale to the ear?" ("Her withered lips moved fast, although no sound issued from them.") "And why should a breach be made in the laws of nature, yet its purpose remain unknown?"

# VII

## DEMONIACAL POSSESSION

THERE is a type of hallucination—namely, Phantasms of the Dead—about which it seems better to say nothing in this place. If such phantasms are seen by "savages" when awake, they will undoubtedly strongly corroborate that belief in the survival of the soul after death, which is undeniably suggested to the early thinker by the phenomena of dreaming. But, while it is easy enough to produce evidence of recognized phantasms of the dead in civilized life, it would be very difficult indeed to discover many good examples in what we know about "savages." Some Fijian instances are given by Mr. Fison in his and Mr. Howitt’s *Kamilaroi and Kurnai*. Others occur in the narrative of John Tanner, a captive from childhood among the "Red Indians." But the circumstance, already noted, that an Australian boy became a wizard because he saw a phantasm of his dead mother, proves that such experiences are not common; and Australian blackfellows have admitted that they, for their part, never saw a ghost, but only heard of ghosts from their elders. Mr. David Leslie, previously cited, gives some firsthand Zulu evidence about a haunted wood, where the *Esemkofu*, or ghosts of persons killed by a tyrannical chief, were heard and felt by his native informant; the percipient was also pelted with stones, as if by a European *Poltergeist*. The Zulu who dies commonly becomes an *Ihlozi*, and receives his share of

sacrifice. The *Esemkofu*, on the other hand, are restless and haunting spirits.¹

Generally, as far as our information goes, it is not the recognized ghosts of the dead seen in waking visions that support the primitive belief in the persistence of the spirit after death. Instead, the primitive thinker bases his faith on the reported phenomena of noises and the physical movement of seemingly untouched objects—the kind of disturbances that cause so many houses in civilized society to be closed or avoided as "haunted." The primitive person naturally attributes such disturbances to "spirits." Therefore, our evidence for recognized ghosts of the dead among primitive peoples is very sparse, so it is unnecessary to examine the much more abundant evidence from civilized societies. The attested facts could, of course, be theoretically explained as the result of telepathy from a mind that is no longer embodied; and if the evidence were as plentiful as that for hallucinations occurring at the same time as a person's death, it would be extremely important. However, it is not so plentiful, and even assuming that it is accurate, various explanations that do not involve anything as unappealing to science as the actions of a disembodied intelligence can be, and have been, proposed.

Therefore, we turn from a subject where civilized testimony is more extensive than that derived from primitive life to a topic where primitive evidence is much more complete than modern civilized records. This topic is what is called <term>Demoniacal Possession</term>.

In the philosophy of <term>Animism</term>, and in the beliefs of many people, both primitive and civilized, spirits of the dead or spirits in general can take up residence in the bodies of living people. Such men or women are described as "inspired" or "possessed." They speak in voices that are not their own and act in a way that is foreign to their natural character.

They are said to deliver prophecies and to display knowledge that they could not have normally acquired—and, in fact, do not consciously possess in their normal state. The primitive person explains all these and similar phenomena with the hypothesis that an outside spirit—perhaps a demon, a ghost, or a god—has taken possession of the patient. The possessed person, being full of the spirit, delivers sermons, oracles, prophecies, and what Americans call "inspirational addresses," before returning to his normal consciousness. Although many such prophets are conscious frauds, others are sincere. Dr. Mason mentions a prophet who converted to Christianity. "He could not account for his former experiences, but said that it certainly seemed to him as though a spirit spoke, and he had to tell what it communicated." Dr. Mason also gives the following anecdote:

> ". . . Another individual had a familiar spirit that he consulted and spoke with; but, upon hearing the Gospel, he claimed to be converted and had no more communication with his spirit. It had left him, he said; it spoke to him no more. After a long trial, I baptized him. I watched his case with interest, and for several years he led an irreproachable Christian life; but, after losing his religious fervor and disagreeing with some of the church members, he moved to a distant village where he could not attend Sunday services. Soon after, it was reported that he was communicating with his familiar spirit again. I sent a native preacher to visit him. The man said he heard the voice that had spoken with him before, but it spoke very differently. Its language was very pleasant to hear and produced a great sense of remorse. It said, 'Love each other; act righteously—act uprightly,' along with other exhortations such as he had heard from the teachers. An assistant was placed in the village near him, at which point the spirit left him again; and ever since then, he has maintained the character of a consistent Christian."¹

This anecdote illustrates what is called by spiritists a "change of control." After receiving and then deserting Christian doctrine, the patient again spoke unconsciously, but under the influence of the faith which he had abandoned. In the same way, we shall find that a modern American "medium," after being for a time constantly in the society of educated and psychological observers, obtained new "controls" of a character more polite and civilized than her old "familiar spirit." <note>1 Hodgson, *Proceedings of the S.P.R.*, vol. xiii. pt. xxxiii. Dr. Hodgson by no means agrees with this view of the case—the case of Mrs. Piper.</note>

It is admitted that the possessed sometimes display an eloquence of which they are incapable in their normal condition. <note>2 *Primitive Culture* ii. 134.</note> In China, possessed women, who never composed a line of poetry in their normal lives, utter their thoughts in verse and are said to give evidence of clairvoyant powers. <note>3 Nevius’s *Demon Possession in China*, a curious collection of examples by an American missionary. The reports of Catholic missionaries are full of such cases.</note>

The book—*Demon Possession in China*—by Dr. Nevius, who was a missionary for forty years, was violently attacked by the medical journals of his native country, the United States. The doctor had the audacity to declare that he could find no better explanation of the phenomena than the theory of the Apostles—namely, that the patients were possessed. Not fearing the judgment of men, he also remarked that the current scientific explanations had the fault of not explaining anything.

For example, "Mr. Tylor suggests that all cases of supposed demoniacal possession are identical with hysteria, delirium, mania, and similar physical and mental derangements." Dr. Nevius, however, gave what he conceived to be the signs of possession, and, in his diagnosis,

Dr. Nevius then observed that, according to Mr. Tylor, "scientific physicians now explain the facts on a different principle," but, says Dr. Nevius, "we search in vain to discover what this principle is." <note>Cited previously, p. 16</note> Dr. Nevius, who had the courage of his convictions, then consulted a work titled *Nervous Derangement* by Dr. Hammond, a professor in the medical school of the University of New York. <note>Putnam, 1881.</note> He found this scientific physician admitting that we know very little about the matter. He knew—which is very gratifying—that "mind is the result of nervous action," and that so-called "possession" is the result of "material disorders of the organs or functions of the system."

Dr. Nevius was ready to admit this latter doctrine in cases of idiocy, insanity, epilepsy, and hysteria; but then, he said, these are not what I call possession. The Chinese have names for all these maladies, "which they ascribe to physical causes," but for possession they have a different name. He expected Dr. Hammond to account for the abnormal conditions in so-called possession, but "he has hardly even attempted to do this." Dr. Nevius next perused the works of Dr. Griesinger, Dr. Baelz, Professor William James, M. Ribot, and, generally, the literature of "alternating personality." He found Mr. James professing his conviction that the "alternating personality" (in popular terms, the demon or familiar spirit) of Mrs. Piper knew a great deal about things which Mrs. Piper, in her normal state, did not and could not know. Thus, after consulting many physicians, Dr. Nevius was no better off and returned to his faith in Diabolical Possession.

He was therefore informed that he had written "one of the most extraordinarily perverted books of the present day" based on the evidence of "transparent ghost stories"—which do not actually occur in his book.

Dr. Nevius's attitude cannot be called strictly scientific. Simply because pathologists and psychologists are unable to explain, or provide the *mechanism* (*modus*) of a set of phenomena, it does not follow that the devil, a god, or a ghost is involved in it.

But this, of course, was exactly the natural conclusion of primitive people.

Dr. Nevius lists the symptoms of possession as follows:

1. The automatic, persistent, and consistent acting out of a new personality, which calls itself <term>shieng</term> (genius) and calls the patient <term>hiang to</term> (incense burner, "medium").
2. Possession of knowledge and intellectual power not owned by the patient (in his normal state), nor explainable by the pathological hypothesis.
3. Complete change of moral character in the patient.

Of these points, the second would, of course, most confirm the primitive belief that a new intelligence had entered into the patient. If he displayed knowledge of the future, or of distant places, the conclusion that a new and wiser intelligence had taken possession of the patient's body would be, to the primitive mind, irresistible. But the more cautious modern person, *even if he accepted the facts*, would be forced to no such extreme conclusion. He would say that knowledge of distant space, or of the past, might be telepathically communicated to the brain of some living person; while, for knowledge of the future, he could resort, along with Hartmann, to contact with the Absolute.

But the question of evidence for the facts is, of course, the only real question. Now, in Dr. Nevius's book, this

# THE MAKING OF RELIGION

Evidence rests almost entirely on the written reports of native Christian teachers, for the Chinese were strictly secretive when questioned by Europeans. “My non-Christian brother, you have a sister who is demon-possessed?” asks the intelligent European. The reply of the non-Christian brother is best left in the obscurity of a remarkably difficult and extensive Oriental language. We are thus forced to rely on the reports of Mr. Leng and other native Christian teachers. They are perfectly modest and rational in style. We learn that Mrs. Sen, a lady who in her normal state was incapable of poetic efforts, spoke in verse in her secondary personality, and discovered the fact that Mr. Leng was on his way to see her when she could not have learned the fact in any normal way. <note>Nevius, p. 33.</note> “They are now crossing the stream, and will be here when the sun is about so high;” which was correct. The other witnesses were examined and confirmed this. <note>*Ibid.* p. 35.</note> Dr. Nevius himself examined Mrs. Kwo when she was possessed; she spoke in verse and was physically limp. <note>*Op. cit.* p. 38.</note>

The narratives are of this type; the patient, on recovering consciousness, knows nothing of what has occurred; Christian prayers are often effective, and there are many anecdotes of objects moving without being touched. <note>See “Fetishism and Spiritualism.”</note>

By a happy accident, as this chapter was passing through the press, a scientific account of a demon-possessed person and his cure was published by Dr. Pierre Janet. <note>*Névroses et Idées Fixes*. Alcan, Paris, 1898. This is the first of a series of works connected with the Laboratory of Psychology at the Salpêtrière in Paris.</note> Dr. Janet has explained, with complete success, everything regarding possession, except for the facts which, in the opinion of Dr. Nevius, were in need of explanation.

The facts in which he was interested did not present themselves in Dr. Janet’s patient, and so Dr. Janet does not explain them.

The simplest plan, here, is to deny that the facts in which Dr. Nevius believes ever present themselves at all; but, if they ever do, Dr. Janet’s explanation does not explain them.

1.  His patient, Achille, did not act out a new personality.
2.  Achille displayed no knowledge or intellectual power which he did not possess in his normal state.
3.  His moral character was not completely changed; he was only more hypochondriacal and hysterical than usual.

Achille was a poor devil of a French tradesman who, like Captain Booth, had violated the laws of strict chastity and virtue. He brooded on this until he became deranged and thought that Satan possessed him. He was convulsed, anesthetic, suicidal, and involuntarily blasphemous. He was not "exorcised" by a prayer or by a command, but after a long course of mental and physical treatment. His cure does not explain the cures in which Dr. Nevius believed. His case did not present the features for which Dr. Nevius asked science for an explanation. Dr. Janet’s essay is the *dernier cri* of science, and leaves Dr. Nevius just where it found him.

Science, therefore, can and does tell Dr. Nevius that his evidence for his facts is worthless, through the lips of Professor W. Romaine Newbold, in *Proceedings, S.P.R.*, February 1898 (pp. 602–604). And the same number of the same periodical shows us Dr. Hodgson

In China, ‘the professional woman sits at a table in contemplation, until the soul of a deceased person from whom communication is desired enters her body and talks through her to the living. . .’ ²

The latter account exactly describes Mrs. Piper. When consulted she passes through convulsions into a trance, after which she talks in a new voice, assumes a fresh personality, and claims to be possessed by the spirit of a French doctor (who does not know French)—Dr. Phinuit. She then displays a varying amount of knowledge of dead and living people connected with her clients, who are usually strangers, often introduced under feigned names. Mrs. Piper and her husband have been watched by detectives, and have not been discovered in any attempts to procure information. She was for some months in England under the charge of the S.P.R. Other ghosts, besides Dr. Phinuit—ghosts more civilized than he—now influence her, and her latest performances are said to exceed her former efforts.³

Volumes of evidence about Mrs. Piper have been published by Dr. Hodgson, who unmasked Madame Blavatsky and Eusapia Paladino.⁴ He was at first convinced that Mrs. Piper, in her condition of trance, obtains knowledge not otherwise and normally accessible to her. It was admitted that her familiar spirit guesses, attempts to extract information from the people who sit with her, and tries deceptively to conceal his failures. The limitations of her trance information, its discontinuity and fitfulness, and its apparent inability to develop beyond a certain point, although they end by arousing one's moral and human impatience with the phenomenon, yet are, from a scientific point of view, among its most interesting peculiarities, since where there are limits there are conditions, and the discovery of them is always the beginning of an explanation.

The binding may have originally been intended to keep the corpse, or ghost, from 'walking.' I do not know if Tahitian prophets were ever tied up to await inspiration. However, I suggest that the frequency of this primitive form of burial—where the corpse is tied up or swathed, sometimes with the head between the legs—and the recurring practice of similarly binding the sorcerer, probably points to an intention of introducing the seer to the society of the dead. The custom, as applied to prophets, might survive even where the burial rite has changed or cannot be determined; likewise, it might survive for corpses where it has fallen out of use for seers. The Scots used to justify their practice of placing the head between the knees—when, bound with a tether made of a corpse's hair, they learned to be second-sighted—by pointing to what Elijah did. The prophet, on the peak of Mount Carmel, 'cast himself down upon the earth, and put his face between his knees.'² But the cases are not identical. Elijah had been hearing a premonitory 'sound of a great rain' in a cloudless sky. He was probably engaged in prayer, not in prophecy.

Kirk, by the way, notes that if the wind changes while the Scottish seer is bound, he is in danger of losing his life. Similarly, children in Scotland are told that if the wind changes while they are making faces, the grimace will become permanent. In the same way, the seer will become what he pretends to be: a corpse.

## VIII

### FETISHISM AND SPIRITUALISM

It has been shown how the doctrine of souls was developed according to anthropological theory. The hypothesis regarding how the souls of the dead were later elevated to the rank of gods, or provided models after which such gods might be creatively fashioned, will be criticized in a later chapter. Here it must suffice to say that the conception of a separable, surviving soul of a dead man was not only not essential to the savage's idea of his supreme god, as it seems to me, but would have been wholly inconsistent with that conception. There exist, however, numerous forms of savage religion in addition to the belief in a Supreme Being, and these contribute their streams to the ocean of faith. Thus, among the kinds of belief that served in the development of Polytheism was Fetishism, which is itself an adaptation and extension of the idea of separable souls. In this regard, like ancestor-worship, it differs from the belief in a Supreme Being, which, as we shall try to demonstrate, is not derived from the theory of ghosts or souls at all.

*Fetish* (*fétiche*) seems to come from the Portuguese *feitiço*, a talisman or amulet, a term applied by the Portuguese to various material objects regarded by the West Africans of the coast with more or less religious reverence. These objects may be held sacred in some degree for a number of inconsistent reasons. They may be tokens, or may be of value in sympathetic magic, or merely odd, and therefore

For our present purpose, as Mr. Tylor says, "to classify an object as a fetish demands an explicit statement that a spirit is considered to be embodied in it, or acting through it, or communicating by it, or, at least, that the people it belongs to do habitually think this of such objects; or it must be shown that the object is treated as having personal consciousness or power, is talked with, worshipped . . ." and so forth. The indwelling spirit may be human, as when a fetish is made out of a friend’s skull, the spirit in which may even be asked for oracles, like the Head of Brân in Welsh legend.

We have tried to show that the belief in human souls may be, in part at least, based on supernormal phenomena which Materialism disregards. We shall now endeavor to make it probable that Fetishism (the belief in souls inhabiting inanimate objects) may also have sources which perhaps are not normal, or which at all events seemed supernormal to savages. We say "perhaps not normal" because the phenomena now to be discussed are of the most puzzling character. We may lean toward the belief in a supernormal cause of certain hallucinations, but the alleged movements of inanimate objects—which probably provide one origin of Fetishism and suggest the presence of a spirit in dead things—leave the inquiring mind in perplexity. We have seen a savage reason for supposing that human spirits inhabit certain lifeless things, such as skulls and other relics of the dead. But how did it come to be thought that a spirit dwelt in a lifeless and motionless piece of stone or wood? Mr. Tylor, perhaps, leads us to a plausible conjecture by writing: "Mr. Darwin saw two Malay women in Keeling Island, who held a wooden spoon dressed in clothes like a doll: this spoon had been carried to the grave of a dead man, and becoming inspired at full moon—in fact, lunatic—it danced about convulsively, like a table or a hat at a modern spirit séance."¹ Now, M. Lefébure has pointed out (in "*Mélusine*") that, according to De Brosses, African conjurers gave an appearance of independent motion to small objects, which were then accepted as fetishes because they were visibly animated. M. Lefébure next compares, as Mr. Tylor does, the alleged physical phenomena of spiritualism—the flights and movements of inanimate objects that are apparently untouched.

The question thus arises: Is there any truth at all in these worldwide and ancient stories of inanimate objects acting like living things? Does <term>fetishism</term> have one of its origins in the actual field of supernormal experience in the <term>X region</term>? We do not intend to answer this question, as the evidence, though practically universal, may be said to rest on deception and illusion. In Melanesia, far enough away, Dr. Codrington found a similar practice, and here the sticks are explicitly said by the natives to be moved by spirits.⁴ The wizard and a friend hold a bamboo stick by each end and ask which man's ghost is afflicting a patient. Among us, a ring is held by a thread over a tumbler, and our unconscious movements swing it until it strikes the hour. How the Karens manage it is less obvious. These savage devices with animated sticks clearly correspond to the more modern 'table-turning.' Here, when the players are honest, the pushing is certainly unconscious.

I have tested this in two ways—first, by trying the minimum of conscious muscular action that would stir a table at which I was alone, and by comparing the absolute unconsciousness of muscular action when the table began to move in response to no voluntary push. Again, I tried with a friend, who said, "You are pushing," when I gently removed my hands altogether, though they seemed to rest on the table, which still revolved. My friend was himself unconsciously pushing. It is undeniable that, to a solitary experimenter, the table *seems* to make little darts of its own will in a curious way. Thus, the unconsciousness of muscular action on the part of savages engaged in the experiment with sticks would lead them to believe that spirits were animating the wood. The same fallacy beset the table-turners of 1855–65 and was, to some extent, exposed by Faraday. Of course, savages would be even more convinced by the dancing spoon of Mr. Darwin's tale, by the dancing sticks of the Zulus, and the rest, whether the phenomena were supernormal or merely worked by unseen strings. The same remark applies to modern experimenters when, as they declare, various objects move untouched, without physical contact.

The best-known modern study on the divining rod is that of M. Chevreul, *La Baguette Divinatoire* (1854). We also have *L’Histoire du Merveilleux dans les Temps Modernes* by M. Figuier (1860). The case of Jacques Aymard, who in the seventeenth century discovered a murderer by using the rod in a truly primitive manner, is well known. In modern England, the rod is used on behalf of private individuals and public institutions (such as Trinity College, Cambridge) to find water.

Professor Barrett has recently published a book of 280 pages in which evidence of both failures and successes is collected.<sup>1</sup> Professor Barrett provides about one hundred and fifty cases, and from reliable sources, he was only able to find twelve failures. He offers a variety of tests designed to detect fraud and chance coincidence, and he publishes the opinions of geologists, whether they are critical or skeptical. Generally, the evidence is what other investigations consider "first-hand." The actual witnesses—often the landowners or the people who needed the water—having been present, provide their testimony. It is certain that the "diviner" is hired by sensible and educated people who are usually too practical to care for theories; they are simply satisfied to get what they want, especially when scientific experts have failed.<sup>2</sup>

In Mr. Barrett’s opinion, the subconscious perception of indications of the presence of water produces an equally unconscious muscular ‘spasm,’ which twists the rod until it often breaks. Yet ‘it is almost impossible to imitate its characteristic movement by any voluntary effort.’ I have myself held the hands of an amateur performer when the twig was moving, and neither by sight nor touch could I detect any muscular movement on his part, much less a spasm. The person was a bailiff on a large estate, and, having accidentally discovered that he possessed the gift, used it when he wanted wells dug for the tenants on the property.

The whole topic is obscure; nor am I concerned here with the successes or failures of the divining rod. But the movements of the twig have never, to my knowledge, been attributed by modern English performers to the operation of spirits. They say ‘electricity.’ Mr. Tylor merely writes:

> ‘The action of the famous divining rod, with its curiously versatile sensitivity to water, ore, treasure, and thieves, seems to belong partly to trickery and partly to more or less conscious direction by more honest operators.’

As the divining rod is the only instance in which automatism—whatever its nature and causes—has been found to be of practical value by practical men, and as it is obviously associated with a number of analogous phenomena, in both civilized and savage life, it certainly deserves the attention of science. But no advance will be made until scientifically trained inquirers themselves arrange and test a large number of experiments. It is worth noting cases in which the rod acts like those of the Melanesians, Africans, and other primitive peoples. A Mr. Thomas Welton published an English translation of ‘La Verge de Jacob’ (Lyon, 1693). In 1851, he asked his servant to bring a stick into the garden that "stood behind the parlor door. In great terror she brought it to the garden, her hand firmly clutching it, and she could not let it go." When Mrs. Welton took the stick, "it drew her with very considerable speed toward nearly the center of the garden," where a well was found. Mr. Welton is unlikely to have known about the recently published examples from primitive cultures. Therefore, the coincidence with the African and Melanesian cases is probably unintentional.

Again, in 1694, the rod was used by Father Menestrier and others, just as it is by primitive peoples, to indicate answers to all sorts of questions through its movements. Experiments of this kind have not been conducted by Professor Barrett or other modern researchers, except by Monsieur Richet, as a way to detect automatic action. But it would be just as sensible to use the twig as it is to use a *planchette* or any other "autoscopic" apparatus. If these tools reveal knowledge unconsciously present in the mind, then simple water-finding should not be the rod's only domain. In the same class as these rods is the forked twig which, in China, is held at each end by two people and made to write in the sand. The little apparatus called a *planchette*, or the other, the *ouija*, is, of course, consciously or unconsciously pushed by the participants. In the case of the twig, as held by water-seekers, the difficulty of moving it consciously while escaping close observation is significant.

The point here is simply the practice of automatism in both civilized and primitive societies—the apparent uncovering of knowledge that is not otherwise accessible through the movements of a stick or a piece of wood. These movements, made without conscious effort or direction, seem to primitive philosophy to be caused by indwelling spirits, which are the sources of Fetishism.

No more than any other theory—indeed, less than some other theories—can it account for the psychical facts which, at the very least, we cannot honestly leave out of our consideration.

We have, therefore, no more to say about the supernormal aspects of the origins of religion. From now on, we are concerned with matters of verifiable belief and practice. We must ask whether, once the <term>doctrine of souls</term> was conceived by early humans, it took precisely the course of development usually indicated by anthropological science.

## IX

### *EVOLUTION OF THE IDEA OF GOD*

To the anthropological philosopher, a ‘plain man’ would naturally pose the question: ‘Having derived your idea of spirit or soul—your theory of Animism—from the idea of ghosts, and having derived your idea of ghosts from dreams and visions, how do you arrive at the Idea of God?’ By ‘God,’ the proverbial ‘plain man’ of controversy means a primal, eternal Being, the author of all things, the father and friend of man, the invisible, omniscient guardian of morality.

The common, though not invariable, reply of the anthropologist might be given in the words of Mr. Everard im Thurn, author of a most interesting work on the Indians of British Guiana:

> ‘From the notion of ghosts,’ says Mr. im Thurn, ‘a belief has arisen, but very gradually, in higher spirits, and eventually in a Highest Spirit; and, keeping pace with the growth of these beliefs, a habit of reverence for, and worship of, spirits. . . . The Indians of Guiana know no God.’ <note>1</note>

As another example of Mr. im Thurn’s hypothesis—that God is a late development from the idea of spirit—one may cite Mr. Payne’s scholarly ‘History of the New World,’ a work of much research: <note>2</note>

> ‘The lowest savages not only have no gods, but do not even recognize those lower beings usually called spirits,

On this theory, ‘the lowest savages’ are devoid of the idea of god or of spirit. Later they develop the idea of spirit, and when they have secured the spirit, as it were, in a tangible object and kept it on board wages <note>maintained with regular offerings of food and drink</note>, then the spirit has attained the dignity, and the savage the conception, of a god. But while a god of this kind is, in Mr. Payne’s opinion, a relatively late development of culture—for the hunting races generally (with some exceptions) have no gods—yet ‘the conception of a creator or maker of all things . . . obviously a great spirit’ is ‘one of the earliest efforts of primitive logic.’ <note>1</note>

Mr. Payne’s own logic is not very clear. The ‘primitive logic’ of the savage leads him to seek a cause or maker of things, which he finds in a great creative spirit. Based on theories such as these, the belief in a moral Supreme Being is a very late (or perhaps very early?) result of evolution, caused by the influence of advancing thought on the original concept of ghosts. This opinion held by Mr. Im Thurn is, broadly speaking, the standard theory among anthropologists. On the other hand, we wish to show that the idea of God—as conceived by an inquisitive ordinary person—appears in a crude but recognizable form in the lowest known levels of savagery. Therefore, it cannot arise from the later speculations of relatively civilized and advanced people based on the original data of ghosts. We shall demonstrate, contrary to the opinions of Mr. Spencer, Mr. Huxley, and even Mr. Tylor, that the Supreme Being—and in at least one instance, the occasional spirits of primitive faith—are active moral influences. <note>The phrase "are active moral influences" is underlined in pencil.</note> What is even more important, we shall make it undeniable that anthropology has simplified its problem by neglecting or ignoring the facts. While the real problem is to explain how the eternal, creative, moral god of the "ordinary person" evolved from ghosts, anthropologists either deny the existence of such a god or being in the beliefs of the lowest savages, ignore it, explain it with theories contradicted by facts, or, at best, explain it away as a result of European or Islamic influences. Now, since the problem is to explain the evolution of the highest conception of God—as far as that concept exists among the most backward races—the problem can never be solved while that highest conception of God is practically ignored.

Mr. Tylor—even though his great work is admittedly much more concerned with the development of the idea of spirit and with the lower forms of animism than with the real *crux*—that is, the evolution of the idea (often obscured by mythology) of a moral, uncreated, undying God among the lowest savages. This neglect by anthropologists has arisen from a single circumstance: they take it for granted that God is always regarded as a Spirit (except in cases where the word for God is applied to a living human being). Thus, having explained the development of the idea of spirit, they regard God as that idea carried to its highest power and as the final step in its evolution. But, if we can show that the early idea of an eternal, moral, creative being does not necessarily or logically imply the doctrine of spirit, then this idea of an eternal, moral, creative being may have existed even before the doctrine of spirit was developed.

We may admit that Mr. Tylor’s account of the process by which gods were evolved from ghosts is a little *touffu* <note>French for "dense" or "overgrown."</note>—rather buried in facts. We "can scarcely see the forest for the trees." We want to know how gods—as makers of things (or most things), fathers in heaven, friends, and guardians of morality who see what is good or bad in the hearts of men—were supposedly evolved out of ghosts or the surviving souls of the dead. We shall demonstrate that such moral, practically all-knowing gods are known to even the lowest savages—Bushmen, Fuegians, and Australians.

Here the inquirer must be careful not to adopt the common opinion that gods improve, morally and otherwise, in direct proportion to the rising levels of culture and civilization. Very well; but where does the great God come from among tribes that have no chief, king, or any distinction of rank, such as the Fuegians, Bushmen, and Australians? The maker and ruler of the world known to these races cannot be the shadow of a king or chief, reflected and magnified through the mist of thought; for these people have no chief or king. This theory (Hume’s) does not work where people have a great God but no king or chief; nor where they have a king but no Zeus or other supreme King-god, as is the case among the Aztecs.

In Mr. Tylor’s theory, we now reach great fetish deities, such as Heaven and Earth, Sun and Moon, and ‘departmental deities’—gods of agriculture, war, and so forth—which are unknown to lower savages.

Or, again, a great phenomenon or force in nature worship—such as the Sun or Heaven—is raised to a position of supremacy. Or speculative philosophy rises from the many to the one by trying to perceive a First Cause through and beyond the universe. Animistic concepts thus reach their furthest limit in the idea of the *Anima Mundi* <note>the Soul of the World</note>. This being may gather all the powers of all polytheistic gods, or he may "loom vast, shadowy, and calm . . . too benevolent to need human worship . . . too merely existent to concern himself with the petty race of men."¹ But he is always animistic.

Now, besides the objections already mentioned in passing, how can we tell that the Supreme Being of primitive peoples was, in its original conception, animistic at all? How can we know that he was originally envisioned as *Spirit*? We shall show that he probably was not; that the question of "spirit or not spirit" was never raised at all. Instead, the Maker and Father in Heaven, prior to the concept of Death, was merely regarded as a deathless *Being*, with no question of "spirit" being raised. If so, animism was not needed for the earliest idea of a moral Eternal being. This hypothesis will lead to some very remarkable conclusions. The notion of a God about whose spirituality nobody has inquired is new to us. To ourselves, and doubtless or probably to people on a certain level of culture, such a Divine Being must be animistic—that is, he must be a "spirit." To take only one case, to which we shall return, the Banks Islanders (Melanesia) believe in ghosts, "and in the existence of Beings who were not, and never had been, human. All alike might be called spirits," says Dr. Codrington; but, *ex hypothesi* <note>according to the hypothesis</note>, the Beings "who never were human" are only called "spirits" by us because our habits of thought do not enable us to envision them *except* as "spirits." They never were men; "the natives will always maintain that he (the *Vui*) was something different, and deny to him the fleshly body of a man," while remaining resolute that he was not a *ghost*.¹

This point will be amply illustrated later, as we study that strangely neglected chapter—that essential chapter—the higher beliefs of the lowest savages. Regarding the existence of a belief in a Supreme Being (not as merely "alleged"), there is as good evidence as we possess for any fact in the ethnographic region.

It is certain that when first approached by curious travelers and missionaries, savages have again and again recognized our God in theirs.

Now, first, there would be nothing strange about the matter if the basic idea of a "Universal Power" came first and was partially replaced by a later practice of worshipping the dead and ghosts. The new religious idea would soon reflect back on the older concept and influence it through its rituals. And, secondly, it is precisely this "Universal Power" that is *not* worshipped with food offerings in places like Tonga (despite what Mr. Huxley says), Australia, and Africa, for example. We cannot avoid the difficulty by saying that in those places, the old spirit of a Universal Power is seen as dead, weak, or as a *roi fainéant* <note>A "do-nothing king"; a ruler who possesses a title but lacks any real power or authority.</note> not worth worshipping. That is not true of a being who punishes sin, teaches selflessness, and is the sole guardian of trust between individuals and nations.

<margin>1 2 3 [horizontal mark] [arrow/checkmark]</margin>
It seems, then, on the whole, that the question an ordinary person asks the anthropologist—"Once you have introduced the idea of a spirit into the mind of a primitive person, how does he develop that into what I call God?"—has not been answered. God cannot be a reflection of human kings in societies where there are no kings. He cannot be a president chosen from a society of many gods where polytheism does not yet exist. He cannot be an idealized first ancestor where people do not worship their ancestors. Furthermore, the spirit of a person who has died—whether real or imaginary—does not fit the usual primitive concept of the Creator. All of this will become much clearer as we examine the highest gods of the most primitive peoples in detail.

Of course, our study does not claim to cover the religion of every primitive group in the world. We are satisfied with using typical and generally well-documented examples. Our scope ranges from the beliefs of the most underdeveloped and poorly equipped nomadic groups to those of societies with aristocracies, hereditary kings, permanent housing, and agriculture, concluding with the Supreme Being of the highly civilized Incas and the Jehovah of the Hebrews.

## X

### *HIGH GODS OF LOW RACES*

To avoid misunderstanding, we must repeat the necessary warnings about accepting evidence regarding the high gods of primitive peoples. A missionary who does not see a demon in every foreign god is likely to welcome signs of an original supernatural revelation—one supposedly obscured by all peoples except the Jews. However, we will not rely much on missionary evidence; when we do, we must be equally on our guard against the anthropological bias within the missionary himself. Having read the works of Mr. Spencer and Mr. Tylor, and finding himself among ancestor-worshippers (as he sometimes does), he is inclined to think that ancestor-worship explains any traces of a belief in a Supreme Being. We must remain vigilant against each and every bias held by observers.

It may also be necessary to point out once again another weak point in all reasoning about primitive religion: namely, that we cannot always determine what may have been borrowed from Europeans. For example, the Fuegians, between 1830 and 1840, were in a very remote location, yet one tribe near the Strait of Magellan worshipped an image called *Cristo*. Fitzroy attributes this obvious trace of Catholicism to a Captain Pelippa, who visited the district some time before his own expedition. It is less probable that Spaniards established a belief in a moral Deity in regions where they left no physical traces of their faith. The Fuegians are not easily converted.

How, then, the Fuegians—who are not proved to be ancestor-worshippers—evolved a being whose strong point is morality out of the malignant ghost of an ancestor, is not easily conceived. The adjacent Chonos ‘have great faith in a good spirit, whom they call Yerri Yuppon, and consider to be the author of all good; him they invoke in distress or danger.’ However starved they may be, they do not touch food until a short prayer has been muttered over each portion, ‘the praying man looking upward.’² They have magicians, but no details are given as to spirits or ghosts. Indeed, Mr. Spencer has suggested that the remarkably complex marriage customs of the Australian Aborigines point to a more refined state in their past history. Of this stage, as we have said, no material traces have ever been discovered, nor can any degeneration be recent. Our earliest account of the Australians is from Dampier, who visited New Holland in the unfortunate year 1688. He found the natives to be "the most miserable people in the world. The <term>Hodmadods</term> <note>A term used by Dampier for the Hottentots.</note> of Monomatapa, though a wretched people, are yet like gentlemen compared to these in terms of wealth; for these people have no houses, sheep, poultry, or fruits of the earth. . . . They have no houses, but lie in the open air." Curiously enough, Dampier testifies to their *unselfishness*, which is the main ethical feature in their religious teaching. "Whether they get a little or a lot, everyone has their share—the young and delicate as well as the old and feeble, who are unable to go out, and the strong and vigorous." Dampier saw no metals used, nor any bows, but only boomerangs ("wooden cutlasses") and lances with points hardened in the fire. "Their place of dwelling was only a fire with a few boughs before it" (the *gunyeh*).

This description remains accurate for most of the traditional Australian tribes, but Dampier appears only to have seen <term>ichthyophagous</term> coastal people.

There is one more important point. In the Bora, or Australian mysteries—during which knowledge of "The Maker" and his commandments is shared—the front teeth of those being initiated are still knocked out. Now, Dampier observed that "the two front teeth of their upper jaw are missing in all of them: men and women, old and young." If this is to be taken quite literally, the Bora rite, in 1688, must have included the women, at least locally. Dampier was on the north-west coast at latitude 16 degrees, longitude 122 1/4 degrees east (Dampier Land, Western Australia). The natives had neither boats, canoes, nor bark logs; but it seems that they had their religious mysteries and their unselfishness two hundred years ago.¹

The Australians have been very carefully studied by many observers, and the results entirely disprove Mr. Huxley’s bold statement that "in its simplest form, such as may be found among the Australian savages, theology is merely a belief in the existence, powers, and nature (usually malicious) of ghost-like entities who may be appeased or scared away; but no actual religious cult can be said to exist. And at this stage, theology is completely separate from ethics."

Statements more bluntly in contradiction of known facts could not be made. The Australians certainly believe in "spirits," which are often malicious and probably regarded in most cases as the ghosts of men. These aid the medicine man and occasionally inspire him. It does not appear that these ghosts are worshipped, and this is denied by Waitz. Furthermore, regarding religious practice, "there is none" in the form of sacrifice to higher gods, as would be expected if these gods were hungry ghosts. The religious practice among the Australians is the worship of the heart, expressed in moral teaching, supposed to be in conformity with the principles
