Indeed, he goes on at once to remark that "*Darumulun* was not, it seems to me, everywhere thought a malevolent being, but he was feared as one who could severely punish those who violated the tribal laws and customs that he was believed to have established."

Punishing violations of his law does not make him a malevolent being by nature. Darumulun "watched the youths from the sky, ready to punish any violation of his laws—whether moral or ritual—with disease or death." His name is so sacred that it is only spoken in whispers, and the anthropologist will note that the names of the deceased are often also forbidden to be spoken. However, the divine name is not restricted or sacred in this way when simple folklore about him is being told. Mr. Howitt’s informants instinctively distinguished between the mythology and the religion of Darumulun.¹ This distinction—the secrecy surrounding the religion versus the openness about the mythology—is crucial, and it explains why we know so little about the inner religious beliefs of early peoples. Mr. Howitt himself knew very little until he was initiated. Before the *white men arrived in Melbourne*, the grandfather of Mr. Howitt’s friend took him out at night and, pointing to a star, said: "You will soon be a man; you see Bunjil <note>the Supreme Being of certain tribes</note> up there, and he can see you and everything you do down here." Mr. Palmer, discussing the Mysteries of Northern Australians (ceremonies performed under divine authority), describes the nature of the moral instruction given. Each boy receives "from one of the elders, advice so kindly, fatherly, and impressive that it often softens his heart and brings him to tears." He

During the Mysteries, Darumulun’s real name may be spoken; at other times, he is called ‘Master’ (*Biamban*) or ‘Father’ (*Papang*), exactly as we say ‘Lord’ and ‘Father.’

It is known that all these things are not due to missionaries, whose instructions would certainly not be conveyed in the *Bora*, or tribal mysteries, which, again, are partly described by Collins as early as 1798, and must have been practiced in 1688. Mr. Howitt mentions, among moral lessons divinely sanctioned, respect for old age, abstinence from lawless love, and avoidance of the sins so popular, poetic, and sanctioned by the example of gods in classical Greece.² A representation is made of the Master, Biamban; and to make such idols, except during the Mysteries, is forbidden ‘under pain of death.’ Those which are made are destroyed as soon as the rites are ended.³ The future life (apparently) is then illustrated by the burial of a living elder, who rises from a grave. This may, however, symbolize the ‘new life’ of the *Mystae* <note>initiates into the sacred mysteries</note>, ‘Worse have I fled; better have I found,’ as was sung in an Athenian rite. The whole result is, by what Mr. Howitt calls ‘a quasi-religious element,’ to ‘impress upon the mind of the youth, in an indelible manner, those rules of conduct which form the moral law of the tribe.’⁴

Many other authorities could be cited for the religious sanction of morals in Australia. An all-knowing being observes and rewards the conduct of men; he is named with reverence, if named at all; his home is the heavens; he is the Maker and Lord of things; his lessons ‘soften the heart.’⁵

The lads about to be initiated (that is, if they have been associating with Christians) are encouraged to expel selfishness and greed. The chief rite, later, is to blindfold every lad with a blanket closely drawn over his head, to make whirring sounds with the *tundun*, or Greek *rhombos*, then to pluck off the blankets and bid the initiates raise their faces to the sky. The initiator points to it, calling out, "Look there, look there, look there!" In this solemn way, they have seen the home of the Supreme Being, "Our Father," Mungun-ngaur (*Mungun* = "Father," *ngaur* = "our"), whose doctrine is then unfolded by the old initiator ("headman") "in an impressive manner."¹ "Long ago there was a great Being, Mungun-ngaur, who lived on the earth." His son Tundun is the direct ancestor of the Kurnai. Mungun initiated the rites and destroyed the earth with water when they were impiously revealed. "Mungun left the earth and ascended to the sky, where he still remains."

Here Mungun-ngaur—a Being not defined as a spirit, but immortal and dwelling in heaven—is the Father, or rather grandfather, not the creator, of the Kurnai. This *may* be interpreted as ancestor worship, but the opposite myth of making or creating is told by the Narrinyeri, Boonorong, Wolgal, Ngarego, Theddora, Coast Murring, and Wiraijuri, who are worshippers of Darumulun. His precepts are:

1. *To obey the old.* (Fifth Commandment.)
2. *To share all with their friends.* (Do to others as you would have others do to you.)
3. *To live peaceably with their friends.*
4. *To not interfere with girls or married women.* (Seventh Commandment.)
5. *To obey the food restrictions.* (Leviticus, *throughout.*)

...no longer be maintained that the Australians have no belief which can be called religious—that is, in the sense of beliefs which govern tribal and individual morality under a supernatural sanction." On this topic, Mr. Howitt’s opinion became more affirmative the more deeply he was initiated.<note>Journal of the Anthropological Institute, volume 13, page 459. The Australians are considered the lowest, most primitive savages, yet no propitiation through food is made to their moral Ruler in heaven, as if he were a ghost.

The laws of these Australian divine beings apply to ritual as well as to ethics, as might naturally be expected. But the moral element is prominent, and the reverence is clear: we have here no mere ghost, appeased by food or sacrifice, or by purely magical rites. His very image (modeled on a large scale in the earth) is no common idol; to create such a thing, except on rare sacred occasions, is a capital offense. Meanwhile, the mythology of the God is treated as a kind of joke, with no sacredness about it.

On the whole, it is evident that Mr. Herbert Spencer, for example, underrates the nature of Australian religion. He cites a case of someone addressing the ghost of a man who recently died, asking him not to bring sickness "or make loud noises in the night," and says: "Here we may recognize the essential elements of a cult." But Mr. Spencer does not allude to the much more essentially religious elements which he might have found in the very authority whom he cites, Mr. Brough Smyth.<note>Ecclesiastical Institutions, page 674.</note> This appears, as far as my scrutiny goes, to be Mr. Spencer’s only reference to Australia in his work *Ecclesiastical Institutions*. Yet the facts which he and Mr. Huxley ignore shed a light very different from theirs on what they consider "the simplest condition of theology."

<meta>This page continues the argument that the religious beliefs of the Australian Aborigines, despite their low material culture, contain high ethical concepts of a supreme being that are often overlooked by anthropologists.</meta>

<page-num>198</page-num>
<header>THE MAKING OF RELIGION</header>

Among the causes of confusion in thinking about religion, Mr. Tylor mentions "the partial and one-sided application of the historical method of inquiry into theological doctrines."¹ Here, perhaps, we see some examples.

In its highest aspect, that "simplest theology" of Australia is free from the flaws of popular theology in Greece. The God discourages sin; he does not set an example of sinning. He is almost too sacred to be named (except in mythology) and far too sacred to be represented by idols. He is not moved by sacrifice—he is never given the opportunity; like Death in Greece, "he alone, of all the Gods, does not love gifts." Thus, the status of theology does not correspond to the status of material and intellectual culture. It would hardly be a paradox to say that the popular Zeus or Ares is a degenerate version of Darumulun, or of the Fuegian being who forbids the slaying of an enemy and almost literally "marks the sparrow’s fall."

If we knew all the mythology of Darumulun, we would probably find it (like much of the myth of Pundjel or Bunjil) to be on a very different level than the theology. There are two currents—the religious and the mythical—flowing together through religion. The former current, the religious one, even among very primitive people, is free from the magical habit of appeasing ghosts. The latter current, the mythological one, is full of magic, empty rituals, and scandalous legends. Sometimes the second stream completely pollutes the first; sometimes they flow side by side, perfectly distinguishable, as in Aztec ethical piety compared with bloody Aztec ritualism. Anthropology has mainly kept its eyes fixed on the impure stream—the lusts, rituals, conjuring, and frauds of priesthoods—while relatively or entirely neglecting (as we have shown) what is honest and reputable.

The worse side of religion is the less sacred part, and therefore it is more obvious. Both elements—the sacred and the profane—coexist in almost all races. Because we completely lack historical information about religious origins, no one can say which element came first, or if one was derived from the other. It is an attractive and seemingly logical idea to suggest that the appeasement of corpses and then of ghosts came first; this idea appeals to certain writers who are biased against all religion, viewing it as an unscientific superstition. But we know very little! The first missionaries in Greenland initially thought there was no trace of belief in a Divine Being there. "But when they came to understand their language better, they found quite the opposite to be true . . . and not only that, but they could clearly gather from a free conversation they had with some completely wild Greenlanders (at a time when they were avoiding any direct appeal to their emotions) that their ancestors must have believed in a Supreme Being and performed some service for him, which their descendants gradually neglected . . ." <note>Cranz, pp. 198, 199.</note> Mr. Tylor does not refer to this as a trace of Christian Scandinavian influence on the Eskimo. <note>*Journal of the Anthropological Institute* xiii. 348–356.</note>

He then stated the argument from design: "Certainly there must be some Being who made all these things. He must be very good too . . . Oh, if I only knew him, how I would love and honor him." # XI

## SUPREME GODS NOT NECESSARILY DEVELOPED OUT OF ‘SPIRITS’

<margin>Two sources of religion</margin>
Before going on to examine the high gods of other low-status groups, I must here again insist on and develop the theory—which is not easily conceived by us—that the Supreme Being of such people belongs to another branch of faith than ghosts, ghost-gods, fetishes, or Totems, and need not be—and probably is not—essentially derived from these. We must try to get rid of our theory that a powerful, moral, eternal Being was, from the start, *ex officio* (by virtue of his position), conceived as a "spirit," and so was necessarily derived from a ghost.

First, what was the process of development?
We have examined Mr. Tylor’s theory. But, to take a practical case: here are the Australians, roaming in small bands, without more formal rulers than "headmen" at most; they are not ancestor worshippers; they are not polytheists; they have no departmental deities to select and elevate; and they are not inclined to speculate on the *Anima Mundi* (the World Soul). How, then, did they bridge the gap between the ghost of a soon-forgotten fighting man and that conception of a Father in Heaven—omniscient and moral—which, under various names, is found all over a huge continent? I cannot see that this problem has been solved or even frankly faced.

The distinction between the creative, all-seeing, undecaying Australian deity, who is not appeased by sacrifice, and the ordinary, fading, easily forgotten, and cheaply appeased

Mr. Jevons has pointed out that, before you can hail a man as a god, you must already have the idea of God. The murder of Captain Cook notoriously resulted from a scientific experiment in theology: "If he is a god, he cannot be killed." So they tried with a dagger, and found that the honest captain was but a mortal British mariner—no god at all. "There are degrees." Mr. Spencer's man-gods become real gods—after death.¹

<margin>(analytical</margin>
Now the Supreme Being of primitive faith, as a rule, never died at all. He belonged to a world that did not know Death.

One cause of our blindness to this point appears to be this: we have from childhood been taught that "God is a Spirit." We, now, can only conceive of an eternal being as a "spirit." We know that legions of primitive gods are now regarded as spirits. And therefore we have never noticed that there is no reason why we should take it for granted that the earliest deities of the first men were supposed by them to be "spirits" at all. not as "spirits," but as "undefined eternal beings." To us, such a being is necessarily a spirit, but he was by no means necessarily so to an early thinker, who may not yet have reached the concept of a ghost.

<margin>Eden</margin>
Anthropologists say that a ghost developed into a god. Now, the very idea of a ghost (distinct from a wraith or fetch) implies the previous death of its owner. A ghost is the phantasm of a dead person. But anthropologists often tell us, and truthfully, that the idea of death as a universal law is unknown to the primitive person. They think diseases and death are things that once did not exist and that, normally, should not occur. In their opinion, these are caused supernaturally by magicians and spirits. Death came into the world by a blunder, an accident, a ritual error, or a decision by a god who existed before death did. Scores of myths are told everywhere on this subject.¹

The primitive Supreme Being, with added power, omniscience, and morality, is the primitive person's idealization of themselves, as they conceive it, *minus* a physical body (as a rule) and *minus* death. He is not necessarily a "spirit," though that term may now be applied to him. He was not originally distinguished as "spirit" or "not spirit." He is a Being, conceived without the question of "spirit" or "no spirit" even being raised; perhaps he was originally conceived before that question could even be raised by men. When we call the Supreme Being of primitive peoples a "spirit," we introduce our own animistic ideas into a concept where they may not have originally existed. Arnold might as well have said: "The British Philistine has no knowledge of God. He believes that the Creator is a magnified non-natural man, living in the sky." The Gippsland, Fuegian, or Blackfoot Supreme Being is just a *Being*—anthropomorphic, but not a <term>mrart</term> or "spirit." The Supreme Being is a <term>wesen</term> (Being) or <term>Vui</term>; we hardly have a term for an immortal existence so undefined. In the original conception, he is a powerful intelligence who existed from the beginning: who was already active long before death entered the world through a breach of his laws, an error in the delivery of a message, a breach of ritual, or some other cause. He was not affected by the entry of death; he still exists.

Modern minds need to become familiar with this indeterminate idea of the primitive Supreme Being, which, logically, may be prior to the evolution of the notion of a ghost or spirit.

But how does it apply when, as among the Kurnai, the Supreme Being is considered an ancestor?

It can very readily be shown that, when the Supreme Being of a primitive people is thus the idealized First Ancestor, he can never have been envisioned by his worshippers as a *ghost* at any time; or, at least, he cannot logically have been so envisioned where the nearly universal belief occurs that death came into the world by accident or needlessly.

Adam is the mythical first ancestor of the Hebrews, but he died, <term>ὑπὲρ μόρον</term> <note>Greek: "beyond what is ordained by fate"</note>, and was not worshipped. Yama, the first of the Aryan men who died, was worshipped by the Vedic Aryans, but admittedly as a ghost-god. Mr. Tylor gives a list of deified first ancestors. The Ancestor of the Mandans did not die and, consequently, is no ghost; <term>emigravit</term>, he "moved west." Where the First Ancestor is

<margin>✓</margin>
Now, ghost-worship and the worship of dead ancestors are impossible before the ancestor is dead and has become a ghost. But the essential idea of Darumulun, Baiame, and most of the high gods of Australia and of other primitive races, is that *they never died at all*. They belong to the period before death came into the world, like Qat among the Melanesians. They arise in an age that did not know death, and had not reflected on phantasms nor developed the idea of ghosts. They could have been conceived of, by the very nature of the case, by a race of immortals who never dreamed of such a thing as a ghost. For these gods, the ghost-theory is not required; it is superfluous and even contradictory. The early thinkers who developed these beings did not need to know that men die (though, of course, they did know it in practice), and even less did they need to have conceived the hypothesis of ghosts through abstract speculation. Baiame, Cagn, and Bunjil, in their worshippers' belief, were *there*: death later intruded among men, but it did not affect these divine beings in any way.

The ghost-theory, therefore, by the evidence of anthropology itself, is not needed for the evolution of the high gods of primitive peoples. It is only needed for the evolution of

The explicitly stated distinction that the high creative gods were never mortal men, while other gods are the spirits of mortal men, is made everywhere. "Ancestors known to be human were not worshipped as [original] gods, and ancestors worshipped as [original] gods were not believed to have been human."<note>Jevons, *Introduction*, p. 197.</note>

Both kinds may have a generic name, such as *kalou* or *wakan*, but this specific distinction is universally made by primitive peoples. On one hand are the original gods; on the other are non-original gods who were once ghosts. Now, this distinction is often calmly ignored; whereas, when any race has developed (like the later Scandinavians) the Euhemeristic hypothesis ("all gods were once men"), that hypothesis is accepted as an historical statement of fact by some writers.

It is part of my theory that the more popular ghost-worship—the souls of people whom men have loved—invaded the possibly older religion of the Supreme Father. Mighty beings, whether originally conceived of as "spirits" or not, later came to be regarded as spirits under the <term>Animistic theory</term>. They even (though not among the most primitive groups) came to be appeased by food and sacrifice. Once <term>Animism</term> prevailed, the alternative for a <term>Supreme Being</term> was either sacrifice (as with more popular ghost deities) or neglect. "The common doctrine of the Old Testament is not that God is a spirit, but that the spirit [*rûah* = 'wind,' 'living breath'] of Jehovah, going forth from him, works in the world and among men."<note>Robertson Smith, *The Prophets of Israel*, p. 61.</note>

To resume: the high gods of primitive societies—moral, all-seeing directors of things and of men—are not explicitly envisioned as spirits at all by their worshippers. The notion of a soul or spirit is out of place here. We can best describe Darumulun, Nàpi, and Baiame as "magnified non-natural men," or undefined beings who existed from the beginning and are eternal. They are, like the indifferent Epicurean gods, *nihil indiga nostri* (needing nothing from us). Because they are not ghosts, they do not crave food from men and receive no sacrifice, as ghosts do, or as gods do who developed out of ghosts, or gods to whom ghost-rituals have been transferred. For this very reason, apparently, Mr. Grant Allen speaks of them as "gods to talk about, not gods to adore; mythological concepts rather than religious beings."<note>*Evolution of the Idea of God*, p. 176.</note> All of this is rather hard on the most primitive people. If they sacrifice to a god, then the god is considered a hungry ghost; if they do not, then the god is "a god to talk about, not to adore." Fortunately, the facts of the <term>Bora ritual</term> and the instruction given there prove that Darumulun and other names refer to gods to adore—through ethical conformity to their will and through solemn ceremony—not merely gods to talk about.

Thus, the highest element in the religion of the most primitive people does not appear to be derived from their theory of ghosts. It is logically conceivable that primitive peoples may have worshipped deities like Baiame and Darumulun before they had developed the notion that Tom, Dick, or Harry has a separable soul, capable of surviving his physical death. Deities of the higher sort—by the very nature of early reflections on death and on its non-original, accidental character—are prior, or may be prior, or cannot be shown not to be prior, to the ghost theory, which is the alleged origin of religion. The ghost theory is not logically required for their evolution; they can exist without it. Yet they—and not the spirits, bogles, Mrarts, *Brewin*, and so forth—are the high gods; the gods who have the most in common (as creators, moral guides, and rewarders and punishers of conduct, though that duty is also occasionally assumed by ancestral spirits) with our civilized conception of the divine. **Our conception of God does not descend from ghosts, but from the Supreme Beings of peoples who do not worship ancestors.**

As it seems impossible to identify any method by which primitive, leaderless, non-polytheistic, and non-metaphysical peoples (if any such exist) evolved the eternal beings who made the world and watch over morality out of ghosts—and as the people themselves unanimously distinguish such beings from ghost-gods—I conclude that such beings were never ghosts. In this case, the Animistic theory seems to me to break down completely. Yet these high gods of primitive peoples preserve, from the earliest ages of the simplest culture, the sketch of a God which our highest religious thought can only attempt to fulfill in its ideal. Regardless of his origin, Jehovah or Allah does not come from a ghost.

### XII

## SAVAGE SUPREME BEINGS

It is among "the lowest savages" that the Supreme Beings are most regarded as eternal, moral (according to the morality of the tribe, or even on a higher level), and *powerful*. I have elsewhere described the Bushman god Cagn, as he was portrayed to Mr. Orpen by Qing, who "had never before seen a white man except in battle." Mr. Orpen obtained the facts from Qing by encouraging him to explain the natives’ pictures on the walls of caves. "Cagn made all things, and we pray to him," in this way: "O Cagn, O Cagn, are we not your children? Do you not see us hunger? Give us food." Regarding ethics, "At first Cagn was very good, but he became spoiled through fighting so many things." "How did he come into the world?" "Perhaps with those who brought the Sun: only the initiated know these things." It appears that Qing was not yet initiated in the dance (corresponding to a high rite of the Australian *Bora*) in which the most secret myths were revealed. <note>Footnote 1</note>

The case of the Andaman Islanders may be especially recommended to believers in the anthropological science of religion. For a long time, these natives were the joy of secular inquirers as the "godless Andamanese." They only provide Mr. Spencer’s *Ecclesiastical Institutions* with a few instances of the belief in ghosts.<note>2</note> Yet when the Andamanese are scientifically studied *in situ* (on site) by an educated Englishman, Mr. Man—who knows their language, has lived with them for eleven years, and presided over our benevolent efforts "to reclaim them from their savage state"—the Andamanese turn out to be quite embarrassingly rich in the higher elements of faith. They have not only a profoundly philosophical religion, but also an excessively absurd *mythology*, like the Australian blacks, the Greeks, and other peoples. If, on the whole, the student of the Andamanese despairs of the possibility of an ethnological theory of religion, he is hardly to be blamed.

The account of Andamanese religion does not align with the anthropological hypothesis. Foreign influence seems to be more than usually excluded by the island's conditions and the guarded nature of the ‘original inhabitants.’ The evidence should make us reflect on the extreme obscurity of the entire problem.

The anthropological study of religion has until now almost entirely overlooked the mysteries of various races, except to the extent that they confirm the entry of young people into the ranks of the adults. Their hidden moral and religious teaching is nearly unknown to us, except in a few instances. It is certain that the mysteries of Greece were survivals of primitive ceremonies, because we know that they included specific primitive rites, such as the use of the *rhombos* to make a whirring noise, and the custom of ritual daubing with dirt; and the sacred *ballets d’action*, in which, as Lucian and Qing say, mystic facts are ‘danced out.’<note>1. *Myth, Ritual, and Religion*, i. 281-288.</note> But, while Greece retained these relics of primitive times, there was something taught at Eleusis which filled minds like Plato’s and Pindar’s with a happy religious awe. Now, a similar ‘softening of the heart’ was the result of the teaching in the Australian *Bora*: the Yao mysteries teach the victory over self; and, until we are admitted to the secrets of all other primitive mysteries throughout the world, we cannot tell whether, among theatrical displays, frivolities, and even excess, high ethical doctrines are not presented under the sanction of religion. The New Life, and perhaps the future life, are undeniably indicated in the Australian mysteries by the simulated Resurrection.

The beings who never were human and never died are <term>Vui</term>; the ghosts are <term>Tamate</term>. Dr. Codrington uses "ghosts" for <term>Tamate</term> and "spirits" for <term>Vui</term>. A <term>Vui</term> is not a spirit that was once a ghost; a story may represent him as if he were a man, "but the native will always maintain that he was something different, and deny that he has the physical body of a man."<note>1. *Journal of the Anthropological Institute*, 267.</note>

This distinction—a ghost on one hand and an eternal being (not a man, nor a ghost of a man) on the other—is fundamental and nearly universal in primitive religion. Anthropology, by ignoring the essential distinction insisted upon in this case by Dr. Codrington, confuses both types under the label of "spirits" and derives both from the ghosts of the dead. The Fijians are at a higher level of material culture than the Melanesians.

Fijian religion, as far as we understand it, resembles others in drawing an impassable line between ghosts and eternal gods. The word *Kalou* is applied to all supernatural beings, as well as to mystic or magical things. It seems to correspond to *mana* in New Zealand and Melanesia, to *wakan* in North America, and to *fée* (enchanted) in old French—as when Perrault says of Bluebeard’s key, "now the key was *fée*." All gods are *Kalou*, but not all things that are *Kalou* are gods. Gods are *Kalou vu*; deified ghosts are *Kalou yalo*. The former are eternal, without a beginning or an end; the latter are subject to frailty and even to death.<note>2. *Williams’s Fiji*, page 218. See Mr. Fison’s remarks cited later.</note>

The Supreme Being, if we can apply that term to him, is Ndengei, or Degei, "who seems to be an embodiment of the abstract idea of eternal existence." This idea is not easily developed from the concept of a human soul that has passed into a ghost and may die again. His myth represents him as a serpent, an emblem of eternity, or as a stone body with a serpent’s head. His only manifestation is expressed through eating. He is so neglected that a song exists about his lack of worshippers and offerings. "We made men," says Ndengei, "and placed them on earth,

The idea of primeval Eternal Beings, as understood by primitive peoples, does not depend on or require the ghost theory. But, as we almost always find ghosts and a Supreme Being together wherever we find either among the most primitive peoples, we have no historical ground for asserting that either is prior to the other. the explanation suggested by Mr. Im Thurn for the problem of religion in Guiana will not fit the facts. It is plain that, *a priori*, another explanation is conceivable. If a people like the Andamanese, or the Australian tribes whom we have studied, had such a conception as that of Puluga, or Baiame, or Darumulun, and then, *later*, developed ancestor-worship with its propitiatory sacrifices and ceremonies, ancestor-worship—as the most recently evolved and infinitely most practical form of cult—would gradually push the belief in a Puluga, or Darumulun, or Cagn into the background. To speak quite plainly, the ancestral spirit can be "negotiated with" by the people in whom he takes a special interest for family reasons. The Father of all men, who treats everyone equally, cannot be "negotiated with," and refuses (until corrupted by the bad example of ancestral ghosts) to make himself useful to one man rather than to another. For these very understandable, simple, and practical reasons, if the belief in a Darumulun came first in evolution, and the belief in a practical, bribable family ghost came second, the ghost-cult would inevitably crowd out the God-cult.¹ The name of the Father and Maker would become a mere survival, a shadow of a name (*nominis umbra*), while worship and sacrifice would go to the ancestral ghost. That explanation would fit the state of religion which Mr. Im Thurn has found, rightly or wrongly, in British Guiana.

But, if the idea of a universal Father and Maker came last in evolution as a refinement, then, of course, it ought to be the newest, and therefore the most fashionable and potent of Guianese cults. Precisely the reverse is said to be the case. Nor can the belief indicated in such names as Father and Maker be satisfactorily ex—

These considerations, however unpleasant to the devotees of Animism, or the ghost theory, are not in themselves illogical, nor do they contradict the theory of evolution; on the contrary, evolution fits them perfectly well. That god thrives best who is most suited to his environment. Any man can decide whether an easy-going, hungry ghost-god with a liking for his family, or a moral Creator who cannot be bribed, is better suited to an environment of not especially scrupulous savages. It is just as easily resolved a question whether a group of not particularly scrupulous savages will readily evolve a moral, unbribable Creator when they already have a serviceable family ghost-god eager to oblige them.

Beyond all doubt, savages who find themselves under the watchful eye of a moral deity whom they cannot "square" <note>In this context, to "square" means to bribe, manipulate, or come to a private arrangement with.</note> will desert him as soon as they have evolved a practicable ghost-god, useful for family purposes, whom they *can* square. No less manifestly, savages who already possess a throng of serviceable ghost-gods will not enthusiastically evolve a moral Creator who despises gifts and only cares for obedience. "There is a great deal of human nature in man," and if Mr. Im Thurn’s description of the Guianese be correct, everything we know of human nature and of evolution assures us that the Father, or Maker, or Ancient of Days came first, and the ghost-gods came last. Unkulunkulu is represented as "the First Man, who broke off in the beginning." "They are ancestor-worshippers," says Dr. Callaway, "and believe that their first ancestor, the First Man, was the Creator." <note>Callaway, p. 1.</note> But they may, like many other peoples, have had a different original tradition and altered it simply because they are now such fervent ancestor-worshippers. Unkulunkulu existed before Death, which came among men in the usual mythical way. <note>Cited work, p. 3.</note> Whether Unkulunkulu still exists is a somewhat debatable question; Dr. Callaway thinks that he does not. <note>Cited work, p. 7.</note> If not, he is an exception to the rule in Australia, the Andaman Islands, among the Bushmen, the Fuegians, and savages in general, who are less advanced in culture than the Zulus. The idea, then, of a Maker of things who has ceased to exist occurs, if at all, not in a relatively primitive religion, but in a relatively late one. Following the analogy of pottery, agriculture, the use of iron, villages, hereditary kings, and so on, the notion of a dead Maker is late, not early. It occurs where men have iron, cattle, agriculture, kings, houses, and a disciplined army—not where men lack these things. The Zulu godless ancestor-worship, then, by the same logic, is—like their material culture—not an early but a late development. The Zulus "hear of a King who is above"—"the heavenly King." <note>Cited work, p. 19.</note> "We did not hear of him first from white men. . . . But he is not like Unkulunkulu, who, we say, made all things."

Ukoto, a very old Zulu man, said: "When we were children, it was said, 'The Lord is in heaven.' . . . They used to point to the Lord on high; we did not hear his name." This patriarch understood Unkulunkulu to refer to immediate ancestors, whose names and family trees he provided.<note>Pp. 49, 50.</note> "We heard it said that the Creator of the world was the Lord who is above; when I was growing up, people always used to point toward heaven."

A very old woman was most reluctant to speak of Unkulunkulu; at last she said, "Ah, it is he, in fact, who is the Creator, who is in heaven, of whom the ancestors spoke." Then the old woman began to chatter humorously about how the white men made all things. Again, Unkulunkulu is said to have been created by Utilexo. Utilexo was invisible, while Unkulunkulu was visible, and so he received credit that was not really his due.<note>P. 67.</note> When the heaven is said to belong to the Chief (the chief being a living Zulu), "they do not believe what they say"; the phrase is merely an exaggerated compliment.<note>P. 122.</note>

Based on this examination of the evidence, it certainly seems just as logical to conjecture that the Zulus once had such an idea of a Supreme Being as lower races hold, and then nearly lost it, as it is to say that the Zulus, though a monarchical race, have not yet developed a King-God out of the crowd of spirits (Amatongo). The Zulus—the Norsemen of the South, so to speak—are a highly practical military race. An abstract Deity was not to their liking. Serviceable family spirits, who continually provided an excuse for a dinner of roast beef, were to their liking. *The less developed races do not commonly kill their flocks for food. A sacrifice is needed as a pretext.* To the gods of the Andamanese, Bushmen, and Australians, no sacrifice is offered. To the Supreme Being of most African peoples, no sacrifice is offered. There is no festivity in the worship of these Supreme Beings—no feasting, at any rate. They are not to be "influenced" by gifts or sacrifices. The Amatongo can be influenced; they are bribable and provide an excuse for a good dinner. Thus, the practical Amatongo are honored, while among the current generation of Zulus, Unkulunkulu is a joke, and the Lord in Heaven is but the shadow of a name. Clearly, this does not point to a recent development of higher ideas, but to a remote one that has now been superseded by spirit-worship.

We shall next see how this view—the opposite of the anthropological theory—works when applied to other races, especially other African races.

<header>THE MAKING OF RELIGION</header>

### XIII
## MORE SAVAGE SUPREME BEINGS

If many of the lowest savages known to us entertain ideas of a Supreme Being such as we find among the Fuegians, Australians, Bushmen, and Andamanese, are there examples—besides the Zulus—of tribes higher in material culture who seem to have had such notions, but have partly forgotten or neglected them? Miss Kingsley, a lively, observant, and unprejudiced, though rambling writer, gives this very account of the Bantu races. Oblivion, or neglect, shows itself by leaving the Supreme Being alone, as he needs no propitiation, while devoting sacrifice and ritual to fetishes and ghosts. That this should be done is perfectly natural if the Supreme Being (who wants no sacrifice) was the first evolved in thought, while venal fetishes and spirits came in as a result of the ghost theory. But if, as a result of the ghost theory, the Supreme Being came last in evolution, he ought to be the most fashionable object of worship, the latest developed, the most powerful, and the one most to be propitiated. He is the reverse.

To take an example: the Dinkas of the Upper Nile (whom Sir Samuel Baker calls "godless") pay a very theoretical kind of homage to the all-powerful Being, dwelling in heaven, from where he sees all things. He is called "Dendid" (great rain, that is, universal benediction?). He is omnipotent, but, being entirely benevolent, he can do no evil; so, because he is not feared, he is not addressed in prayer. The evil

> ‘ At the beginning, when Dendid made all things,
> ->He created the Sun,<-
> And the Sun is born, and dies, and comes again!
> ->He created the Stars,<-
> And the Stars are born, and die, and come again!
> ->He created Man,<-
> And Man is born, and dies, and returns no more! ’

It is like the lament of Moschus.<note>Lejean, *Rev. des Deux Mondes*, April 1862, p. 760. Citing for the chant, Beltrame, *Dizionario della lingua denka*, MS.</note>

Russegger compares the Dinkas, and all the neighboring peoples who hold the same beliefs, to modern Deists.<note>Waitz, ii. 74.</note> They are far from atheism and from ritual worship! Suggestions about an ancient Egyptian influence are made, but popular Egyptian religion was not monotheistic, and priestly thought could scarcely influence the ancestors of the Dinkas. M. Lejean says these peoples are so practical and utilitarian that missionary religion takes no hold on them. Mr. Spencer does not provide the ideas of the Dinkas, but it is not easy to see how the overly benevolent Dendid could have evolved out of ghost-propitiation, "the origin of all religions." Rather, the Dinkas, a practical people, seem to have simply forgotten to be grateful to their Maker; or they have decided—more to the credit of their clear heads than the warmth of their hearts—that he does not want gratitude. Like the French philosopher, they cultivate *l’indépendance du cœur* (independence of the heart), being in this matter strikingly unlike the Pawnees.

Let us now take a case in which ancestor worship, and no other form of religion (beyond mere superstitions), has been declared to be the practice of an African people. Mr. Spencer gives the example of the natives of the south—

This figure is preferred over older spirits who are now forgotten; such old spirits may, however, have a mountaintop for a home, as a great chief is better remembered. The mountain god is prayed to for rain; higher gods were probably similar local gods in an older habitat of the Yao.<note>*Ecclesiastical Institutions*, 681.</note>

Such is, in the main, Mr. Spencer's summary of Mr. Duff Macdonald's report. He omits whatever Mr. Macdonald says about a Being among the Yao who is similar to the Dendid of the Dinka, or the Darumulun of Australia, or the Huron Ahone. Yet analysis reveals, in Mr. Macdonald's report, many traces of such a Being, even though Mr. Macdonald himself believes that ancestor worship is the source of the local religion. Thus, Mulungu, or Mlungu, used as a proper name, "is said to be the great spirit, *msimu*, of all men—a spirit formed by adding all the departed spirits together."<note>*Africana*, i. 66.</note> This is a remarkable reach of primitive philosophy and indicates (says Mr. Macdonald) "a grasping after a Being who is the totality of all individual existence. . . . If it fell from the lips of civilized men instead of savages, it would be regarded as philosophy. Expressions of this kind among the natives are partly traditional and partly dictated by the big thoughts of the moment." It is indeed philosophy, but a philosophy dependent on the ghost theory.

I will go on to show that the Wayao have—though Mr. Spencer omits him—a Being who precisely corresponds to Darumulun, if stripped (perhaps) of his ethical aspect. On this point we are left in uncertainty, simply because Mr. Macdonald could not ascertain the secrets of his

mysteries which, in Australia, have been revealed to a few Europeans.

Where Mulungu is used as a proper name, it "certainly points to a personal Being, who is sometimes said by the Wayao to be the same as Mtanga. At other times he is a Being who possesses many powerful servants, but is himself kept quite far from the scene of earthly affairs, like the gods of Epicurus."

This is, of course, exactly the feature in African theology that interests us. The Supreme Being—despite the power that his supposed position as the latest evolution of the ghost-world should naturally give him—is neglected, either because he is half-forgotten or for philosophical reasons. For these reasons, Epicurus and Lucretius made their gods *otiosi* (unconcerned), and the Wayao, with their concept of a universal collective spirit, are quite significant philosophers.

"This Mulungu" or Mtanga, "in the world beyond the grave, is represented as assigning spirits to their proper places," though we are not informed whether this is for ethical reasons or not.<note>1 Africana, i. 67.</note> Santos (1586) says "they acknowledge a God who, in both this world and the next, deals out retribution for the good or evil done in this."

"In the native hypothesis about creation, 'the people of Mulungu' play a very important part." These ministers of his who carry out his will are therefore regarded as existing before the current world, as is Mulungu himself. Therefore, in the opinion of the Wayao, they cannot be the ghosts of the dead at all, nor can we properly call them "spirits." They are *beings*—eternal, creative, but undefined. The word Mulungu, however, is now applied to the spirits of individuals; but whether the word means "sky" (according to Salt) or "ancestor" (according to Bleek), it cannot be used to prove that Mulungu himself was originally envisioned as a "spirit."

For, clearly, if we suppose that the idea of powerful, undefined beings came first in evolution and was followed by the idea of ghosts, then that ghost idea might have been applied to explaining the pre-existing creative powers.

Mtanga is "localized" by some as the god of Mangochi, a sort of Olympus left behind by the Yao during their migrations. Here, some believe, his voice can still be heard. "Others say that Mtanga was never a human being . . . he was involved in the first introduction of humans into the world. He is credited with . . . making mountains and rivers. He is closely associated with a year of plenty. He is called <term>Mchimwene juene</term>, 'a very great chief.' He has a kind of evil counterpart, <term>Chitowe</term>, but this being, the Satan of this belief system, 'is a child or subject of Mtanga'—essentially an evil angel."<note>1 *Africana*, i. 71, 72.</note>

The thunder god, <term>Mpambe</term>—called <term>Njasi</term> (lightning) in <term>Yao</term>—is also a minister of the Supreme Being. "He is sent by Mtanga with rain." Europeans are thought to be cleverer than the locals because we "stayed longer with the people of God (<term>Mulungu</term>)."

I do not find evidence that, although associated with good crops, <term>Mtanga</term> or <term>Mulungu</term> receives any sacrifice or appeasement. "The chief addresses his own god";<note>2 i. 88.</note> the chief "will not concern himself with his great-great-grandfather; he will present his offering to his own immediate predecessor, saying, 'O father, I do not know all your relatives; you know them all: invite them to feast with you.'"<note>3 i. 68.</note>

"All the offerings are intended to address some need of the spirit." Mtanga, on the other hand, is *nihil indiga nostri* <note>Latin: "needs nothing from us."</note>.

A village god is given beer to drink, just as <term>Indra</term> received <term>Soma</term>. A deceased chief is appeased with human sacrifices. I find no trace of any offering given to Mtanga. His mysteries are

...really unknown to Mr. Macdonald; they were laughed at by a traveled and "emancipated" Yao.<note>1 *Africana*, i. 130.</note>

"These rites are supposed to be kept strictly secret by the initiated, who often say that they would die if they revealed them."<note>2 *Ibid.*</note>

How can we pretend to understand a religion if we do not know its secret? That secret, in Australia, provides the certainty of the ethical character of the Supreme Being. Mr. Macdonald says about the initiator (a grotesque figure):

"He delivers lectures and is said to give much good advice . . . the lectures condemn selfishness, and a selfish person is called *mwisichana*, that is, 'uninitiated.'"

There could not be better evidence of the presence of the ethical element in religious mysteries. Among the Yao, as among the Australian Kurnai, the central secret lesson of religion is the lesson of our Lord.

It is not stated that Mtanga instituted or presides over the mysteries. Judging from the analogy of Eleusis, the Bora, the American Indian initiations, and so on, we may expect this to be the belief; but Mr. Macdonald knows very little about the matter.

The legendary tales say "all things in this world were made by 'God.'" "At first there were not people, but 'God' and beasts." "God" here is Mlungu. The other statement is apparently derived from existing ancestor-worship, where people who died became "God" (Mlungu). But God exists prior to death, for the Yao have a version of the common myth regarding the origin of death, and also of sleep: "death and sleep are one word; they are of one family." God dwells on high, while a malevolent "great one," who disturbed the mysteries and killed the initiated, was turned into a mountain.<note>3 i. 279-301.</note>

In spite of information that is admittedly incomplete, I have extracted from Mr. Spencer’s chosen authority a mass of facts pointing to a Yao belief in an eternal being, the maker of mountains and rivers. This being existed before humans; he is not subject to death—which appeared late among them—and is benevolent. He is not appeased by sacrifice (as far as the evidence shows) and is moral (if we may judge by the similarity to other mysteries), and yet he occupies the religious background while the foreground is held by the spirits of the recently deceased. To prove Mr. Spencer’s theory, he should have provided a full account of this being and shown how he was developed from ghosts, which are forgotten in inverse proportion to their distance from the current generation. I imagine that Mr. Spencer would find a middle point between an ordinary ghost and Mtanga in the spirit of a chief associated with a mountain, where the location and place-name preserve the ghost’s name and memory. But it is, I think, a long way from such a chief’s ghost to the pre-human, angel-served Mtanga.

Of ancestor worship and ghost worship, we have abundant evidence. But the position of Mtanga raises one of those delicate and crucial questions that cannot be solved by ignoring their existence. Is Mtanga evolved from an ancestral ghost? If so, why—as the greatest of divine beings, the ‘Very Chief,’ who has powerful ministers under him—is he left without offerings, unless it is through moral discourses during the mysteries? Since he is a much more advanced concept than the ghost of a real father, he ought to be much later in evolution, more recently conceived, and more widely worshipped. How do we explain his lack of worship? Was he originally imagined as a ghost at all? If so, by what strange but consistent logic of primitive peoples is he regarded as existing before humans, and—though a ghost—existing before the concept of death? Is it not certain that such a being could be con-

Light is thrown on these problems by a successor to Mr. Spencer’s authority, Mr. Duff Macdonald of the Blantyre Mission. This gentleman, the Rev. David Clement Scott, has published *A Cyclopedic Dictionary of the Mang’anja Language in British Central Africa*.¹ Looking at ancestral spirits first, we find *Mzimu*, "spirits of the departed, supposed to come in dreams." Though they dwell in the spirit world, they also haunt thickets; they inspire *Mlauli* (prophets) and make them rave and utter predictions. Offerings are made to them. Here is a prayer: "Watch over me, my ancestor, who died long ago; tell the great spirit at the head of my race, from whom my mother came." There are small hut-temples, and the chief directs the sacrifices of food or animals. There are religious pilgrimages, including sacrifice, to mountains. God, like the people in this region, has various names, such as *Chiuta*, "God in space and the rainbow sign across"; *Mpambe*, "God Almighty" (or rather "pre-excellent"); *Mlezi*, "God the Sustainer"; and *Mulungu*, "God who is spirit." *Mulungu* means God, "not spirits or a fetish." "You cannot use the plural, as God is One," say the natives. "There are no idols called gods, and spirits are the spirits of people who have died, not gods." Idols are *Zitunzi-zitunzi*. "Spirits are supposed to be with *Mulungu*." God made the world and man. Our author says, "when the chief or people sacrifice, it is to God," but he also says that they sacrifice to ancestral spirits. There is some confusion of

Mr. Scott does not seem to know more about the Mysteries than Mr. Macdonald, and his article on Mulungu does not enlighten us much. Does Mulungu, as a Creative God, receive sacrifice or not?¹ Mr. Scott provides no instance of this under *Nsembe* (sacrifice), where ancestors or the hill-dwelling ghosts of chiefs are offered food; yet, as we have seen, under *Mulungu*, he states that the chiefs and people do sacrifice to God. He appears to be confusing the Creator with spirits, and this part of his evidence cannot be relied upon. "At the back of all this" (sacrifice to spirits) "there is God." If I understand Mr. Scott, sacrifices are actually made only to spirits, but he is trying to argue that, after all, a theistic conception lies behind the animistic practice, thereby inserting his theory into his facts. His theory would, in fact, be better supported if sacrifice were not offered to the Creator, but this had not occurred to Mr. Scott.

It is clear, in any case, that the religion of the Africans in the Blantyre region has an element not easily derived from ancestral spirit-worship—an element not observed by Mr. Spencer.

No one who has followed the examples already cited will be surprised by what Waitz calls the "surprising result" of recent inquiries among the great African peoples. Among the branches where foreign influence is least suspected, we discover, behind their more conspicuous fetishism and superstitions, something which we cannot exactly call Monotheism, yet which tends in

Waitz’s remarks on the Supreme Being of the Negro are well worth noting, due to his unconcealed astonishment at the discovery.

Wilson’s observations on North and South Guinea religion were published in 1856. After commenting on the delicate task of finding out what a primitive religion really is, he writes: “The belief in one great Supreme Being, who made and upholds all things, is universal.”¹ The names of the being are translated as “Maker,” “Preserver,” “Benefactor,” and “Great Friend.” Although composed of all good qualities, the being has allowed the world to “come under the control of evil spirits,” who alone receive religious worship. Although he leaves things uncontrolled, the chief being (as in Homer) still ratifies oaths at a treaty and is invoked to punish criminals when ordeal water is to be drunk. To this extent, then, he has an ethical influence. “Grossly wicked people” are buried outside of the regular burial ground. <term>Fetishism</term> prevails, along with <term>spiritualism</term>, and Wilson thinks that mediums might pick up some good tricks in Guinea. He gives no examples. Their inspired men do things “that cannot be accounted for” through the use of narcotics.

The South Guinea Creator, Anyambia (meaning “good spirit”?), is good but capricious. He has a good deputy, Ombwiri (spelled “Mbuiri” by Miss Kingsley); he alone has no priests but communicates directly with men. The neighboring Shekuni have mysteries of the Great Spirit. No details are given. This great being, Mwetyi, witnesses covenants and punishes perjury. These people are ancestor-worshippers, but their Supreme Being is not said to receive

sacrifice, as ghosts do. However, he is so far from being powerless, like Unkulunkulu, that if it were not for the fear of his wrath, "their national treaties would have little or no force."¹ Since we have no information about the mysteries, we naturally know nothing of other moral influences that are, or may be, exercised by these great, powerful, and not entirely <term>otiose</term> <note>inactive or retired from worldly affairs</note> beings.

The celebrated traveler Mungo Park, who visited Africa in 1805, had excellent opportunities to understand the natives. He did not rush through the land with a large armed force; instead, alone or almost alone, he paid his way with brass buttons. "I have conversed with people of all ranks and conditions regarding their faith," he says, "and can pronounce, without the slightest shadow of doubt, that the belief in one God and in a future state of reward and punishment is entire and universal among them." This cannot strictly be called monotheism, as there are many subordinate spirits who may be influenced by "magical ceremonies." But if monotheism means a belief in only one Spirit, or religious regard paid to only one Spirit, it exists nowhere—not even in Islam.

Park thinks it remarkable that "the Almighty" only receives prayers at the new moon (he says nothing of sacrifice to the Almighty), and that, being the creator and preserver of all things, He is "of so exalted a nature that it is idle to imagine the feeble supplications of wretched mortals can reverse the decrees and change the purpose of unerring Wisdom." The new moon prayers are mere matters of tradition: "our fathers did it before us." "Such is the blindness of unassisted nature," says Park, who is not satirizing, in the manner of Jonathan Swift, the prayers of Presbyterians back home on the Yarrow.

We encounter our old problem: How has this God, whose concept involves so much philosophy, developed from these hungry ghosts? The influence of Islam can hardly be suspected, since Allah is addressed, of course, in endless prayers, while the African god receives none. Indeed, it would be more plausible to say that Muhammad borrowed Allah from the widespread belief we are studying than to say the African’s Supreme Being was borrowed from Allah.

As we have seen, Park had many opportunities for informal discussion with the people on whose mercy he relied.

> ‘But the Africans do not often make their religious opinions the subject of conversation; when questioned, in particular, concerning their ideas of a future state, they express themselves with great reverence, but try to shorten the discussion by saying, “*Mo o mo inta allo*” (“No man knows anything about it”).’¹

Park himself, in extreme distress and almost in despair, happened to observe the delicate beauty of a small moss plant. Reflecting that the Creator of such a fragile thing could not be indifferent to any of His creatures, he took heart and reached safety.² He did not share the African philosophy, making it less likely that he invented it. The new moon prayer, said in a whisper, was reported to Park ‘by many different people’ as containing ‘thanks to God for his kindness during the existence of the past moon, and to request a continuation of his favor during the new one.’ This, of course, may prove Islamic influence and contradicts the general tendency of the religious philosophy as it has been described.

We now come to a theory of the Supreme Being among a certain African race that would be completely fatal to my whole hypothesis on this topic, if it could be proven factually correct, and if it could be extended so as to apply to the Australians, Fuegians, Andamanese, and other very primitive peoples. It is the hypothesis that the Supreme Being is a "loan-god," borrowed from Europeans.

The theory is very clearly set forth in Major Ellis’s ‘Tshi-speaking Peoples of the Gold Coast.’¹ Major Ellis’s opinion matches that of Waitz in his ‘Introduction to Anthropology’ (an opinion to which Waitz does not seem dogmatic)—namely, that "the original form of all religion is a raw, unsystematic polytheism," where nature is populated by hostile powers or spirits, and everyone worships whatever he thinks is most dangerous or most useful. There are few general, but many local or personal, objects of worship.² Major Ellis only encountered this passage after he had formed his own ideas by observing the Tshi race. We do not pretend to guess what "the original form of all religion" may have been; but we have given, and shall continue to give, abundant evidence for the existence of a higher faith than this among peoples much lower in material culture than the Tshi races, who possess metals and an organized priesthood. They inhabit the forests of the Gold Coast in small villages (except for Coomassie and Djuabin). The mere mention of Coomassie shows how much more advanced in civilization the Tshis (Ashantis and Fantis) are than the naked, homeless Australians. Their inland communities, however, are "mere specks in a vast expanse of impenetrable forest." The coastal people have been in contact with Europeans for centuries, but the "Tshi-speaking races are now

Nevertheless, Major Ellis explains their Supreme Being as the result of European influence! *A priori*, this appears highly improbable. That a belief should sweep over all these spots in the impenetrable forest, spreading from the coastal tribes in contact with Europeans, and that this belief—though the most recent—should be infinitely the least powerful, cannot be regarded as a plausible hypothesis. Moreover, according to Major Ellis's theory, the Supreme Beings of races that only recently came into contact with Europeans for the first time—Supreme Beings kept jealously apart from European knowledge and revered in the secrecy of ancient mysteries—must also, by the same logic, be the result of European influence. Unfortunately, Major Ellis gives no evidence for his statements about the past history of the Tshi religion. He must have sources, and references would be welcome.

Gold Coast men can only approach gods through priests.¹ This is a sign of degeneration.

Obviously, if religion began in a form that was relatively pure and moral, it must degenerate as civilization advances under the influence of priests who "exploit" the lucrative aspects of faith and see no profit in the pure elements of belief and practice. The fact that the lucrative elements in Christianity were exploited by the clergy, while ethics were neglected, was precisely the complaint of the Protestant Reformers. The Apostles' Creed was free from these lucrative elements, and a similar freedom characterizes the religion of Australia or that of the Pawnees. We cannot, therefore, possibly expect to find the "original" state of religion among a people dominated by a money-grubbing priesthood, such as the Tshi peoples. Even if religion begins as pure as snow, it would be corrupted by priestly trafficking in its profitable <term>animistic</term> aspects. Furthermore, a priesthood develops relatively late in the history of a culture.

Major Ellis categorizes Tshi gods as:
1. General, worshipped by an entire tribe or multiple tribes.
2. Local deities of river, hill, forest, or sea.
3. Deities of families or corporations.
4. Tutelary deities of individuals.

The second class, according to the natives, were appointed by the first class, who are "too distant or indifferent to interfere ordinarily in human affairs." Similarly, the Huron god, Ahone, punishes nobody. He is all "sweetness and light," but "has a partner, Mr. Jorkins," called Okeus. Based on our hypothesis, this indifference of high gods suggests the displacement of the great, disinterested God by corrupt animistic competition. All of class II "appear to have been originally malignant." Though, in native belief, class I was prior to and "appointed" class II, Major Ellis thinks that the malignant spirits of class II were

Major Ellis then asserts that when Europeans reached the Gold Coast in the fifteenth century, they "appear to have found" a northern god, Tando, and a southern god, Bobowissi, still being worshipped. Bobowissi creates thunder and rain, lives on a hill, and receives—or once received—human sacrifices. Later, Major Ellis must contrast Bosman’s account of fetishism (1700) with his own observations. According to Bosman’s native source of information, men then selected their own fetishes. These are *now* selected by priests. Either Bosman’s source was wrong, or the priesthood has expanded its field of business. Major Ellis argues that the revolution from amateur to priestly selection of fetishes could not occur in 190 years "over a vast tract of country, among peoples living in semi-isolated communities, in the midst of pathless forests, where there is but little opportunity for the exchange of ideas, and where we know they have been uninfluenced by *any higher race*."

It is not very easy to believe that Nyam, under all his names, was picked up from the Portuguese and passed apparently from Negroes to Bantu all over West Africa, despite the isolation of the groups and the resistance of the priesthood.

Nyam, like Major Ellis’s class I, appoints a subordinate god to do his work: he is truly good and governs the malevolent spirits.³

It is clear that Major Ellis is endeavoring to explain a phenomenon of very wide distribution by a single solution (namely, the borrowing of a God from Europeans)—a solution that is both improbable and inadequate. Nyankupon cannot be explained separately from Taaroa, Puluga, Ahone, Ndengei, Dendid, and Ta-li-y-Tooboo—gods to be described later—who cannot, by any stretch of probability, be considered of European origin. All of these represent the original Supreme Being, who, as culture advanced, was more or less completely stripped of his ethical influence and crowded out by the horde of useful, greedy ghosts or ghost-gods whose service is lucrative. Nyankupon makes no claim to be, or to have been, a "spirit." <note>Ellis, p. 29.</note>

Major Ellis’s theory is a natural result of his belief that a mess of polytheism was "the original state of religion." If so, there was not much room for the natural development of Nyankupon, in whom "the missionaries find a parallel to the Yahweh of the Jews." <note>The same work, p. 28.</note> According to our theory, Nyankupon takes his place in the regular process of theism being corrupted by animism.

In all missionary accounts of indigenous religion, we must guard against two kinds of bias. One is the bias that causes the observer to deny any religion to the native race, except for devil-worship. The other is the bias that leads him to look for traces of a pure, primitive religious tradition. Yet we cannot help but observe this reciprocal phenomenon: missionaries often find a native name and idea that correspond so closely to their own conception of God that they adopt the idea and the name in their teaching. On the other hand, when the indigenous people first hear the missionaries' account of God, they recognize it—as did the Hurons and Bakwain—as something that has always been familiar to them. This is recorded in very early pre-missionary travels, such as in the book by William Strachey on Virginia (1612), to which we now turn. The God found by Strachey in Virginia cannot, by any stretch of speculation, be regarded as the result of contact with Europeans. Yet he almost exactly corresponds to the African <term>Nyankupon</term>, who is dismissed as a "<term>loan-god</term>." For the belief in relatively pure creative beings—whether they are morally adored without sacrifice or simply neglected—is so widely diffused that anthropology must either ignore them, account for them as "loan-gods," or abandon its current theory!

# XIV

## AHONE. TI-RA-WÁ. NÀ-PI. PACHACAMAC.
## TUI LAGA. TAA-ROA

In this chapter, it is my objective to place certain American Creators alongside the African beings whom we have been examining. We will range from the Hurons to the Pawnees and Blackfeet, and end with Pachacamac, the supreme being of the ancient Inca civilization, along with Tui Laga and Taa-roa. It will be shown that the Hurons have been accidentally deprived of their benevolent Creator by a bibliographical error, while that Creator corresponds very well with the Peruvian Pachacamac, who is often regarded as a mere philosophical abstraction. The Pawnees will show us a Creator involved in a sacrificial ritual, which is uncommon, while the Blackfeet present a Creator who is not imagined as a spirit at all and, according to our theory, represents a very early stage of the theistic concept.

The Ahone-Okeus creed is clear. God (Ahone) is all-powerful and good, yet calamities trouble humanity. How are these to be explained? Clearly as penalties for men’s sins, inflicted not by Ahone, but by his subordinate, Okeus. But that official can be, and is, appeased by sacrifices—offerings which would be impious, or at the very least useless, to offer to the Supreme Being, Ahone. It is a logical creed, but how could the Supreme Being have evolved out of the ghost of a "people-devouring king" like Powhatan? The facts, which are quite well-documented, do not fit the anthropological theory. It should be noted that Strachey’s Ahone is a much less mythological concept than the one which, based on strong evidence, he attributes to the Indians of the Potomac River. Their Creator is described as "a divine Hare," who receives their souls into Paradise, from where they are reborn on earth again, as in Plato’s myth. They also regard the four winds as four gods. How the god took the mythological form of a hare is explained in various ways.<note>¹ See Brinton, *Myths of the New World*, for a linguistic theory.</note>

Meanwhile, the Ahone-Okeus creed corresponds to the Nyankupon-Bobowissi creed. Since the American faith was certainly not borrowed from Europe, it is less likely that the African creed was borrowed.

To illustrate the general theory presented here, we may now look at two tribal religions among the North American Indians. The first is that of the horse-riding Pawnee, who, thirty years ago, lived on the Loup Fork in Nebraska. The buffalo have since been destroyed, the lands seized, and the Pawnee driven into a "Reservation," where they are, or lately were, cheated and oppressed in the usual way. They were originally known to Europeans as four groups, the fourth being the Skidi or Wolf Pawnee. They seem to have come into

If, then, they are of Mexican origin, we might expect to find traces of Aztec ritual among the Pawnees.

Long after they obtained better weapons, they used flint-headed arrows for killing the only two beasts which it was lawful to sacrifice: the deer and the buffalo. They have long been both a hunting and an agricultural people. Corn was given to them originally by the Ruler: their god, *Ti-ra-wá*, "the Spirit Father." They offer the sacrifice of a deer with particular solemnity and are a very prayerful people. The priest "held a relationship with the Pawnees and their deity not unlike that occupied by Moses toward Jehovah and the Israelites." A feature of their ritual is the sacred bundles of unknown contents, brought from their original home in Mexico. The Pawnees were created by *Ti-ra-wá*. They believe in a happy afterlife, while the wicked die, and that is the end of them. They cite their dreams of the dead as an argument for a life beyond the grave. "We see ourselves living with *Ti-ra-wá*!" An earlier evil race, which did not know *Ti-ra-wá*, was destroyed by him in the Deluge; evidence is found in large fossil bones, and it would be an interesting inquiry whether such fossils are always found where the story of a "sin-flood" occurs. If so, fossils must be universally distributed.

Disease is caused by evil spirits, and many American soldiers were healed by Pawnee doctors, even though their injuries had refused to yield to the treatment of the United States Army Surgeons.<note>Major North, for a long time the U.S. Superintendent of the Pawnees.</note>

The miracles performed by Pawnee medicine men, witnessed by Major North, far surpass what is told of Indian magic. But this was forty years ago, and it is probably too late to learn anything of these astounding performances of naked men on the hard floor of a lodge. "Major North told me" (Mr. Grinnell) "that he saw with his own eyes the doctors make the corn grow," the doctor not manipulating the plant, as in the Mango trick, but standing apart and singing. Mr. Grinnell says: "I have never found anyone who could even suggest an explanation."

This art places great power in the hands of the doctors, who exhibit many other wonders. It is notable that in this religion we hear nothing of ancestor-worship; everything that has been stated regarding ghosts has been reported. We find the worship of an all-powerful being, in whose ritual sacrifice is the only feature that suggests ghost-worship. The popular tales and historical memories of the last generation entirely support, through their references, Mr. Grinnell’s account of the Pawnee faith. In this faith, the ethical element mainly consists of a sense of dependence on and touching gratitude to *Ti-ra-wá*, as shown in fervent prayer. He abhors theft, he applauds valor, he punishes the wicked by annihilation, and the good dwell with him in his heavenly home. He is addressed as *A-ti-us ta-kaw-a*, "Our father in all places."

It is not easy to see how this Being developed from ancestor worship, of which we find no traces among the Pawnees. To argue for ancestor worship among the Sioux, it is common to quote a remark by an interpreter named Prescott: "Sometimes an Indian will say, 'Wah negh on she wan da,' which means, 'Spirits of the dead have mercy on me.' Then they will add what they want. That is about the extent of an Indian’s prayer."<note>Schoolcraft, iii. 237.</note> Obviously, when we compare Mr. Grinnell’s account of Pawnee religion—based on his own observations and those of Major North and Mr. Dunbar (who has written on the language of the tribe)—we are on much safer ground than when we follow a dismissive, half-educated European.

The religion of the Blackfoot Indians appears to be a cruder form of the Pawnee faith. Whether the differences arise from tribal character, from decline, or because the Blackfoot belief is in an earlier and more primitive condition than that of the Pawnees, it is not easy to be certain. As in China, there exists a difficulty in deciding whether the Supreme Being is identical with the great nature-god (in China, the Heaven; among the Blackfeet, the Sun); or if he preceded him in conception, or was later substituted for him, or placed beside him. Blackfoot mythology is base, crude, and—except in tales of Creation—is mocking. As in Australia, there is a specific difference in tone between mythology and religion.

The Blackfoot territory extends east from the summit of the Rocky Mountains to the mouth of the Yellowstone River on the Missouri, then west to the Yellowstone sources, across the Rocky Mountains to the Beaverhead, and from there back to their summit.

<page-num>259</page-num>

<sig>s 2</sig>

As for spirits, the Blackfeet believe in—or at least tell stories about—ghosts, which behave much like those in our old-fashioned ghost stories. They haunt people in a rather playful and irresponsible manner. The souls or shadows of respectable people go to the bleak country called the Sand Hills, where they live in a dull, monotonous kind of Sheol <note>A term referring to a shadowy underworld or place of the dead.</note>. The shades of the wicked are "earth-bound" and mischievous, especially the ghosts of men killed in battle. They cause paralysis and madness but fear the interiors of lodges; they only "tap on the lodge-skins." Like many Native American tribes, the Blackfeet have a legend similar to that of Eurydice. A man grieving for his dead wife finds his way to the underworld, is pitied by the dead, and is allowed to take the woman back with him under certain ritual prohibitions, one of which he unfortunately breaks. The prevalence of this deeply touching story among Native Americans, and its close resemblance to the tale of Orpheus, is one of the most curious facts in mythology. Mr. Grinnell’s friend Young Bear, when lost with his wife in a fog, heard a Voice: "It is well. Go on, you are going right." "The top of my head seemed to lift up. It felt as if many needles were being driven into it. . . . This must have been a ghost." Since his wife also heard the Voice, it was likely human rather than a hallucination.

Animals receive the usual degree of friendly respect from the Blackfeet. They also have a developing polytheism, categorized as "Above Persons, Ground Persons, and Under-Water Persons." Among the first group, Thunder is the most important and is worshipped. There is also the Cold Maker—a white figure on a white horse—the Wind, and so forth.

The Creator is Nà-pi, or Old Man. Dr. Brinton believes he is a personification of Light, but Mr. Grinnell considers it absurd to attribute such an abstract concept to the Blackfeet. Nà-pi is simply a primal, immortal Being.

Chiefs were elected based on their conduct, courage, and charity.

Although weapons and tools were buried with the dead or displayed on platforms, and although great men were left to sleep in their lodges—which were never to be entered by the living from then on—there is no trace known to me of persistent ancestor worship. As many Blackfeet change their names every year, ancestral names are not likely to become the names of gods.

These two cults and beliefs, Pawnee and Blackfoot, may be regarded as fairly well-authenticated examples of non-Christianized American religion among races on the borderland of agriculture and hunting. It would be difficult to maintain that ghost-worship or ancestor-worship is a powerful factor in the evolution of the deathless Tir-a-wá or the immortal Creator Nà-pi, who has nothing of the spirit about him, especially since ghosts are not worshipped. <note>Grinnell’s *Blackfoot Lodge-Tales* and *Pawnee Hero Stories*.</note>

The question then arises: Is Pachacamac a form of the same creative being whom we find among the lowest savages, or is he the result of philosophical reflection? The latter was Garcilasso's opinion. "The Incas and their Amautas" (learned class) "were philosophers." <note>*Op. cit.* i. 106.</note>

"Pacha," he says, means universe, and "cama" means soul. Pachacamac, then, is *Anima Mundi*. "They did not even take the name of Pachacamac into their mouths," or did so only seldom and reverently, just as the Australians will not, in religious matters, mention Darumulun. The position of <term>Pachacamac</term> and the Sun is very nearly that of the Blackfoot Creator <term>Nà-pi</term> and the Sun, or of <term>Shang-ti</term> and the Heaven in China. We have the Creative Being whose creed is invaded by that of a worshipped aspect of nature, and whose cult, quite logically, is *nothing*, or nearly *nothing*. There are also, in different strata of the <term>Inca</term> empire, ancestor-worship, or mummy-worship, Totemism and polytheism, with a vague mass of *huaca = Elohim, kalou, wakan.*

Perhaps it would not be too rash to conjecture that <term>Pachacamac</term> is not merely a philosophical abstraction, but a survival of a Being like <term>Nà-pi</term> or <term>Ahone</term>. <term>Cieza de Leon</term> calls <term>Pachacamac</term> ‘a devil,’ whose name means ‘creator of the world’! <note>Cieza de Leon, p. 253.</note> The name, when it was uttered, was spoken with genuflections and signs of reverence. So closely did <term>Pachacamac</term> resemble the Christian Deity, that <term>Cieza de Leon</term> declares the devil to have forged and insisted on the resemblance! <note>Markham’s translation, p. 253.</note> It was possible for Spanish missionaries to use <term>Pachacamac</term>—as the Jesuits among the <term>Bantu</term> used <term>Mpungu</term>—as a leverage point for the introduction of Christianity. They preferred to regard <term>Pachacamac</term> as a fraudulent fiend. Now <term>Nzambi Mpungu</term>, among the <term>Bantu</term>, is certainly not a creation of a learned priesthood, for the <term>Bantu</term> have no learned priests, and <term>Mpungu</term> would be useless to the greedy conjurers whom they do consult, as he is not propitiated. On grounds of analogy, then, <term>Pachacamac</term> may be said to resemble a savage Supreme Being, somewhat etherealized either by <term>Garcilasso</term> or by the <term>Amautas</term>, the learned class among the subjects of the <term>Incas</term>. He does not seem, even so, much superior to the <term>Ahone</term> of the <term>Virginians</term>.
