The best version is that of Christoval de Molina, who was chaplain of the hospital for the natives and wrote between 1570 and 1584.¹ Christoval assembled a number of old priests and other natives who had taken part in the ancient services and collected their evidence. He calls the Creator ('not born of woman, unchangeable and eternal') by the name Pachayachachi, 'Teacher of the world,' and 'Tecsiviracocha,' which Garcilasso dismisses as meaningless.² He also tells the tale of Inca Yupanqui and the Lord of the Sun but says that the Incas already had knowledge of the Creator. To Yupanqui, he attributes the erection of a gold image of the Creator, which is utterly denied by Garcilasso.³ Christoval declares—again contradicted by Garcilasso—that sacrifices were offered to the Creator. Unlike the Sun, Christoval says, the Creator had no woman assigned to him, 'because, as he created them, they all belonged to him' (p. 26), which, of course, is an idea that would also make sacrifice superfluous.

Christoval gives prayers in Quichua, in which the Creator is addressed as *Uiracocha*.

Christoval assigns images, sacrifice, and even human sacrifice to the Creator Uiracocha. Garcilasso denies that the Creator <term>Pachacamac</term> had any of these things; he denies that Uiracocha was the name of the Creator, and he denies it even though he knew that the Spaniards made the assertion.⁴ Who is right? Uiracocha, says Garcilasso, is one thing, with his sacrifices; the Creator, <term>Pachacamac</term>, without sacrifices, is another—he is GOD.

Mr. Markham thinks that Garcilasso, writing when he did and not consciously exaggerating, was nevertheless less trustworthy (though 'wonderfully accurate') than Christoval.

# THE MAKING OF RELIGION

Garcilasso, however, is "scrupulously truthful."¹ "The excellence of his memory is perhaps best shown in his topographical details. . . . He does not make a single mistake," in the topography of three hundred and twenty places! A scrupulously truthful gentleman, endowed with an amazing memory and a master of his native language, flatly contradicts the version of a Spanish priest who also appears to have been careful and honorable.

I shall now show that Christoval and Garcilasso have different versions of the same historical events, and that Garcilasso bases his refutation of the Spanish theory of the Inca Creator on his version of this historical tradition, which follows:

The Inca <term>Yahuarhuaccac</term>, like George II, was at odds with his Prince of Wales. He therefore banished the Prince to Chita and made him serve as a shepherd of the llamas of the Sun. Three years later, the disgraced Prince came to court with what the Inca regarded as a cock-and-bull story of an apparition of the kind technically styled "<term>Borderland</term>." Whether he was asleep or awake he did not know, but he saw a bearded, robed man holding a strange animal. The apparition declared himself to be <term>Uiracocha</term> (Christoval’s name for the Creator), a Child of the Sun—by no means <term>Pachacamac</term>, the Creator of the Sun. He announced a distant rebellion and promised his aid to the Prince. Upon hearing this narrative, the Inca replied in the tone of Charles II when he said of Monmouth, "Tell James to go to hell!"² The predicted rebellion, however, broke out; the Inca fled, the Prince saved the city, dethroned his father, and sent him into the country. He then adopted the throne name <term>Uiracocha</term> from the apparition, grew a beard, and dressed like the apparition, to whom he built a temple that was roofless and unique in its construction.

In that place, he had an image of the god, for which he himself gave frequent sittings. When the Spaniards arrived—who were bearded men—the Indians called them Uiracochas (as all the Spanish historians say). To flatter them, the Indians falsely declared that Uiracocha was their word for the Creator. Garcilasso debunks the Spanish etymology of the name using the language of Cuzco, which he "learned from birth." "The Indians said that the prominent Spaniards were children of the Sun to turn them into gods, just as they said they were children of the apparition, Uiracocha."<note>Garcilasso, ii. 68.</note> Moreover, Garcilasso and Cieza de Leon agree in their descriptions of the statue of Uiracocha. Both assert that the Spaniards believed it represented an early Christian missionary, perhaps St. Bartholomew.<note>Cieza de Leon, p. 357.</note> Garcilasso had seen the mummy of the Inca Uiracocha and relates the whole story from his uncle's oral account, adding many native comments on the court revolution described.

To Garcilasso, then, the prayers to Uiracocha in Christoval’s collection are a native adaptation to Spanish bias; even in those prayers, the name Pachacamac appears.<note>Rites, pp. 28, 29.</note>

Now, Christoval has obtained a variation of Garcilasso’s narrative, which, in Garcilasso's version, contains plenty of humor and human nature. According to Christoval, it was not the Prince (later Inca Uiracocha) who saw the apparition, but rather Inca Uiracocha’s son—the "Prince of Wales" of that period, so to speak—who later became Inca Yupanqui.

Garcilasso corrects Christoval. Uiracocha saw the apparition, as Father Acosta correctly says, and Yupanqui was not the son but the grandson of this Inca Uiracocha.<note>Acosta, book vi. ch. 21; Garcilasso, ii. 88, 89.</note> Uiracocha’s own son was Pachacutec, which simply means "Revolution"; "they say, as a common saying, *Pachamcutin*, which means 'the world changes.'"

Christoval’s version of the story is especially gratifying in one way. Yupanqui saw the apparition in a *piece of crystal*; ‘the apparition vanished, while the piece of crystal remained. The Inca took care of it, and they say that he afterwards saw everything he wanted in it.’ The apparition, in human form and in Inca dress, claimed to be the Sun; and Yupanqui, when he came to the throne, ‘ordered a statue of the Sun to be made, as nearly as possible resembling the figure he had seen in the crystal.’ He commanded his subjects to ‘reverence the new deity, as they had previously worshipped the Creator,’ <note>*Rites*, p. 12.</note> who, therefore, existed before Uiracocha.

Interesting as a proof of Inca crystal-gazing, this legend of Christoval’s cannot compete as evidence with the accounts of Acosta and Garcilasso. The reader, however, must decide whether he prefers Garcilasso’s unpropitiated Pachacamac, or Christoval’s Uiracocha, human sacrifices, and all. <note>*Ibid.*, p. 54.</note>

Mr. Tylor prefers the version of Christoval, making Pachacamac a title of Uiracocha. <note>*Primitive Culture*, ii. 337, 338.</note> He thinks that we have, in Inca religion, an example of ‘a subordinate god’ (the Sun) ‘usurping the place of the supreme deity,’ and ‘the rivalry between the Creator and the divine Sun.’ In China, as we shall see, Mr. Tylor thinks, on the other hand, that Heaven is the older god, and that Shang-ti, the Supreme Being, is the usurper.

The truth in the Uiracocha *versus* Pachacamac controversy is difficult to determine. I confess a preference for Garcilasso, who is so truthful and so wonderfully accurate, rather than for the Spanish priest. It should be noted that Christoval says ‘Chanca-Uiracocha was a *huaca* (sacred place) in Chuqui-chaca.’ <note>*Rites*, p. 29.</note> Now Chuqui-chaca is the very place where, according to Garcilasso, the Inca

Uiracocha built a temple to "his uncle, the Apparition." <note>Garcilasso, ii. 69.</note> Uiracocha, then, the deity who receives human sacrifice, would be a late, royally introduced ancestral god—not a real rival to the Creator, who receives no sacrifice at all. Since he was bearded, his name would be easily transferred to the bearded Spaniards, whose arrival the Inca Uiracocha was said to have predicted. But to call several or all Spaniards by the name given to the Creator would be absurd. Mr. Tylor and Mr. Markham do not refer to the passage in which Christoval obviously obtains a wrong version of the story of the apparition.

There is yet another version of this historical legend, written forty years after Christoval's date by Don Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua. He ranks after Garcilasso and Christoval, but before earlier Spanish writers such as Acosta, who did not know Quichua. According to Salcamayhua, the Inca Uiracocha was like James III: fond of architecture and opposed to war. He gave the kingdom to his illegitimate son, Urca, who was defeated and killed by the Chancas. Uiracocha intended to abandon the contest, but his legitimate son, Yupanqui, saw a handsome youth on a rock who promised him success in the name of the Creator and then vanished. The Prince was victorious, and the Inca Uiracocha retired into private life. This appears to be a mixture of the stories of Garcilasso and Christoval. <note>*Rites and Laws*, p. 91 and following.</note>

It is not, in itself, a point of much importance whether the Creator was called Uiracocha (which, if it means anything, means "sea of grease!"), or whether he was called Pachacamac, "maker of the world," or by both names. The important question is whether the Creator received human sacrifices (according to Christoval) or none at all (according to Garcilasso). As to Pachacamac, we must consult

Mr. Payne, who has the advantage of being a Quichua scholar, considers that Pachacamac combines the conception of a general spirit of living things with that of a Creator or maker of all things. "Pachacamac and the Creator are one and the same," but the conception of Pachayachacic, "ruler of the world," "belongs to the later period of the Incas." <note>Payne, volume 1, page 459.</note> Mr. Payne appears to prefer Christoval’s legend of the Inca crystal-gazer to the rival version of Garcilasso. Garcilasso must, if Mr. Payne is right, have been a deliberate liar, unless, indeed, he was deceived by his Inca kinsfolk. The reader can now estimate for himself the difficulty of knowing much about Peruvian religion, or, indeed, of any religion. For, if Mr. Payne is right about the lowest savages having no conception of God, or even of spirit, though the idea of a great Creator, a spirit, is one of the earliest efforts of "primitive logic," we, of course, have been merely fabling throughout.

Garcilasso’s evidence, however, seems untainted by Christian attempts to find a primitive divine tradition. Garcilasso may possibly be refining on facts, but he asks for no theory of divine primitive tradition in the case of Pachacamac, whom he attributes to philosophical reflection.

No authority can be better than that of traditional sacred chants found among a people who will not sing them before one of their Mexican masters.

Let us examine a case of anthropological bias. The Fijians, as we learned from Williams, have ancestral gods and also a unique form of creative being, Ndengei, or, as Mr. Lorimer Fison calls him, Degei. Mr. Fison writes: "It is clear that the Fijians humanized their gods because they had once existed on earth in human form. . . . Like other primitive people, the Fijians deified their ancestors." Yet the Fijians "may have forgotten the names of their ancestors three generations back"! How in the world can you deify a person whom you do not remember? Moreover, only malevolent chiefs were deified, so apparently a Fijian god is really a well-born human scoundrel, so significant that *he* for one is not forgotten—just as if we worshipped the wicked Lord Lyttelton! Of course, a god like Ahone could not be made out of such materials as these, and, in fact, we learn from Mr. Fison that there are other Fijian gods of a different origin.

> "It is probable that there were, here and there, gods who were the creation of the priests who ministered to them and were not the spirits of dead chiefs. Such was the god of the Bure Tribe on the Ra coast, who was called Tui Laga or 'Lord of Heaven.' When the missionaries first went to convert this town, they found the pagan priest to be their staunch ally. He declared that they had come to preach the same god that he had been preaching, the Tui Laga, and that more had been revealed to them than to him concerning the mysteries of the god."

Mr. Fison is reminded of St. Paul at Athens: "The one whom you worship in ignorance, him I proclaim to you."¹

At this point, critics might naturally remark that whether the savage Supreme Being is celebrated, as by the Comanches, who offer puffs of smoke; or is apparently half-forgotten, as by the Algonquins and Zulus; whether he is appeased by sacrifice (which is very rare indeed), or only by behavior, I still claim him as the probable evolutionary descendant of the primitive, undifferentiated, not necessarily "spiritual" Being found in creeds like those of the Australians.

It is consistent with the universal primitive theory of Death, whereas the animistic hypothesis is, in this case, inconsistent. Finally, as has been said before, if we accept my opinion that there are <gloss>two streams of religious thought</gloss>—one arising from the concept of an undifferentiated Being who is eternal, moral, and creative, and the other arising from the ghost-doctrine—it stands to reason that the latter, being better suited to daily needs and experiences (both normal and supernatural), might contaminate the former. This would introduce sacrifice and food offerings into the rituals of Beings who, by the original conception, "need nothing of ours." At the same time, once the concept of "spirit" was attained, it would inevitably be attached to the idea of the Supreme Being, even if he was not at first conceived of as a spirit. We know from our own experience how difficult it has become for us to imagine an eternal, powerful, and immortal being as anything other than a spirit. Yet this way of viewing the Supreme Being merely as *being*, and not as spirit, must have existed, assuming that the idea of spirit finds its expression in the concept of a "ghost." By their very definition, the high gods of indigenous peoples are not ghosts, and never were ghosts, but existed before death.

Here, let me introduce as an example a Supreme Being who is not from the lowest primitive level. Metaphysically, his description is more refined, but morally he is stained with the worst crimes of the hungry ghost-god or a deity modeled on the lines of animism. Taa-roa was "uncreated, existing from the beginning, or from the time he emerges from the *po*, or world of darkness." Now this kind of horror, human sacrifice, is unknown, I think, in early religions of Supreme Beings, such as those in Australia, among the Bushmen, the Andamanese, and so on. I therefore suggest that in an advanced polytheism, such as that of Polynesia, the evil sacrificial rites unpracticed by primitive groups come to be attached even to the worship of the Supreme Being. Ghosts and ghost-gods demanded food, and food was therefore also offered to the Supreme Being.

It was found difficult, or impossible, to induce Christian converts in Polynesia to repeat the old prayers. They began, trembled, and abstained. They had a ritual "for almost every act of their lives," a thing unfamiliar to more primitive peoples. In fact, beyond all doubt, religious criminal acts—from human sacrifice to the burning of Joan of Arc—increase as religion and culture move away from the stage of the Bushmen and Andamanese to the stage of Aztec and Polynesian culture. The Supreme Being is replaced in advancing civilization, and under the influences of animism, by ruthless and insatiable ghost-gods, full of the worst human qualities. Thus, there is what we may really call a moral and religious degeneration that inevitably accompanies early progress.

We shall now try to demonstrate that this is the case—that the first advances in culture necessarily introduce religious degeneration. But we may observe, in passing, that our array of moral or noble supreme beings of primitive peoples (the first that came to hand) will, for some reason, not be found in anthropological treatises on the Origin of Religion. ## XV

### *THE OLD DEGENERATION THEORY*

If any supporter of the anthropological theory has read this far into the argument, he will likely have often whispered to himself, "The old degeneration theory!" Regarding this, Dr. Brinton remarked in 1868:

> "The assumption that in ancient times and in very unenlightened conditions, before mythology had developed, a monotheism existed which was later revived by reformers at various times, is a belief that should have vanished when the pleasures of savage life and the praises of a state of nature stopped being the favorite subjects of philosophers."<note>¹ *Myths of the New World*, p. 44.</note>

"The old degeneration theory" practically, and mistakenly, resulted in two assumptions—as Mr. Tylor says—"first, that the history of culture began with the appearance on earth of a semi-civilized race of men; and second, that from this stage culture has proceeded in two ways—backward to produce savages, and forward to produce civilized men."<note>² *Primitive Culture* i. 35.</note> That hypothesis is proven false by everything we know about evolution.

The hypothesis tentatively supported here makes no such assumptions at all. It is a positive fact that among some of the lowest savages there exists, not a doctrinal and abstract Monotheism, but a belief in a moral, powerful, kind, and creative Being; this faith is found side-by-side with a belief in ghosts that are not worshipped, totems,

<summary>The author clarifies that his argument is not the "old degeneration theory," which mistakenly assumed that humanity began in a semi-civilized state before declining into savagery. Instead, he points to the factual existence of high moral deities among even the most primitive peoples as a complex reality that exists alongside other beliefs like animism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that certain primitive beliefs in a creative Supreme Being are more morally "pure" than those of more advanced cultures, suggesting that the development of ancestor worship and spirit-propitiation actually introduced more "degenerate" practices like sacrifice.</meta>

Now, it is a simple matter of fact, and not an assumption, that the Supreme Being of many relatively more advanced primitive cultures differs from the Supreme Being of certain less advanced cultures. This difference lies in the neglect he suffers, the detached "epicurean" repose attributed to him, and his relative lack of moral control over human conduct. In his place, a crowd of ghosts and spirits—believed to be powerful and helpful in daily life—attract people's attention and worship, and are paid through sacrifice—even through human sacrifice.

Turning to races even higher in material culture, we find a crowd of hungry and cruel gods.

On this point, Mr. Jevons remarks—in agreement with my own observations—that "human sacrifice appears at a much earlier period in rites for the dead than it does in rituals for the gods."¹ The dead chief requires servants and wives in the afterlife <note>Hades</note>, who are offered to him. The Australians show some elements of cannibalism but do not, as a general rule, offer any human victims. Therefore, to this extent, ancestor worship introduced a sadly "degenerate" ritual when compared to the moral faith in gods who do not require feeding.

In some cases, human sacrifice was probably extended to the gods either by a cannibalistic civilized race, like the Aztecs, or by way of *piacula* <note>expiatory sacrifices</note>; the god was conciliated for human sin by the offering of what man valued most, with the "jealousy" of the god being appeased in a similar way. But these are relatively advanced concepts that are not found, to my knowledge, among the most primitive and least developed races. Therefore, the progression toward the idea of a spirit

Undeniably, these hungry, cruel gods are a degeneration from the Australian "Father in Heaven," who receives no sacrifice except for that of men's lusts and selfishness; who desires obedience, not the fat of kangaroos; who needs nothing of ours; and who is neither fed nor bribed. Thus, in this specific respect, the degeneration of religion from the Australian or Andamanese standard to the Dinka standard—and infinitely more to the Polynesian, Aztec, or popular Greek standard—is as undeniable as any fact in human history.

Anthropology has only avoided recognizing this circumstance by establishing a rule—demonstrably not based on facts—that "the divine sanction of ethical laws . . . belongs almost or entirely to religions above the savage level, not to the earlier and lower creeds;" and that "savage Animism is almost devoid of that ethical element which to the educated modern mind is the very mainspring of practical religion." ¹

Indeed, I have argued that the God of "low savages" who provides the divine sanction of ethical laws is *not* of animistic origin. But even where Mr. Im Thurn finds nothing in Guiana but Animism of the lowest conceivable type, he also finds in that Animism the only or most powerful moral restraint on human conduct.

This question will be discussed later; but, unless new facts are discovered, we must accept the version of the Pentateuch or resort to conjecture.

Darumulun is, so far, in line with our own ideas of divinity because he is not localized. He does not dwell in temples made with hands; it is not likely that he should, when his worshippers have neither house, tent, nor tabernacle. As Mr. Robertson Smith says, “where the God had a house or a temple, we recognize the work of men who were no longer pure nomads, but had begun to establish fixed homes.” By the nature of Australian society, Darumulun could not be tied to a temple; consequently, temple rituals—and the myths created to explain those rituals—could not arise. Nor could Darumulun be attached to a specific district, just as “the nomad Arabs could not adopt the concept of a god as a landowner and apply it to their own tribal deities, for the simple reason that in the desert, private property in land was unknown.”¹

Darumulun is thus not capable of degenerating into “*a local god, such as Baal, or lord of the land*,” because this “*involves a series of ideas unknown to the primitive life of the savage hunter*,” like the widely spread Murring tribes.²

Nor could Darumulun be tied down to a place in the Semitic fashion—first by manifesting himself there, then by receiving an altar of sacrifice there, and finally a sanctuary—for Darumulun receives no sacrifice at all.

Mr. Robertson Smith has pointed out, again, the way in which the different political developments of the East and West affected the religion of Greece and of the Semites. In Greece, monarchy fell early on to the aristocratic families. The result was ‘a divine aristocracy of many gods, modified only by a faint memory of the old kingship in the not very effective sovereignty’ (or <term>prytany</term>) ‘of Zeus. In the East, the national god tended to acquire a truly monarchical influence.’¹

Australia escaped polytheistic degeneration by having no aristocracy, unlike Polynesia, where aristocracy—as in early Greece—had developed polytheism. The Australians knew of ghosts and spirits, but not polytheistic gods nor specialized deities of war, agriculture, or art. The early people had no agriculture, and their social condition was not divided into specialized departments. In yet another way, political progress produces religious degeneration, if we consider polytheism to be a decline from the concept of a single, relatively supreme moral being. To form a nation, several tribes must unite. Each has its own god, and the nation is likely to accept them all equally into its pantheon. Thus, if worshippers of Baiame, Pundjel, and Darumulun merged into a single nation, we might find all three gods living together in a new polytheism. In fact, granting a relatively pure starting-

Thus, on the whole, Darumulun—or other Supreme Beings of the lowest known savages, men roaming wild when first encountered on a continent inhabited by older types of animals than ours—was (as we define purity) on a much higher plane than the gods of the Greeks and Semites in their earliest known forms. Setting mythology aside and looking only at worship, the God of the Murring or the Kurnai, whose precepts soften the heart, who knows the heart’s secrets, who teaches chastity, respect for age, and unselfishness, who is not restricted by space or place, and who receives no blood from slaughtered humans or beasts, is a concept from which the ordinary polytheistic gods of far more refined peoples have clearly declined. The animistic superstitions wildly based on the belief in the soul have not corrupted him. Furthermore, the social conditions of aristocracy, agriculture, and architecture have not turned him into one of a polytheistic crowd of greedy gods, nor tied him like a Baal to a specific estate, nor confined him to a temple built by human hands. He cannot appear as a ‘God of Battles;’ no *Te Deum* can be sung to him for victory in a cause that might be unjust, for he is the Supreme Being of a specific group of allied local tribes. One of these tribes has no more claim on him than another, and the group as a whole does not, as a body, wage war on another foreign group. The social conditions of his worshippers, then, preserve Darumulun from the obvious stains on the reputation of gods found among much more advanced races.

Once more, the idea of Animism allows for endless expansion. A spirit can be placed anywhere—in any stone, stick, bush, person, hill, or river. A god created on the animistic model can be assigned to any department of human activity, down to sports, or lusts, or the domain of Cloacina. Thus religion becomes a mere

Thus, from every point of view, and on every side, Animism is full of the seeds of religious decline, which do not and cannot exist in what I take to be the earliest known form of the theistic concept: that of a Being about whose metaphysical nature—whether spirit or not—no questions were asked, as Dr. Brinton noted long ago.

That concept alone could neither provide the moral motive of "a soul to be saved," nor satisfy the metaphysical instinct of progressing humanity. To meet these needs—to provide a "soul" with its moral stimulus, and to offer a phrase or idea by which the Deity could be viewed (*that is*, as a *spirit*) by advancing thought—Animism was necessary. The blending of the theistic and the animistic beliefs was essential to religion. However, in the process of animistic development under advancing social conditions, decline was necessarily implied. Therefore, a decline of the theistic concept occurred for a while. The facts are the evidence; and only a sufficient number of contradictory facts can destroy the old theory of Degeneration when it is presented in this form.

It must be repeated that on this theory an explanation is given of what the old Degeneration hypothesis does not explain. Granting a primal religion relatively pure in its beginnings, why did it degenerate?

Arguing elsewhere against this idea, I have asked: What was the *modus* <note>method or manner</note> of degeneration which produced similar results in Christianity, and in African and other religions? How did it work? I am not aware that Mr. Max Müller has answered this question. But how degeneration worked—namely, by Animism replacing Theism—is conspicuously plain on our theory.

Take the early chapters of Genesis, or any primitive creation myth you please. Deathless man is face to face with the Creator. He cannot decline in religion. He cannot offer sacrifice, for the Creator obviously needs nothing, and again, as there is no death, he cannot kill animals for the Creator. But, in one way or another, usually by the breach of a taboo, Death enters the world. Then comes, through the process of evolution, belief in hungry spirits, and belief in spirits who may inhabit stones or sticks; again, there arise priests who know how to appease spirits and how to tempt them into sticks and stones. These arts become profitable and are backed by the cleverest men, and by the apparent evidence of prophecies by convulsionaries <note>individuals who experienced religious fits or seizures</note>. Thus, every known kind of degeneration in religion is inevitably introduced as a result of the theory of Animism. We do not need a hypothesis of Original Sin as a cause of degeneration, and, if Mr. Max Müller’s doctrine of the Infinite were viable, we have supplied, in Animism—under advancing social conditions—what he does not seem to provide: a cause and *modus* of degeneration. Fetishism would thus be really 'secondary,' *ex hypothesi* <note>according to the hypothesis</note>, but as we nowhere find Fetishism alone, without the other elements of religion, we cannot say, historically, whether it is secondary or not. ## XVI

### *THEORIES OF JEHOVAH*

All speculation on the early history of religion tends to end in the effort to see how far the conclusions can be made to illustrate the faith of Israel. Thus, the theorist who believes in ancestor worship as the key to all creeds will see in Jehovah a developed ancestral ghost, or a kind of fetish-god attached to a stone—perhaps an ancient sepulchral stele <note>a carved stone slab used for commemorative purposes</note> of some desert sheikh. The exclusive admirer of the hypothesis of Totemism will find evidence for his belief in the worship of the golden calf and the bulls. The partisan of nature worship will insist on Jehovah's connection with storms, thunder, and the fire of Sinai. On the other hand, whoever accepts our suggestions will be inclined to see, in the early forms of belief in Jehovah, a version of the widely diffused concept of a Moral Supreme Being, at first (or, at least, when our information begins) envisioned in human-like form, but gradually cleansed of all local traits by the unparalleled and unique inspiration of the great Prophets. They, as far as our knowledge extends, were strangely indifferent to the animistic element in religion—to the doctrine of surviving human souls—and so, of course, to that element of Animism which is invaluable: the purification of the soul in the light of the hope of eternal life. Just as the Prophets' hunger for righteousness is intense, so their hope of finally satisfying that hunger in an eternity of sinless bliss and enjoyment of God is admittedly

inconspicuous. In short, they have carried Theism to its austere extreme—"though He slay me, yet will I trust in Him"—while remaining unconcerned about the rewards of Animism. This is certainly a strange result for a religion which, according to the anthropological theory, has Animism as its basis.

We therefore examine certain forms of the animistic hypothesis as applied to account for the religion of Israel. The topic is one in which special knowledge of Hebrew and other Oriental languages seems absolutely indispensable; but anthropological speculators have not been Oriental scholars (with rare exceptions), while some Oriental scholars have borrowed from popular anthropology without much critical discrimination. These circumstances must be our excuse for venturing onto this difficult ground.

It is probably impossible for us to trace with accuracy the rise of the religion of Jehovah. "The wise and learned" dispute endlessly over the dates of documents, over the amount of later doctrine inserted into the earlier texts, and over the nature, source, and quantity of foreign influence—Chaldean, Accadian, Egyptian, or Assyrian. We know that Israel had, at an early age, the conception of the moral Eternal; we know that, at an early age, that conception was contaminated and anthropomorphized; and we know that it was rescued, to a great degree, from this corruption, while always retaining its original ethical aspect and sanction. Why matters went this way in Israel and not elsewhere we do not know, except that such was the will of God in the mysterious education of the world. How mysterious that education has been is best known to all who have studied the political and social results of Totemism. On the face of it, it is a perfectly crazy and degrading belief—on the face of it, it meant nothing

An example of anthropological theory concerning Jehovah was put forth by Mr. Huxley. <note>Science and Hebrew Tradition.</note> Mr. Huxley’s general idea of religion as it exists on the lowest known level of material culture—through which the ancestors of Israel must have passed like other people—has already been criticized. He denied to the most backward races both a religious cult and a religious sanction for ethics. He was demonstrably, though unintentionally, in error regarding the facts, and therefore could not start from the idea that Israel, in the lowest historically known condition of savagery, possessed—or, like other races, might possess—the belief in an Eternal Being that promotes righteousness.

It is clear that, for whatever reason, ancestor-worship among the Hebrews was, at most, rudimentary. Otherwise, it would have been clearly denounced by the Prophets along with the other heresies of Israel. Therefore, because it was at most rudimentary, ancestor-worship in Israel could not have developed immediately into the worship of Jehovah.

Though ancestor-worship among the Hebrews could not be fully developed according to Mr. Spencer—due to their nomadic habits—it *was* fully developed according to the Reverend A. W. Oxford. He writes, "Every family, like every ancient Roman and Greek family, was firmly held together by the worship of its ancestors; the hearth was the altar, and the head of the family was the priest. . . . The bond that kept the families of a tribe together was its common religion: the worship of its reputed ancestor. The chief of the tribe was, of course, the priest of the cult." Of course; but what a pity that Mr. Huxley and Mr. Spencer omitted facts so invaluable to their theory! And how does the Reverend Mr. Oxford know this? Well, "there is no direct proof," oddly enough, of such a marked feature in Hebrew religion, but we are referred to 1 Samuel 20:29 and Judges 18:19. 1 Samuel 20:29 has Jonathan say that David wants to go to a family sacrifice—that is, a family dinner party. This hardly supports the large assertions made by Mr. Oxford. His second citation is so unfortunate that it contradicts his observation that "of course" the chief of the tribe was the priest of the cult. This particular example of *Elohim* was a phantasm of the dead, but *Elohim* is also used for the highest Divine Being; therefore, the highest Divine Being is of the same genus as a ghost—so Mr. Huxley reasons. "The difference which was supposed to exist between the different *Elohim* was one of degree, not of kind." <note>1. *Science and Hebrew Tradition*, p. 299.</note>

"If Jehovah was thus supposed to differ only in degree from the undoubtedly animal-shaped or human-shaped 'gods of the nations,' why is it to be assumed that he also was not thought to have a human shape?" He *was* thought to have a human shape at one time by some theorists; no doubt exists on that point. That, however, is not where we object. We object when, because an hallucination of the Witch of Endor (probably still incompletely developed) is called *Elohim* by her, the highest *Elohim* is said by Mr. Huxley to differ from a ghost only in degree, not in kind. *Elohim*, or *El*, the creator, differs from a ghost in kind because he, in Hebrew belief, never was a ghost; he is immortal and without beginning.

He and other "original gods" that he created are carefully and absolutely distinguished from the *atua*, which are "the human soul after its separation from the body." All Tongan gods are *atua* (*Elohim*), but not all *atua* are "original gods." These original gods are not served by priests and are not offered food or drink offerings, unlike the highest God, Tá-li-y-Tooboo, the Eternal of Tonga. "He occasionally inspires the How" (the elective King), but often a How is not inspired by Tá-li-y-Tooboo at all, just as Saul, in the end, was no longer inspired by Jehovah.

Surely there is a difference in kind between an eternal, immortal God and a ghost, even though both are called *atua* or *Elohim*—the unknown X.

Many people call a ghost "supernatural"; they also call God "supernatural," but I believe they would admit that there is a difference in kind between the ghost of a dead man and the Deity. We have shown, or tried to show, that the concepts of "ghost" and "Supreme Being" are different, not only in nature but in origin. The ghost comes from and depends on the theory of animism; the Supreme Being, as originally conceived, does not. All Gods are *Elohim*, *kalou*, or *wakan*; but not all *Elohim*, *kalou*, or *wakan* are Gods.

A ghost-god should receive food or drink offerings. Mr. Huxley says that Tá-li-y-Tooboo did so. In the case of Tá-li-y-Tooboo, "there is no cup filled for the god." <note>Mariner, ii. 205.</note> "Before any cup is filled the man by the side of the bowl says: 'The Kava is in the cup'" (which it is not), "and the *mataboole* answers, 'Give it to your god;'" but the Kava is *not* in the cup, and the Tongan Eternal receives no oblation.

The sacrifice, says Mr. Huxley, meant "that the god was either a deified ghost, or, at any rate, a being of like nature to these." <note>Science and Hebrew Tradition, p. 335.</note> But as Tá-li-y-Tooboo had no sacrifice, contrary to Mr. Huxley's assertion, he was not "a deified ghost, or a being of like nature to these." To the lower, non-ghostly Tongan gods the animistic habit of sacrifice had been extended, but not yet to the Supreme Being.

Ah, if Mr. Gladstone, or the Duke of Argyll, or some bishop had made a misstatement of this kind, how Mr. Huxley would have crushed him! But it is a mere error of careless reading, such as we all make daily.

It is obvious that we cannot prove Jehovah to be a ghost by the parallel of a Tongan god, who, by ritual and by definition, was *not* a ghost. The proof therefore rests on the anthropomorphized pre-prophetic accounts, and on the ritual, of Jehovah. But man naturally "anthropomorphizes" his deities: he does not thereby demonstrate that they were once ghosts.

As regards the sacrifices to Jehovah, the sweet savor which he was supposed to enjoy (contrary to the opinion of the Prophets), these sacrifices afford the best presumption that Jehovah was a ghost-god, or a god constructed on ghostly lines.

If then (as in the case of Taa-roa), a Supreme Being does receive sacrifice, we may argue that a piece of <term>animistic ritual</term>—not connected with the Supreme Being in Australia or the Andaman Islands, and not connected with his creed in Virginia or Africa (where ghost-gods do receive sacrifice)—may in other regions be transferred from ghost-gods to the Supreme Being, who never was a ghost. There seems to be nothing unbelievable or illogical in the theory of such <term>transference</term>.

Men may come to bestow sacrifices on a God who never was a ghost (sacrifices which are not made to Baiame and the others) because, being in the habit of appeasing one set of bodiless powers in this way, they may not think it polite or safe to leave another set of powers out. By his very nature, man must attribute some human passions and qualities to all gods, unless—like many primitive peoples—he leaves his High God strictly alone and becomes a slave to fetishes and spirits. But that practice argues against the <term>ghost-theory</term>.

In the attempt to explain the sacrifices to Jehovah in this way—namely, by <term>transference</term>—we encounter a difficulty of our own making. If the Israelites did not sacrifice to ancestors (as we have shown there is very little reason to suppose they did), how could they transfer to Jehovah the rite which, according to our hypothesis, they are not proven to have offered to ancestors?

We then find a historical tradition of secular contact between Israel and Egypt, from which Israel emerges with Jehovah for God and a system of sacrifices. Regarding Jehovah as a revived memory of the moral Supreme Being whom Israel must have known in extremely remote ages (unless Israel was less favored than Australians, Bushmen, or Andamanese), we might look on the sacrifices to him as an adaptation from the practices of religion among races more settled and more civilized than Israel.¹

Speculation on subjects so remote must be conjectural, but our suggestion would, perhaps, account for sacrifices to Jehovah, paid by a race which, by reason of "nomadic habits," was never much given to ancestor-worship, but had been in contact with great sacrificing, polytheistic civilizations. One might look for examples of such a thing in any known race, at any stage of culture. Peru will not provide an example—it is not the Creator, Pachacamac, but the Sun who is the god of the Inca family. If, on the other hand, Jehovah was a Kenite god, the Kenites were a semi-Arab Semitic people connected with Israel and might very well have retained traditions of a Supreme Being which, in Egypt, were likely to be obscured by foreign religions, as the book of Exodus asserts. The learned Stade, to be sure, may doubt Israel’s stay in Egypt, but that revolutionary opinion is not necessarily binding for us and presents several difficulties.

Whatever all this may mean, it does not look as if Zipporah expected such rites as circumcision in the faith of a Kenite husband, nor does it support the idea that the <term>sacra</term> of Moses were of Kenite origin.

Regarding criticism, one may protest against presenting a theory to the manual-reading intellectual middle classes that is as vague, contradictory, and (by any analogy) as impossible as the one Mr. Oxford collects from German writers. Of course, the entire subject, which is handled so dogmatically, is merely a matter of differing opinions among scholars. Thus, M. Renan derives the name of Jehovah from Assyria, specifically from ‘Aramaized Chaldeanism.’¹ In that case, the name existed long before the residence in Egypt. But then again, perhaps Jehovah was a local god of Sinai, or a provincial deity in Palestine.² He was known to very ancient sages, who preferred names like El Shaddai and Elohim. In short, we have no certainty on the matter.³

Perhaps I hardly need to say that I have no outdated prejudice against Biblical criticism. Certainly, the Bible must be studied like any other collection of documents—linguistically, historically, and through the comparative method. For example, the leading ideas of Wellhausen are notable for their shrewdness; even the most ordinary layman can see that. But one may protest against criticizing the Bible, or Homer, using methods similar to those used to prove that Shakespeare was actually Bacon. One must also protest against presenting inconsistent and probably unfounded critical hypotheses with the dogmatic brevity found in cheap handbooks.

Furthermore, where does the moral element in Jehovah come from? Mr. Huxley thinks it possibly originated from the ethical practices and theories of Egypt. In the Egyptian *Book of the Dead*, ‘a kind of guide to the spirit world,’ there are moral chapters; the spirit tells his judges in Amenti which sins he has not committed. Many of

From the mysteries of Mtanga or Pundjel, he might have also learned—had he been present—to love his neighbor as himself. If the creed of Jehovah, or of El, retained only as much ethics as is under divine sanction among the Kurnai people, adapting it from the *Book of the Dead* was unnecessary.

Caring for the departed, the ritual of the <term>Ka</term>, and the intense preoccupation with the afterlife—which are the essential characteristics of the *Book of the Dead* far more than its morality—are things Israel cared nothing about. They brought none of these animistic things, or very little of them, out of the land of Egypt. Moses was certainly very selective; he took only the morality of Egypt. But since Mr. Huxley offers this opinion tentatively, acknowledging there is no secure historical authority regarding Moses, it hardly answers our question: Where did the moral element in Jehovah come from? One might guess that it was a survival of the primitive, divinely sanctioned ethics of the ancient ancestors of the Israelites. These ethics were known to them—just as they are to the Kurnai—before they had a pot, a bronze knife, seeds to sow, sheep to herd, or even a tent over their heads. In the eternal plan, Israel was chosen to keep that flame burning, however obscured by the smoke of sacrifice—that flame which illuminates the darkest places of the earth: "a light to bring revelation to the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel." History cannot tell us how that flame was lit or from where that light shines, and anthropology can only speculate. Here, scientific ignorance is wiser than the overconfidence of popular science, with its ghosts, fetish-stones, and gods that sprang from

It appears, then, if our general suggestion is accepted, that what occurred in the development of the Hebrew religion was precisely what the Bible tells us did occur. This must inevitably seem highly paradoxical to our generation, but the entire direction of our proposed system supports this paradox. If nomadic, primitive Israel possessed the higher religious concepts proven to exist among several of the most primitive known races, these concepts might have been revived by a brilliant leader. During a crisis in the tribe's history, they could have become the rallying point for a new national sentiment. Though somewhat obscured by exposure to "the idols of Egypt" and limited and localized by the very national spirit they encouraged, these concepts were purified and expanded far beyond any local, tribal, or national boundaries—extended as far as the *flammantia mœnia mundi* <note>The flaming walls of the world</note>—by the historically unique genius of the Prophets. Combined with the doctrine of our Lord, and enhanced by the addition of <term>Animism</term> in its pure and invaluable form—the reward of faith, hope, and charity in eternal life—the faith of Israel enlightened the world.

All this is exactly what happened, according to the Old and New Testaments. All this is precisely what, according to our hypothesis, might be expected to occur if—out of the many races which, in their most primitive culture, had a basic concept of a Moral Creative Being who was relatively supreme—one race underwent the education of Israel, showed Israel's relative indifference to <term>Animism</term> and ghost-gods, listened to the Prophets of Israel, and gave birth to one greater than Moses and the Prophets.

To this result the <term>Logos</term> <note>The Word or Reason</note>, as Socrates says, has led us through the path of <term>anthropology</term>.

## XVII

### CONCLUSION

We may now look back at the path which we have tried to cut through the jungles of early religions. It is not a highway, but the track of a lone explorer; and this essay claims to be no more than a sketch—not an exhaustive survey of creeds. Its limitations are obvious, but they may be stated here. The higher and even the lower polytheisms are only mentioned in passing, as our object is to keep clearly in view the concept of a Supreme, or practically Supreme, Being, from the lowest stages of human culture up to Christianity. In polytheism, that concept is necessarily obscured, showing itself dimly either in the *Prytanis*, or President of the Immortals, such as Zeus; or in Fate, behind and above the Immortals; or in Mr. Max Müller’s *Henotheism*, where the god addressed—*Indra*, *Soma*, or *Agni*—is, for the moment, envisioned as supreme and is adored in something like a monotheistic spirit; or, finally, in the etherealized deity of advanced philosophical speculation.

It has not been necessary for our purpose to dwell on these civilized religions. Granting our hypothesis of an early Supreme Being among primitive peoples—obscured later by ancestor worship and ghost-gods, but not often absolutely lost to religious tradition—barbaric and civilized polytheisms easily fall into place and are easily understood. Space forbids a discussion of all known religions; only typical specimens have been

On its higher plane, it appears to consist of the worship of Heaven as a great fetish-god—a worship that may well have begun in days, as Dr. Brinton says, "long before man had asked himself, 'Are the heavens material and is God spiritual?'"—perhaps, for all we know, before the idea of "spirit" had even evolved. The Chinese religion of Heaven is also colored by Chinese political conditions; Heaven (<term>Tien</term>) corresponds to the Emperor and tends to be confused with <term>Shang-ti</term>, the Emperor above. "Dr. Legge accuses Confucius," says Mr. Tylor, "of a tendency to substitute, in his religious teaching, the name of <term>Tien</term> (Heaven) for the one known to more ancient religion and used in older books—<term>Shang-ti</term>, the personal ruling deity." If so, China also has its ancient Supreme Being who is not merely a divinized aspect of nature.

> "It seems, rather, that the sage was, in fact, upholding the tradition of the ancient faith, thus acting according to the character on which he prided himself—that of a transmitter, not a creator; a preserver of old knowledge, not a new revealer."¹

This, of course, is purely a question of evidence to be settled by <term>Sinologists</term>. If the personal Supreme Being, <term>Shang-ti</term>, occupies in older documents the position held by <term>Tien</term> (Heaven) in Confucius’s later system, why should we say that Confucius, by promoting Heaven in place of <term>Shang-ti</term>, was restoring an older concept?

As matters stand, it seems to me probable that ancient China possessed a Supreme Personal Being, more remote and original than Heaven, just as the Zuñis do. On the lower plane, Chinese religion is overrun, as everyone knows, by Animism and ancestor-worship. This is so powerful that it has given rise to a native theory of <term>Euhemerism</term>. The departmental deities of Chinese polytheism are explained by the Chinese on Euhemeristic principles:

> ‘According to legend, the War God, or Military Sage, was once, in human life, a distinguished soldier; the Swine God was a hog-breeder who lost his pigs and died of sorrow; the God of Gamblers was a ruined gambler.’ <note>Abridged from Tylor's *Primitive Culture*, volume 2, page 119.</note>

These are not statements of fact, but reflections of Chinese Euhemeristic theory. On that hypothesis, Confucius should now be a god; but of course he is not; his spirit is merely localized in his temple, where the Emperor worships him twice a year just as ancestral spirits are worshipped.

Every theorist will force facts into harmony with his system, but I do not see that the Chinese facts are contrary to mine. On the highest plane is either a personal Supreme Being, <term>Shang-ti</term>, or there is <term>Tien</term>, Heaven (with Earth, the parent of men), neither of them necessarily owing anything in their origin to Animism. The distinction drawn here is so great and obvious that to prove the case of the German girl, we need better evidence than Coleridge's rumor of a rumor—cited, as it is, by Hamilton, Maudsley, Carpenter, Du Prel, and the usual collection of manuals.

I wish I saw a way for orthodox, unimaginative psychology to escape its dilemma.

After offering these considerations to anthropologists and psychologists—which I purposely repeat—we historically examined the relationship between science and "the marvelous." We showed, for example, how Hume, following his *a priori* theory of the impossible, would have declined to investigate certain occurrences because they were "miraculous," whereas to Charcot, those same occurrences were ordinary incidents in medical experience.

Next, we examined and critiqued the anthropological theory of religion as expounded by Mr. Tylor. We then gathered from his work a series of alleged supernormal phenomena in primitive beliefs, all of which contribute to the foundation of animistic religion. Through several chapters, we pursued the study of these phenomena, choosing primitive examples and placing them alongside civilized testimony regarding similar experiences. Our conclusion was that such civilized experiences—if they occurred among primitive people as they are universally said to do—would help to originate and strongly support the primitive doctrine of souls, which is the basis of religion in the theory of English anthropologists. But regardless of the primitive doctrine of "spirits" (whether they actually exist or not), the evidence points to the existence of human faculties not accounted for in current systems of materialism.

All this, it must be emphatically insisted upon, is proposed "with all reservations." While these four stages—say (1) the Australian unpropitiated Moral Being, (2) the African neglected Being, who is still somewhat moral, (3) the relatively Supreme Being involved in human sacrifice, as in Polynesia, and (4) the Moral Being reinstated philosophically, or in Israel—do suggest steps in evolution, we do not wish to base any hard-and-fast system of ascending and descending degrees upon our current evidence. Nothing excites my own suspicion regarding my provisional hypothesis more than its symmetry. It really seems to fit the facts, as they appear to me, too neatly. I would suggest, however, that ancient savage sacred hymns and practices in the mysteries are actually more like "documents"—at least more so than the casual observations of some travelers, or the gossip extracted from natives who have been in close contact with Europeans.

Supposing that the arguments in this essay were to meet with some acceptance, what effect would they have, if any, on our thoughts about religion? What is their practical tendency? The least certain effect would be, I hope, to prevent us from accepting the anthropological theory of religion, or any other theory, as a foregone conclusion. I have tried to show how dim our knowledge is, how weak our evidence often is, and that—finding among the lowest savages all the elements of all religions already developed in different degrees—we cannot, historically, say that one is earlier than another. This point of priority we can never historically settle. If we met savages with ghosts and no gods, we could not be sure that they did not once possess a God and then forgot Him. If we met savages with a God and no ghosts, we could not be historically certain that a higher creed had not obliterated a lower one. For

For these reasons, dogmatic decisions regarding the *origin of* religion seem unworthy of science. They will appear even more futile to any student who agrees with me enough to doubt whether the highest gods of the most primitive races could be developed, or can be shown to have developed, through the ghost theory. To someone who reaches this point, the entire animistic doctrine of ghosts as the single seed of religion will appear to be in jeopardy. The main practical result, then, will be a hesitation to accept the latest scientific opinion, even when backed by great names and published in introductory textbooks.

<margin>1</margin>
According to the hypothesis offered here for criticism, there are two main sources of Religion: (1) the belief—how it was attained we do not know <note>The hypothesis of St. Paul does not seem to be the most unsatisfactory.</note>—in a powerful, moral, eternal, omniscient, 
<margin>and immortal</margin>
Father and Judge of men; (2) the belief (probably developed from both normal and supernormal experiences) in something in man that may survive the grave. This second belief is not, logically, required as the basis for the first, in its seemingly earliest form. For all we know, it may be the later of the two beliefs chronologically. But this belief, too, was necessary to religion: first, because it eventually provided a formula through which developing minds could conceive of the Mighty Being involved in the former creed; and next, because it elevated man's conception of his own nature. Through the second belief, he becomes the child of the God in whom he perhaps already trusted, and in whom he has his being—a being not destined to perish with the death of the body. Man is thus not only the child but the heir of God, a 'nurseling of immortality,' capable of entering into eternal life. It is unnecessary to dwell on the moral influence of this belief.

In the religion of our Lord and the Apostles, these two currents—faith in one righteous God and concern for the individual soul—were purified and joined together. "God is a Spirit, and those who worship Him must worship Him in spirit and in truth." Man is also a spirit and, as such, is in the hands of a God who cannot be appeased by human sacrifice or monastic rituals. We know how this doctrine was later disrupted by what was essentially animism, and by the sacrifices and rituals of the Medieval Church. Being too eager "to be all things to all men," the noble and charitable Mother of Christendom allowed the earlier animism to return in new forms, such as the worship of saints, pilgrimages, and popular ceremonies—things separate from, yet often mistakenly thought to be substitutes for, living a righteous life and practicing the selflessness commanded even in primitive rituals. These things, such as masses for the beloved dead, were established because of both the tenderness and the stubbornness of human hearts.

Modern thought has deanthropomorphized <note>stripped away human-like qualities</note> what remained of the anthropomorphic in religion. In the end, it has left us for God, at most, "a stream of tendency making for righteousness," or an unknown and unknowable energy—the ghost of a ghost. Against this part of modern scientific teaching, the earlier position of this essay suggests an objection. By the aid of the tradition of and belief in <term>supernormal phenomena</term> among primitive peoples, and by attested phenomena of the same kinds of experience among more advanced cultures, I have ventured to try to suggest that “we are not merely brain;” that man has his part—we know not how, in we know not what—and has faculties and vision hardly restricted by the limits of his normal scope. The evidence for all this deals with matters often trivial, like the electric sparks rubbed from a deer’s hide, which are nevertheless related to an infinite, essential power of the universe. Not being able to explain away these facts, or to offer here what would necessarily be a premature theory regarding them, I regard them—though they seem shadowy—as grounds for hope, or, at least, as signs that men do not yet need to despair. This is not the first time that the weak things of the earth have been chosen to confound the strong. Nor have men who held this opinion always been the weakest; not among the feeblest are Socrates, Pascal, Napoleon, Cromwell, Charles Gordon, St. Theresa, and Joan of Arc.

I am fully aware that the “superstitious” nature of the earlier part of this essay must damage any impact which the argument of the latter part might possibly have on critical opinion. ## APPENDIX A
### OPPOSITIONS OF SCIENCE

The most elaborate reply to the arguments for telepathy, based on the Report of the Census of Hallucinations, is that of Herr Parish in his *Hallucinations and Illusions*.¹ Herr Parish is currently opposed to the theory that the Census establishes a telepathic cause in the so-called "coincidental stories," which were put forward, as he says, "with due reserve and based on an astonishing mass of materials, to some extent critically handled."

He first objects to an allowance of twelve hours for the coincidence of a hallucination and a death; but if we reflect that twelve hours is very little time even in a year, it must be admitted that coincidences within twelve hours *donnent à penser* <note>give cause for thought</note>, even if we reject the theory that, assuming a real telepathic impact occurs, it may need time and quiet to develop into a complete hallucination.

We do not need to linger over the very strange cases from Munich, as these are not among the selected thirty in the Report. Herr Parish then focuses on that hallucination of memory in which we feel as if everything currently happening has happened before. Most of us may have experienced being reminded, by some association of ideas during the day, of a dream from the previous night that we had forgotten. For instance, while looking at a bridge over a brook and thinking about how I would fish it, I remembered that I had dreamed the previous night of casting a fly for practice on a lawn. No one would think of disputing the fact that I actually had such a dream,

¹ Walter Scott.

<summary>This appendix begins a rebuttal to Herr Parish’s skepticism regarding the "Census of Hallucinations," specifically defending the significance of hallucinations that coincide with a death within a twelve-hour window. The author also discusses "hallucinations of memory" and the common experience of remembering forgotten dreams through daily associations.</summary>

<keywords>telepathy, Census of Hallucinations, Herr Parish, coincidental hallucinations, hallucination of memory, psychological research, paranormal skepticism</keywords>

forgot it and remembered it when reminded of it by an association of ideas. But if the forgotten dream had been "fulfilled" and recalled to memory only at the moment of fulfillment, science would deny that I ever had such a dream at all. The alleged dream would be described as a "hallucination of memory." It would be said that when something occurred, I had the not very unusual sensation of "This has occurred to me before," and the sensation would become a false memory that it *had* occurred—in a dream. I believe this theory will be proposed not when an ordinary dream is recalled by a waking experience, but only when the dream coincides with and precedes that experience, which is something dreams are not supposed to do. Scientifically speaking, such coincidental dreams are necessarily "false memories." Now, how does this theory of false memory bear on coincidental hallucinations?

The insane, it seems, are likely to have the false memory "This occurred before," and then claim that the event was revealed to them in a vision. <note>1. Parish, p. 278.</note> It might be recommended that the insane make a note of the vision and have it properly witnessed *before* the event. The same remark applies to the "presentiments" of the sane. But it does *not* apply if Jones tells me, "I saw my great-aunt last night," and news arrives *after* this remark that Jones’s aunt died that same night in Timbuktu. Yet Herr Parish (p. 282) seems to think that the argument of false memory fits perfectly, even when a hallucination has been reported to another person before its fulfillment. Of course, everything depends on the honesty of the narrator and the person to whom he told his story. To take a case given: <note>2. Ibid. pp. 282, 283.</note> suppose Brown, traveling with his wife, dreams that a rabid dog bit his son on the elbow at home. He tells his wife. Upon arriving home, Brown finds that it was true. Herr Parish appears to argue as follows:

Brown dreamed nothing at all, but he becomes excited when he hears the bad news at home; through a false memory, he thinks he has a recollection of it. He says to his wife, "My dear, didn’t I tell you last night that I had dreamed all this?" and his equally excited wife replies, "True, my Brown, you *did*, and I said it was only one of your dreams." And now *both* believe that the dream occurred.

This is very plausible, is it not? Science would only say nothing about it if the dream had *not* been fulfilled—if Brown had remarked, "Goodness, my dear, seeing that horse reminds me that I was dreaming last night of driving in a dog-cart." For then Brown was not excited.

None of this exquisite reasoning regarding dreams applies to waking hallucinations reported before the alleged coincidence, unless we accept a collective hallucination of memory in the seer or seers, and also in the people to whom their story was told.

But it is obvious that memory is inclined to become <term>mythopoeic</term>, to the point of exaggerating the closeness of a coincidence and adding romantic details. We do not need Herr Parish to tell us *that*; we encounter this circumstance in all narratives based on memory, whatever the topic, even in Herr Parish’s own writings.

We must admit that the public, in ghostly stories as in all narratives on any topic, is prone to "fanciful additions." Therefore, as Herr Parish justly remarks, we should "maintain a very skeptical attitude toward all accounts" of <term>veridical</term> hallucinations. "Not that we should dismiss them as old wives’ fables—an all-too-common method—or even doubt the narrator’s good faith." We should treat them like tales of big fish that get away; sometimes there is good corroborative evidence that they *really were* big fish, and sometimes not. We shall return to these false memories.

Was there a coincidence at all in the Society’s cases printed in the Census? Herr Parish thinks three of the selected twenty-six cases are very dubious. In one case, there is a possible margin of four days; another (wrongly numbered, by the way) does not appear at all among the twenty-six. In the third, Herr Parish is wrong in his statement.<margin>¹ Page 287, Mr. Sims, *Proceedings*, x. 230.</margin> This is a fine example of skeptical sloppiness and, accompanied by the miscitation of the second case, shows that inaccuracy is not entirely on the side of the seers. However, the case is not very good, as the two percipients imagined that the date of the event was more recent than it really was. Unfortunately, Herr Parish only criticizes these three cases—as we have noted, with varying accuracy. He had no room for more.

He then offers the astonishing statement that, "in the view of the English authors—a view that is, of course, assumed in all calculations of this kind—a hallucination persists just as long in the memory and is just as easily recalled in response to a question, whether the experience made only a slight impression on the observer, or affected them deeply, as would be the case, for instance, if the hallucination had been found to coincide with the death of a close relative or friend."¹ This assertion by Herr Parish is so incorrect that the Report specifically says that "as years recede into the distance," the proportion of hallucinations that are remembered compared to those which are forgotten, or at least ignored, "is very large." Yet Herr Parish claims that, in all calculations, it is assumed that hallucinations are just as easily recalled whether they are impressive or not! Once more, the Report says (p. 246), "*It is not the case*" that coincidental (and impressive) hallucinations are as easily forgotten as non-coincidental and non-impressive ones. The editors therefore multiply the non-coincidental cases by four, arguing that no coincidental cases ("hits") are forgotten, while three out of four non-coincidentals ("misses") are forgotten, or may be supposed likely to be forgotten. Immediately after declaring that the English authors assume all hallucinations are equally well remembered (which is the exact opposite of what they actually do say), Herr Parish admits that the authors multiply the "misses" by four, "influenced by other considerations" (p. 289). By what other considerations? They give their reason (that very reason which Herr Parish says they refuse to consider), namely, that "misses" are four times as likely to be forgotten as "hits." "To go into the reason for adopting this plan would lead us too far," he writes. Why, it is the very reason which, he says, is not favored by the English authors!

# APPENDIX A 341

How strangely far from being "coincident" with plain facts, or "veridical" at all, is this scientific criticism! Herr Parish says that a "view" (which does not exist) is "of course assumed in all calculations;" and, on the very same page, he says that it is *not* assumed! "The witnesses of the report—influenced, it is true, by other considerations" (which is not the case), "have sought to turn the point of this objection by multiplying the whole number of (non-coincidental) cases by four." Then the "view" is *not* "assumed in all calculations," as Herr Parish has just asserted.

What led Herr Parish, an honorable and clear-headed critic, into this maze of incorrect and contradictory assertions? It is interesting to try to trace the causes of such non-veridical illusions, to find the *points de repère* <note>reference points</note> of these literary hallucinations. One might suggest that when Herr Parish "rewrote the chapters" of his German edition, as he says in his preface to the English version, he accidentally left in a passage based on an earlier paper by Mr. Gurney,¹ not observing that it was no longer accurate or appropriate.

After this odd passage, Herr Parish argues that a "veridical" hallucination is regarded by the English authors as "coincidental," even when external circumstances have made that very hallucination a probable occurrence by producing "tension of the corresponding nerve element groups." That is to say, a person is in a condition—a nervous condition—likely, *a priori*, to produce a hallucination. A hallucination is produced, quite naturally; and so, if it happens to coincide with an event, the coincidence should not count—it is purely accidental.²

Here is an example. A lady, facing an old sideboard, saw a friend with no coat on, and in a waistcoat with a back of shiny material. Within an hour she was taken to where her friend lay dying, without a coat, and in a waistcoat with a shiny back.³ Here is the scientific explanation of Herr Parish: "The shimmer of a reflecting surface [the sideboard?] formed the occasion for the hallucinatory emergence of a subconsciously perceived shiny black waistcoat [the quotation is incorrect, of course], and an individual subconsciously associated with that impression—"

Herr Parish’s explanation would be brilliantly satisfactory if it were only true to the printed words that lay before his eyes when he wrote. There was no “shiny black waistcoat” in the case, but a waistcoat with a *shiny back*. Gentlemen, and especially old gentlemen who travel in bath-chairs (like the man in this story), do not habitually take off their coats and show the backs of their waistcoats to nineteen-year-old ladies in England. And if Herr Parish had cared to read his case, he would have found it expressly stated that the lady “had never seen the man without his coat” (and so could not associate him with an impression of a shiny back on his waistcoat) until after the hallucination, when she saw him without his coat on his deathbed. The case is dismissed, then, by the aid of the “fanciful additions” to which Herr Parish justly objects. He first gives the facts incorrectly and then explains an occurrence which, as he reported it, did not happen and was not claimed to have happened.

I confess that, if Herr Parish’s version were as correct as it is essentially inaccurate, his explanation would leave me doubtful. For the circumstances were that the old gentleman of the story lunched daily with the young lady’s mother. Suppose that she were familiar (which she was not) with the shiny back of his waistcoat; she still saw him daily, and she was also in the habit of seeing the (hypothetically) shiny surface of the sideboard daily. That being the case, she had every day the materials, both subjective and objective, for the hallucination. Yet it only occurred once, and then it precisely coincided with the death agony of the old gentleman and with his coatless condition. Why only that once? *That is the miracle!* “How much for this little waistcoat?” as the man asked David Copperfield.

His next argument is essentially that hallucinations are always merely a type of dream.<gloss>1</gloss> He attempts to prove this by the large number of coincidental hallucinations which occurred under "sleepy" circumstances. One man went to bed early and woke up early; another was "roused from sleep;" two ladies were sitting up in bed, feeding their babies; a man was reading a newspaper on a sofa; a lady was lying awake at seven in the morning; and there are eight other English cases of people "awake" in bed during an hallucination. Now, in Dr. Parish’s opinion, we must argue that they were *not* awake, or at least not fully awake; therefore, the hallucinations were merely dreams. Dreams are so frequent that coincidences in dreams can be dismissed as pure flukes. People may say, certainly, "I am used to dreams and do not notice them; *this was a unique experience.*" But we must not pay attention to what people say.

Yet I fear we must pay attention to what they say. At least, we must remember that sleeping dreams are, above all things, the most easily forgotten; while a vivid hallucination—occurring when we, at least, believe ourselves to be awake—seems to us to be on a completely different level of impact, and (*believe one who has experienced it*) is truly very difficult to forget. Herr Parish cannot be allowed, therefore, to use the standard eighteenth-century argument—"They are all just dreams!" For the two types of dreams—those in sleep and those in apparent wakefulness—seem to the subject to be fundamentally different. And they truly are different. It is the essence of an ordinary nightly dream that we are unconscious of our actual surroundings and conscious of a fantastic environment. It is the essence of being wide awake to be conscious of our actual surroundings. In an ordinary dream, nothing real competes with its visions. When we are conscious of our surroundings, everything real does compete with any hallucination. Therefore, an hallucination that competes with reality while we are conscious of our physical environment is fundamentally different from an ordinary dream. Science gains nothing by arbitrarily declaring that two experiences so radically different are

He reaches this conclusion from an anecdote reported—as a not uncommon phenomenon—by a friend of Miss X. But the phenomenon occurred when Miss X was not crystal-gazing at all! Someone says that Miss X was not in her normal consciousness on a certain occasion when she was not crystal-gazing, and that this condition is familiar to the observer. Therefore, argues Herr Parish, nobody is in their normal consciousness when crystal-gazing.

In vain might "so good an observer as Miss X" think herself fully awake (as she does) when crystal-gazing, because once, when she happened to have "her eyes fixed on the window," her expression was "associated" by a friend "with something uncanny," and she afterwards spoke "in a dreamy, far-away tone" (p. 297). Miss X, though extremely "wide awake," may have looked dreamily at a window and seen mountains and marvels. But the point is that she was not voluntarily gazing at a crystal for amusement or experiment—perhaps trying to see how a microscope affected the pictures—or to entertain a friend.

I appeal to the spirits of Aristotle and Bacon against the scientific logic used by Herr Parish. Here is his syllogism:

A. is occasionally dreamy when not crystal-gazing.
A. is human.
Therefore, every human being, when crystal-gazing, is more or less asleep.

...calculations, namely, our good old friend, *the association of ideas* (p. 302). Our side cannot prove the *absence* of the *association of ideas*. Certainly we cannot; but ideas in endless millions are being associated all day long. A hundred thousand different, unnoticed associations may bring Jones or Brown to my mind. But I do not, therefore, see Brown or Jones, who is not there. Still less do I see Dr. Parish, or Nebuchadnezzar, or a monkey, or a salmon, or a golf ball, or Arthur's Seat (all of which may be brought to my mind by the association of ideas), when they are not present.

Suppose, then, that once in my life I see the absent Jones, who dies in that hour (or within twelve hours). I am puzzled. Why did Association choose that day, of all days in my life, for her solitary freak? And, if this choice of freaks by Association occurs among other people—say, two hundred times more often than chance allows—the freak begins to suggest that it may have a cause.

Not even the circumstance cited by Herr Parish—that a drowsy tailor, "sewing on in a dream," poor fellow, saw a client in his shop while the client was dying—solves the problem. The tailor is not said even once to have seen a customer who was *not* dying; yet he writes, "I was accustomed to work all night frequently." The tailor thinks he was asleep because he had been making irregular stitches, and perhaps he was. But, out of all his late-night watches and all his customers, association only formed *one* hallucination, and that was of a dying client whom he supposed to be perfectly well. Why on earth is association so fond of dying people—granting the statistics, which are "another story"? The explanation explains nothing. Herr Parish only moves the difficulty back a step, and, since we cannot live without the association of ideas, they are taken for granted by our side. Association of ideas does not cause hallucinations, as Mrs. Sidgwick remarks, though it may determine their contents.

He, therefore (by virtue of his excitement), now *believes* you told him about seeing your unhappy relative. This kind of false memory is very common. Two cases are recorded by Kraepelin among the insane. Are you sure you quite understand my reasoning?"

I understand it perfectly, but I do not see how it seems like good logic to Herr Parish.

The other theory is even more amusing. Jones never had a hallucination before. ‘*The rarity and the degree of interest compelled by it*’ made Jones ‘*connect it with some other prominent event,*’ say, the death of his aunt, which actually occurred, say, nine months later. But this is a simple matter of *evidence*, which it is the business of the S.P.R. to evaluate.

If anything external could encourage a belief in coincidental and veridical hallucinations, it would be these ‘Oppositions of Science.’ If a learned and fair opponent can find no better proofs than logic and the (unconscious) perversions of facts—such as the logic and the statements of Herr Parish—the case for telepathic hallucinations may seem strong indeed.
