I grant, too, that a census of 17,000 inquiries may only have ‘skimmed the cream off’ (p. 87). Another dip of the net, bringing up 17,000 fresh answers, might alter the whole aspect of the case, one way or the other. Moreover, we cannot get scientific evidence through this method of inquiry. If the public were interested in the question and understood its nature, and if everybody who had an hallucination immediately recorded it in writing, duly attested on oath before a magistrate by persons to whom he reported it before the coincidence was known—and if all such records, coincidental or not, were kept in the British Museum for fifty years—then an examination of them might teach us something. But all this is quite impossible. We may form a belief for ourselves on this point of veridical hallucinations, but beyond that, it is impossible to advance. Still, Science might examine her evidence more closely!

## APPENDIX B

### *THE POLTERGEIST AND HIS EXPLAINERS.*

In the chapter on ‘Fetishism and Spiritualism,’ it was suggested that the movements of inanimate objects, apparently without contact, may have been one of the causes leading to fetishism—to the opinion that a spirit may inhabit a stick, a stone, or any other object. We added that whether such movements were caused by trickery or not was not essential, as long as the savage did not discover the fraud.

The evidence for the genuine supernormal character of such phenomena was not discussed, so that we might preserve the continuity of the general argument. The history of such phenomena is too long to be stated here. The same reports are found ‘from China to Peru,’ from the Eskimo to the Cape, from Egyptian magical papyri to yesterday’s provincial newspaper.<note>A sketch of the history will be found in the author’s *Cock Lane and Common Sense*.</note>

About 1850–1870, phenomena that had previously been reported as sporadic and spontaneous occurrences were domesticated and organized by Mediums, generally American. These were imitators of the enigmatic David Dunglas Home, who was certainly a most oddly gifted man, or a most successful fraud. A good deal of scientific attention was given to these occurrences; Mr. Darwin, Mr. Tyndall, Dr. Carpenter, and Mr. Huxley had all glanced at the phenomena and been present at séances. In most cases, the exhibitions—given in the dark or in very bad light—were blatant frauds and were regarded as such by the scientists who looked into them. A series of exposures culminated in the recent detection of Eusapia Paladino by Dr. Hodgson and other members of the S.P.R. <note>Society for Psychical Research</note> at Cambridge.

There was, however, one apparent exception. The chief mystagogue, Home, though by no means a clever man, was never caught in the fraudulent production of fetishistic phenomena. This is stated here because several third-hand stories of Home being caught in fraud are in circulation, and it is hoped that a well-documented, first-hand case of detection may be brought forward.

Regarding Home’s successes with Sir William Crookes, Lord Crawford, and others, more remains to be said; but first we will examine the attempted explanations for alleged physical phenomena occurring without the presence of a paid or even a recognized ‘medium.’ It will appear, I believe, that the explanations for evidence so widespread, so consistent, so old, and so new are far from satisfactory. Our conclusion would be simply that we should keep an eye on such phenomena if they are reported to recur.

> Mr. Tylor says, "I am well aware that the problem [of these phenomena] is one to be discussed on its merits, in order to arrive at a clear opinion on how far it may be connected with facts insufficiently appreciated and explained by science, and how far with superstition, delusion, and pure trickery. Such investigation, pursued through careful observation in a scientific spirit, would seem likely to shed light on some interesting psychological questions."

Acting on Mr. Tylor’s suggestion, Mr. Podmore proposes two explanations: (1) fraud; (2) hallucinations caused by excited expectation and by the *Schwärmerei* <note>Enthusiasm or fanaticism</note> resulting from sitting in hushed hope of marvels.

To address fraud first: Mr. Podmore has collected and analyzed eleven recent sporadic cases of moving objects.<note>The best source is his article on ‘Poltergeists.’ *Proceedings* xi. 45–116. We will limit ourselves to this example. This case appears to have been first reported in the *Retford and Gainsborough Times* "early in March," 1883 (actually March 9). The newspaper reports contain no theory that explains White’s breaking of his own furniture and pottery, nor Rose’s securing her own dismissal from a house where she was kindly received by willfully destroying the property of her hostess. An amateur published a theory involving silk threads attached to light items and thick cords to heavy ones, though no trace of these was found by witnesses who examined the flying objects. An elaborate machinery of pulleys fixed in the ceiling, the presence of a trickster in a locked pantry, apparent errors in the account of the flight of the objects, and a number of accomplices were all involved in this local explanation, with the person explaining it admitting that he could not imagine *why* the tricks were played. Six or eight pounds’ worth of goods were destroyed, and it is not surprising that poor Mrs. White wept over her shattered penates <note>The Latin term 'penates' refers to household gods or cherished domestic items.</note>.

The destruction began, of course, while White was away. The girl Rose gave the newspaper the same account as the other witnesses; however, just as White thought she was the cause, she suspected White, even though she admitted that he was not at home when the trouble started.

Mr. Podmore, reviewing the case, says, “The phenomena described are quite inexplicable by ordinary mechanical means.”¹ Yet elsewhere² he suggests that Rose herself, “as the instrument of mysterious agencies, or simply as a half-witted girl, gifted with abnormal cunning and love of mischief, may have been directly responsible for all that took place.” That is to say, a half-witted girl could accomplish (excluding “mysterious agencies”) “what is quite inexplicable by ordinary mechanical means,” even though, according to the policeman, she was not even present on some occasions. Such discrepancies are common in all evidence regarding even the most ordinary events. In any case, according to Mr. Podmore’s theory, a half-witted girl can do what "is quite inexplicable by ordinary mechanical means." There is not a shadow of evidence that the girl Rose had the supposed advantage of being "half-witted"; she is described by Mr. Podmore merely as "the child of an imbecile mother." The phenomena began, in one isolated case (the tilted table), before Rose ever entered the house. She was admitted out of kindness and served as a maid; it was not in her interest to break the crockery or upset the furniture. The troubles, which began before the girl’s arrival, were apparently active even when she was not present. Even if she were present, she could not have caused them "by ordinary mechanical means," and there was admittedly no trace of any extraordinary mechanical means. The disturbances stopped after she was dismissed; nothing else connects her to them.

Therefore, Mr. Podmore’s attempt at a natural explanation involving fraud carries no weight. He must exaggerate the significance of such discrepancies—which occur in all human testimony on every subject—as a form of disproof. He emphasizes the five-week interval between the events and his own collection of testimony. However, contemporary accounts appeared in local newspapers, and he fails to compare that contemporary evidence with the later testimony, as we have done. There is one discrepancy that suggests a witness (not cited here) came to believe he had seen what he had only heard others talking about. Finally, after abandoning the idea that mechanical means could possibly have produced these effects, Mr. Podmore relies on the alleged cunning of a half-witted girl, despite there being no evidence that she was half-witted. The alternative is that the girl was "the instrument of mysterious agencies."

So much for the hypothesis of fraud, which has produced identical results from China to Peru and from Greenland to the Cape.

We now turn to the other cause that acts alongside it in Mr. Podmore’s theory: hallucination. "Many of the witnesses described the articles as moving slowly through the air, or exhibiting some peculiarity in their flight."

Before criticizing this explanation, let us examine the English case mentioned by Mr. Podmore.

The most curious modern case I know of is not a recent one, but it occurred in broad daylight in the presence of many witnesses, and the phenomena continued for weeks. The events took place in 1849, and the record was expanded by Mr. Bristow, a witness, from an account he wrote in 1854. The setting was Swanland, near Hull, in a carpenter's shop where Mr. Bristow worked with two colleagues. To be brief, they were pelted by scraps of wood about the size of a common matchbox. Each man blamed the others until that explanation became impossible. The workrooms and the space above were searched to no avail. The pieces of wood sometimes danced along the floor, but more commonly sailed gently along or "moved as if carried on gently heaving waves." This continued for six weeks. One piece of wood "came toward me from a distant corner of the room, moving in a path that could be described as a geometrical square or a corkscrew about eighteen inches in diameter. . . . A piece was never seen coming through the doorway." Mr. Bristow considers this period "the most remarkable episode in my life" (June  Hull 27, 1891). The phenomena "did not depend on the presence of any single person or any specific number of people."

Visiting Swanland in 1891, Mr. Sidgwick found one surviving witness of these events, who asserted that the objects could not have been thrown because of their unusual flight paths, which he described in the same way as Mr. Bristow. If they were thrown, the thrower must have had a natural talent for "pitching" in <term>base-ball</term>. This witness, named Andrews, was mentioned in Mr. Bristow's report but was not cited by him as a source for confirmation. The people he did cite were found to be either dead or had emigrated. The villagers held a superstitious theory

This case has a certain interest regarding Mr. Podmore's surmise that all such phenomena arise from trickery, which produces excitement in the spectators; this excitement then begets hallucination, and the hallucination takes the form of seeing thrown objects move in an unnatural way. Thus, if I keep throwing things about and you do not detect this stratagem, you get excited and, consequently, hallucinated; you then believe you see the things move in spirals, or undulate as if on waves, or hop, float, or glide in an impossible way. The uniformity of these hallucinations is so consistent that these phenomena are described in similar terms by witnesses (hallucinated, of course) in both old and new times, as in cases cited by Glanvil, Increase Mather, Telfer (of Rerrick), and generally in works of the seventeenth century. Nor is this uniform hallucination confined to England. Mr. Podmore quotes a German example, and I received similar testimony (regarding the flight of an object around a corner) from a gentleman who employed Esther Teed, "the Amherst Mystery," in his service. He was not excited, for he was engaged in his usual work in his stable when the incident occurred unexpectedly as he was looking after his livestock. One may add the case of Cideville (1851) and Sir W. Crookes's evidence, as well as that of Mr. Schhapoff.

Mr. Podmore must, therefore, suppose that in states of excitement, the same peculiar form of hallucination develops itself uniformly in America, France, Germany, and England (not to mention Russia), and persists through different ages. This would be a novel and valuable psychological law. Moreover, Mr. Podmore must hold that "excitement" lasted for six weeks among the carpenters in the shop at Swanland, one of whom writes like a man of much intelligence and has prospered to become a master in his craft. It is difficult to believe that he was excited for six weeks, and we still marvel that excitement produces the same uniformity of hallucination, affecting policemen, carpenters, marquises, and a Fellow of the Royal Society (F.R.S.). We are referring to Sir W. Crookes's case.

been very rare. The best examples are the experiments of Sir William Crookes, F.R.S., with Home.<note>¹ See Sir W. Crookes's *Researches in Spiritualism*.</note> He demonstrated, by using a machine built for that purpose which registered automatically, that in Home's presence, a balance was affected by as much as two pounds while Home was not touching the table where the machine was placed. He also saw objects float in the air with a motion like a piece of wood on small ocean waves (clearly excitement producing hallucination, in Podmore's view), while Home was at a distance, with other spectators holding his hands and his feet visibly enclosed in a kind of cage. Crookes was professionally celebrated for the accuracy of his observations, these circumstances are difficult to explain, and these are only a few cases among many.

I venture to believe that, upon reflection, Mr. Podmore will doubt whether he has discovered a universal law of excited misperception, or whether the remarkable and certainly unintentional coincidence of testimony regarding the strange flight of objects points instead to an ‘abnormal agency’ that is uniform in its effects. Contagious hallucination cannot affect witnesses in many different lands and eras who are unaware of each other's existence, nor could they fake their reports to match accounts they had never heard.

We now turn to the peculiarities of the so-called Medium, such as floating in the air, changes in body size, and escaping injury when handling or walking on fire. Mr. Tylor says nothing about Sir William Crookes’s cases (1871), but speaks of the alleged levitation, or floating in the air, of both primitive and civilized men. These are recorded in Buddhist and Neoplatonic writings, among North American Indians, in Tonkin (where a Jesuit saw and described the phenomena in 1730), in the *Acta Sanctorum*, and among modern spiritualists. In 1760, Lord Elcho, while in Rome, was present at the trial for canonizing an unnamed saint and heard witnesses swear to having seen the holy man levitated. Sir W. Crookes testifies to having seen Home float in the air on several occasions. “I was sitting with Mr. Home, Lord Adare, and a cousin of his. During the session, Mr. Home went into a trance, and in that state was carried out of the window in the room next to where we were, and was brought in through our window. The distance between the windows was about seven feet six inches, and there was not the slightest foothold between them, nor was there more than a twelve-inch projection at each window, which served as a ledge to put flowers on. We heard the window in the next room lifted up, and almost immediately after we saw Home floating in the air outside our window. The moon was shining full into the room; my back was to the light, and I saw the shadow on the wall of the window sill, and Home’s feet about six inches above it. He remained in this position for a few seconds, then raised the window and glided into the room feet first and sat down.

“Lord Adare then went into the next room to look at the window from which he had been carried. It was raised about eighteen inches, and he expressed his wonder how Mr. Home had been taken through so narrow an opening. Home said, still entranced, ‘I will show you,’ and then with his back to the window he leaned back and was shot out of the opening, head first, with his body rigid, and then returned quite quietly. The window is about seventy feet from the ground.” The hypothesis of a mechanical arrangement of ropes or supports outside has been suggested, but it does not cover the facts as described.

Mr. Podmore, who quotes this, offers the explanation that the witnesses were excited, and that Home “thrust his head and shoulders out of the window.” But, if he did, they could not see him do it, for he was in the next room. A brick wall was between them and him. Their first view of Home was “floating in the air outside our window.” It is not very easy to maintain that a belief for which the collective evidence is so large and universal, such as the belief in <term>levitation</term>, was caused by a series of saints, sorcerers, and others thrusting their heads and shoulders out of windows where the observers could not see them. Nor in Lord Crawford’s case is it easy to suppose that three educated men, if hallucinating, would all be hallucinated in the same way.

The theory of hallucination does not apply to Mr. Hamilton Aïdé and M. Alphonse Karr, neither of whom was a scientist. Both were highly skeptical of Home and went to Nice to see and, if possible, expose him. Home was a guest at a large villa in Nice; M. Karr and Mr. Aïdé were two of a party in a large, brightly lit salon where Home received them. A large, heavy table, far from their group, moved toward them. M. Karr then went under a table that rose into the air and carefully examined the space beneath it, while Mr. Aïdé observed it from above. Neither of them could find any explanation for the phenomenon, and they walked away together—annoyed, disappointed, and criticizing Home. <note>Mr. Aïdé provided me with this information. He recorded the events in his diary at the time.</note>

In this case, there was neither excitement nor a desire to believe, but rather a strong wish to disbelieve and to expose Home. If two such witnesses could be hallucinated, we must significantly expand our understanding of the limits of the human capacity for experiencing hallucinations.

One unusual phenomenon reported in Home’s case has little to do with any plausible theory of spirits. He was said to stretch, or become elongated, while in a trance. <note>*Report of the Dialectical Society*, p. 209.</note> Mr. Podmore explains that "perhaps he really stretched himself to his full height"—one of the easiest ways imaginable to perform a miracle. Iamblichus records the same phenomenon occurring in those who were possessed. <note>See Porphyry, in Parthey’s edition (Berlin, 1857), iii. 4.</note> Iamblichus adds that they were sometimes widened as well as lengthened. Now, M. Féré notes that "any part of the body of a hysterical patient may change in volume, simply because the patient’s attention is fixed on that part." <note>*Bulletin de la Société de Biologie*, 1880, p. 399.</note> It is possible that the elongation of Home and the ancient Egyptian mediums was an extreme case of this "change in volume." If this could be proven with examples, Home’s elongation would no longer be considered a "miracle." However, it would follow that in this case the observers were not hallucinated, and the assumption would be that they were not hallucinated in other cases either. Indeed, this argument applies universally.

There is another class of "physical phenomena" that has no direct bearing on our subject. Many people throughout history are said to have handled or walked through fire, not only without suffering pain but without any injury to the skin. Iamblichus mentions this as one of the peculiarities of his "possessed" men; and in *Modern Mythology* (1897), I collected first-hand evidence for this feat in classical times, as well as in India, Fiji, Bulgaria, Trinidad, the Straits Settlements, and many other places. The evidence comes from travelers, officials, missionaries, and others, and is supported (for what photographic testimony is worth) by photographs of the performance. Holding glowing coals in his hand and sharing the ability to do so with others was part of Home’s repertoire. Lord Crawford saw it done on eight occasions and personally received a glowing coal from Home’s hand without being harmed. A friend of mine, however, still has a blister from the injury sustained during the process. Sir William Crookes’s evidence follows:

> "At Mr. Home’s request, while he was in a trance, I went with him to the fireplace in the back drawing room. He said, 'We want you to notice particularly what Dan is doing.' Accordingly, I stood close to the fire and leaned down toward it when he put his hands in.
>
> "Mr. Home then waved a handkerchief in the air two or three times, held it above his head, and then folded it up and laid it on his hand like a cushion. Putting his other hand into the fire, he took out a large lump of coal, red-hot at the bottom, and placed the red part on the handkerchief. Under normal circumstances, it would have caught fire. In about half a minute, he took it off the handkerchief with his hand, saying, 'As the power is not strong, if we leave the coal longer it will burn.' He then placed it on his hand and brought it to the table in the front room, where everyone except me had remained seated."

Mr. Podmore explains that on one occasion only two candles and the fire provided light, and that Home’s hands were "possibly" protected by some "non-conducting substance." He does not explain how this substance was applied to Lord Crawford’s hands, nor does he tell us what this valuable substance might be. None is known to science, though it seems to

It is not necessary to believe Sir W. Crookes’s assertions that he saw Home perform the fire tricks, for we can fall back on the lack of light (only two candles and the firelight), as well as on the law of hallucination caused by excitement. I could detect no trace of injury to the skin, which was soft and delicate, like a woman’s. Neither were there signs of any preparation having been previously applied. I have often seen conjurers and others handle red-hot coals and iron, but there were always palpable signs of burning." <note>¹ Crookes, *Proceedings*, ix. 308.</note>

The interesting point, historically, is the combination in Home of the entire *repertoire* of the possessed men in Iamblichus. We certainly cannot get rid of the fire trick by aid of a hypothetical "non-conducting substance." Until the "substance" is tested experimentally, it is not a <term>vera causa</term>. We might as well say "spirits" at once. Both that "substance" and those "spirits" are equally "in the air." Yet Mr. Podmore’s "explanations" (which are not satisfactory to himself) are conceived so thoroughly in the spirit of popular science—one of them casually discovering a new psychological law, a second contradicting the facts it seeks to account for, a third generously inventing an unknown substance—that they ought to be welcomed by reviewers and lecturers.

It seems wiser to admit our ignorance and suspend our belief.

Here, the useless chapter of explanations ends. Fraud is a *vera causa* <note>A Latin term meaning "true cause," used in science to refer to an explanation known to exist in nature.</note>, but it is a hypothesis difficult to apply when it is admitted that the effects could not be caused by ordinary mechanical means. Hallucination, caused by excitement, is a *vera causa*, but its remarkable uniformity—as described by witnesses from different lands and ages who knew nothing of each other—makes us hesitate to accept a sweeping hypothesis of hallucination. The case for it is not confirmed when we have the same reports from witnesses who were certainly not excited.

This extraordinary bundle of reports, then—practically identical accounts of facts that paralyze belief—this bundle made up of statements from so many ages and countries, can only be "filed for reference." But it is clear that any savage who shared the experiences of Sir W. Crookes, Lord Crawford, Mr. Hamilton Aïdé, M. Robert de St. Victor at Cideville, and Policeman Higgs at Worksop would believe that a spirit might inhabit a stick or stone; believing this, he would be a Fetishist. Thus, the probable origin even of Fetishism lies in a region of which we know nothing—the *x* region.

## APPENDIX C

### *CRYSTAL-GAZING*

Since the chapter on crystal-gazing was set in type, a work by Dr. Pierre Janet has appeared, titled ‘*Les Névroses et les Idées Fixes.*’¹ It contains a chapter on crystal-gazing. The opinion of Dr. Janet—as that of a scholar familiar at the Salpêtrière hospital with ‘neurotic’ visionaries—cannot help but be interesting. Unfortunately, the essay must be regarded as seriously diminished in value by Dr. Janet’s unusual treatment of his subject. Nothing is more necessary in this research than accuracy of reporting. Now, Dr. Janet has taken a set of Miss X’s experiences or experiments from her interesting essay, which was already cited. He has attributed them not to Miss X, but to various people—for example, to *a young girl*, *a poor seer*, and *a somewhat mystical person*. He has altered the facts in the spirit of a romance and has triumphantly provided the explanation of memory revival, which was originally identified by Miss X herself.

Throughout his paper, Dr. Janet appears as the calm man of science pronouncing judgment on the visionary whims of ‘haunted’ young girls and disappointed female seers. No such people were involved; no such hauntings, supposed premonitions, or ‘disillusions’ occurred. The romantic and ‘marvelous’ circumstances are myth-making additions resulting from Dr. Janet’s own memory or imagination. His scientific explanation is the one he attributes to his trio of the *young girl*, *poor seer*, and *somewhat mystical person*.

Because he is heavily involved in the study of ‘neurotic’ and hysterical patients, Dr. Janet thinks that they are most likely to see crystal visions. Perhaps they are; and one doubts if their descriptions are more to be trusted than

Not having any acquaintances in neurotic circles, I am unable to say whether such persons provide more cases of the faculty of crystal vision than ordinary people; while one would think their word is much less to be trusted than that of men and women in excellent health. The crystal visions which I have cited from my own knowledge (and I could cite dozens of others) were seen by men and women engaged in the ordinary duties of life. Students, barristers, novelists, lawyers, schoolmasters, schoolmistresses, and golfers—to all of whom the topic was perfectly new—have all exhibited the faculty. It is curious that a thirteenth-century Arabian author, Ibn Khaldun, cited by M. Lefébure, offers the same account of *how* the visions appear as that given by Miss Angus in the *Journal of the S.P.R.*, April 1898. M. Lefébure’s citation was sent to me in a letter.

I append M. Lefébure’s quotation from Ibn Khaldun. The original is translated in ‘*Notices and Extracts of the Manuscripts of the Imperial Library,*’ I. xix. p. 643–645.

> ‘Ibn Khaldun admits that certain men have the faculty of foretelling the future.
>
> ‘“Those,” he adds, “who look into transparent bodies, such as mirrors, bowls filled with water and other liquids; those who inspect the hearts, livers, and bones of animals... all these people also belong to the category of diviners, but, because of the imperfection of their nature, they occupy a lower rank. To pull back the veil of the senses, the true diviner does not need great effort; as for the others, they try to reach the *goal* by attempting to concentrate all their *perceptions* into a single sense. Since sight is the noblest sense, they give it preference; fixing their gaze on an object with a smooth surface, they consider it with attention until they perceive there the thing they wish to announce. Some people believe that the image perceived in this manner is drawn on the surface of the mirror; but they are mistaken. The diviner looks fixedly at this surface...

...until it disappears and a curtain, like a mist, comes between him and the mirror. On this curtain, the things he wishes to see are drawn, and this allows him to give indications—either positive or negative—about what is desired to be known. He then recounts his perceptions just as he receives them. While in this state, diviners do not perceive what is actually seen in the mirror; instead, a different mode of perception arises within them which operates not through sight, but through the soul. It is true that, *for them, the soul's perceptions so closely resemble those of the senses that they are deceived; a fact which, furthermore, is well known.* The same thing happens to those who examine the hearts and livers of animals. We have seen some of these individuals obstruct the *operation of the senses* by using simple *fumigations*, and then use *incantations*<note>1</note> to give the soul the *required disposition*; they then recount what they have perceived. These forms, they say, appear in the air and represent people: they teach the diviners, through emblems and signs, the things they seek to know. Individuals of this class are less detached from the influence of the senses than those of the previous class.

The words he speaks are sometimes true and sometimes false. Indeed, as the diviner wishes to compensate for his natural imperfections, he uses methods quite foreign to his perceptive faculty which do not align with it in any way. Therefore, truth and error appear to him simultaneously; thus, one should place no trust in his words. Sometimes he even resorts to suppositions and conjectures in the hope of hitting upon the truth and deceiving those who question him.'

# APPENDIX D

## CHIEFS IN AUSTRALIA

In the remarks on Australian religion, it is argued that chiefs in Australia are, at most, very inconspicuous, and that a dead chief cannot have evolved into a Supreme Being. Attention should be called, however, to Mr. Howitt’s remarks on Australian ‘Head-men,’ in his treatise on ‘The Organization of Australian Tribes’ (pp. 103–113). He attributes more power to ‘Head-men’ than Mr. Curr does in his work, ‘The Australian Race.’ As a rule, the headmen attain whatever influence they possess through seniority, provided it is accompanied by courage, wisdom, and, in some cases, magical skills. There are signs of a tendency to keep the office (if it may be called one) within the same family line. ‘But figures like Vich Ian Vohr or Chingachgook are not to be found in Australian tribes’ (p. 113). I do not observe that the *manes* or ghost of a deceased headman receives any worship or service intended to establish him in the tribal memory, and thus lead to the evolution of a deity, although one headman was powerful throughout the entire Dieyri tribe across three hundred miles of territory. Such a person, if honored after death, might conceivably develop into a hero, if not into a creative being. But we must wait for evidence that any posthumous reverence was paid to this man, Ialina Piramurana (New Moon). Mr. Howitt’s essay is in the ‘Transactions of the Royal Society of Victoria for 1889.’

<vocab>Australia, religion, chiefs, Head-men, Mr. Howitt, Mr. Curr, Dieyri tribe, Ialina Piramurana</vocab>

<summary>This appendix explores the level of power held by Australian tribal "Head-men" and whether their status could eventually lead to their worship as deities. The author concludes that while some headmen held significant territorial influence, there is currently no evidence that they were worshipped after death in a way that would produce a Supreme Being.</summary>

## History, Politics, Polity, Political Memoirs, etc.

**Abbott.**—*A HISTORY OF GREECE.* By EVELYN ABBOTT, M.A., LL.D.
Part I.—From the Earliest Times to the Ionian Revolt. Crown 8vo., 10s. 6d.

**Acland and Ransome.**—*A HANDBOOK IN OUTLINE OF THE POLITICAL HISTORY OF ENGLAND TO 1896.* Chronologically Arranged. By the Right Hon. A. H. DYKE ACLAND, M.P., and CYRIL RANSOME, M.A. Crown 8vo., 6s.
